title: P versus NP
open: Is P = NP? Equivalently, does every problem whose solutions can be verified efficiently also admit solutions that can be found efficiently?
status: Open since 1971 (Cook–Levin), and one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems (2000), carrying a USD 1,000,000 Clay Millennium prize. All known techniques provably fail: relativization (Baker–Gill–Solovay 1975), natural proofs (Razborov–Rudich 1997), and algebrization (Aaronson–Wigderson 2009). Key works include S. Cook, "The complexity of theorem-proving procedures", STOC 1971; L. Levin, "Universal sequential search problems", Problems of Information Transmission 1973; R. Razborov, S. Rudich, "Natural proofs", JCSS 1997 (DOI:10.1006/jcss.1997.1494); S. Aaronson, A. Wigderson, "Algebrization: a new barrier in complexity theory", TOCT 2009 (arXiv:0806.1347); Clay Mathematics Institute, "P vs NP Problem", claymath.org/millennium/p-vs-np.
solved_when: A proof that P = NP, or a proof that P ≠ NP, is established.
why: It is the single most consequential question in computer science, separating feasible verification from feasible computation across all of mathematics, and it underpins the foundations of cryptography.
key_works: S. Cook, "The complexity of theorem-proving procedures", STOC 1971; L. Levin, "Universal sequential search problems", Problems of Information Transmission 1973; R. Razborov, S. Rudich, "Natural proofs", JCSS 1997 (DOI:10.1006/jcss.1997.1494); S. Aaronson, A. Wigderson, "Algebrization: a new barrier in complexity theory", TOCT 2009 (arXiv:0806.1347); Clay Mathematics Institute, "P vs NP Problem", claymath.org/millennium/p-vs-np

title: NP versus coNP
open: Does NP equal coNP — that is, can every statement whose negation has a short verifiable proof also itself be given a short verifiable proof? Formally, the question is whether complements of NP problems always admit polynomial-size certificates.
status: Open since the 1970s and widely believed false; a separation would imply P ≠ NP. No oracle is known to offer insight, though duality phenomena in linear and semidefinite programming exhibit partial worlds where the collapse holds. Background appears in S. Cook, "The complexity of theorem-proving procedures", STOC 1971, and S. Arora, B. Barak, "Computational Complexity: A Modern Approach", Cambridge 2009, ch. 3-5.
solved_when: NP is proven equal to coNP, or a language in NP is proven to have no complement in NP.
why: A separation would rule out short certificates of unsatisfiability (short SAT refutations), bounding proof systems and many verification tasks; it would also imply P ≠ NP.
key_works: S. Cook, "The complexity of theorem-proving procedures", STOC 1971; S. Arora, B. Barak, "Computational Complexity: A Modern Approach", Cambridge 2009, ch. 3-5

title: One-way functions existence
open: Do one-way functions exist — functions that are easy to compute but hard to invert on average? By Impagliazzo's equivalence, this asks whether easy average-case hard problems exist, and fails precisely when P = NP ∩ coNP.
status: Open. Existence of one-way functions would imply P ≠ NP, but not conversely. Impagliazzo's five worlds (1995) frame the possible relationships between average-case hardness and cryptography; see Impagliazzo, "A personal view of average-case complexity," CCC 1995, and Goldreich, "Foundations of Cryptography vol. 1," Cambridge 2001.
solved_when: A proof that one-way functions exist (which would also establish P ≠ NP), or a proof that they do not, e.g. via showing P = NP ∩ coNP rules them out.
why: One-way functions are necessary and sufficient for much of modern cryptography, and their existence is the minimal complexity assumption underlying private-key cryptography.
key_works: R. Impagliazzo, "A personal view of average-case complexity", CCC 1995; O. Goldreich, "Foundations of Cryptography vol. 1", Cambridge 2001

title: BPP versus P (derandomization)
open: Does every problem solvable by a randomized polynomial-time algorithm also admit a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm — that is, is BPP equal to P? Equivalently, can randomness always be eliminated from efficient computation at only polynomial cost?
status: BPP = P is widely believed. Impagliazzo–Wigderson (1997, "P = BPP if E requires exponential circuits", STOC 1997, DOI:10.1145/258533.258590) shows BPP = P follows if E requires 2^Ω(n) circuits; the problem is equivalent to building sufficiently strong pseudorandom generators from hard functions. Full derandomization is known to require circuit lower bounds that are themselves open. See also Nisan–Wigderson, "Hardness vs randomness", JCSS 1994.
solved_when: BPP = P is proved; the known route is via pseudorandom generators strong enough to fool all polynomial-time randomized algorithms, e.g., by showing E requires 2^Ω(n)-size circuits (the Impagliazzo–Wigderson condition).
why: It settles whether randomness is ever essential for efficient computation, and the hardness-versus-randomness framework behind it underpins the pseudorandom generator constructions used throughout derandomization and cryptography.
key_works: R. Impagliazzo, A. Wigderson, "P = BPP if E requires exponential circuits", STOC 1997 (DOI:10.1145/258533.258590); N. Nisan, A. Wigderson, "Hardness vs randomness", JCSS 1994

title: Circuit lower bounds for NEXP
open: Does NEXP have polynomial-size circuits? Formally, prove that NEXP is not contained in P/poly — or even that MA_EXP is not contained in P/poly in the non-uniform setting, which itself remains open.
status: The best known result is Williams (2010), proving NEXP ⊄ ACC0. The general P/poly bound resists all known techniques, and the natural proofs barrier applies to much stronger targets. Key works: R. Williams, "Nonuniform ACC circuit lower bounds", JACM 2014 (arXiv:0907.4753); E. Allender et al. on barriers; R. Ryan Williams survey "Some Estimated Likelihoods for Computational Complexity" (arXiv:1502.07816) (verify).
solved_when: A proof that NEXP ⊄ P/poly, or failing that, that MA_EXP ⊄ P/poly.
why: This is the front line of circuit lower bounds: any superpolynomial circuit lower bound for NEXP would be the first "real" lower bound beyond ACC0 and would open a path toward P vs NP.
key_works: R. Williams, "Nonuniform ACC circuit lower bounds", JACM 2014 (arXiv:0907.4753); E. Allender et al. on barriers; R. Ryan Williams survey "Some Estimated Likelihoods for Computational Complexity" (arXiv:1502.07816) (verify)

title: Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (SETH)
open: Does solving k-SAT on n variables require essentially 2^n time as k grows — formally, does the SETH constant s_inf = lim_{k→∞} s_k equal 1?
status: Open since 1999 (Impagliazzo–Paturi). Known: the sparsification lemma reduces dense k-SAT instances to sparse ones; SETH implies lower bounds for dozens of problems, such as ruling out n^(2-ε) improvements for Edit Distance. Key works: R. Impagliazzo, R. Paturi, "On the complexity of k-SAT", JCSS 2001; ETH chapter in "Fine-Grained Complexity" course notes by V. Williams.
solved_when: It is proved (or refuted) that s_inf = lim_{k→∞} s_k equals 1; equivalently, a decision on whether k-SAT with unbounded k admits algorithms asymptotically faster than 2^n as k grows.
why: SETH is the load-bearing assumption of fine-grained complexity; its failure would collapse a web of conditional lower bounds, including the n^(2-ε) drag reductions for Edit Distance and dozens of other problems.
key_works: R. Impagliazzo, R. Paturi, "On the complexity of k-SAT", JCSS 2001; ETH chapter in "Fine-Grained Complexity" course notes by V. Williams (verify)

title: Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH)
open: Is there no algorithm solving 3-SAT in time 2^{o(n)}? In other words, does 3-SAT require genuinely exponential time in the number of variables?
status: Open since 1999; it is implied by the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (SETH), and it contrasts with subexponential algorithms known for restricted formula classes (Schöning 1999). Key works: R. Impagliazzo, R. Paturi, "On the complexity of k-SAT", JCSS 2001.
solved_when: A proof that no 2^{o(n)}-time algorithm exists for 3-SAT resolves it affirmatively; a subexponential algorithm for 3-SAT refutes it.
why: ETH is the foundation for the widespread belief that NP-hard problems admit no subexponential algorithms, and it serves as the base assumption for countless reductions in parameterized complexity.
key_works: R. Impagliazzo, R. Paturi, "On the complexity of k-SAT", JCSS 2001

title: 3SUM conjecture
open: Is there a truly subquadratic algorithm for deciding whether n given integers contain three that sum to zero? Formally, does an O(n^{2-ε})-time algorithm exist for some constant ε > 0?
status: Open since Gajentaan–Overmars (1995) popularized it. The best known algorithms are slightly subquadratic: n^2/polylog due to Baran–Demaine–Pătraşcu (2008), improved to n^2 (log log n)^{O(1)} / log^Ω(1) n by Chan (2018); a near-linear quantum algorithm is known (Ambainis 2007).
solved_when: An algorithm decides 3SUM on n integers in O(n^{2-ε}) time for some constant ε > 0, or the conjecture is refuted by a matching lower-bound argument.
why: The conjecture anchors quadratic conditional lower bounds for dozens of problems in computational geometry and string algorithms, and serves as a rare unconditional "hard core" candidate in fine-grained complexity.
key_works: A. Gajentaan, M. Overmars, "On a class of O(n^2) problems in computational geometry", CGTA 1995; T. Chan, "More logarithmic-factor speedups for 3SUM, (median,+)-convolution, and some geometric 3SUM-hard problems", SODA 2018 (arXiv:1708.03063)

title: APSP subcubic barrier
open: Is there a truly subcubic (n^{3-ε}) algorithm for All-Pairs Shortest Paths in weighted graphs?
status: Open for decades. Best known ~n^3 / 2^{Ω(sqrt log n)} by Williams (2014) building on Chan; equivalent subcubic-hard class (Vassilevska Williams–Williams 2010: APSP, negative triangle, etc. all subcubic-equivalent).
why: Central to the fine-grained web; many graph problems are subcubically equivalent to it.
key_works: V. Vassilevska Williams, R. Williams, "Subcubic equivalences between path, matrix and triangle problems", FOCS 2010 (arXiv:1011.4901); R. Williams, "Faster all-pairs shortest paths via circuit complexity", STOC 2014 (arXiv:1312.6680)

title: Integer factorization complexity
open: Is there a polynomial-time classical algorithm for factoring integers? Failing that, can factoring be done substantially faster than the subexponential L_N[1/3] running time of the number field sieve?
status: Open. The best classical algorithm is the number field sieve, running in time exp((~1.9)(ln N)^{1/3}(ln ln N)^{2/3}); quantumly, Shor's algorithm (FOCS 1994) factors in polynomial time. Despite decades of effort no classical polynomial-time algorithm is known, and factoring is not even known to be NP-hard — it is believed to lie outside P but within NP ∩ coNP. Key works: P. Shor, "Algorithms for quantum computation: discrete logarithms and factoring", FOCS 1994; A. Lenstra et al., "The number field sieve", 1993.
solved_when: Either a classical polynomial-time factoring algorithm is exhibited, or an algorithm asymptotically beating exp((~1.9)(ln N)^{1/3}(ln ln N)^{2/3}) time is given.
why: RSA's security rests on the hardness of factoring, so a classical polynomial-time algorithm would break most deployed public-key cryptography.
key_works: P. Shor, "Algorithms for quantum computation: discrete logarithms and factoring", FOCS 1994; A. Lenstra et al., "The number field sieve", 1993

title: Graph isomorphism complexity
open: Is graph isomorphism solvable in polynomial time? Equivalently, does GI lie in P?
status: Open. The best known bound is quasipolynomial time n^{polylog n} (Babai 2016, arXiv:1512.03547, with Helfgott's simplification). GI is not believed NP-complete, since that would collapse the polynomial hierarchy (Boppana–Håstad–Zachos). Practical solvers such as nauty and Traces handle huge instances; see also Köbler, Schöning, Torán, "The Graph Isomorphism Problem: Its Structural Complexity", Birkhäuser 1993.
solved_when: A polynomial-time algorithm for deciding graph isomorphism is given, or GI is proved to lie outside P.
why: GI is the canonical "NP-intermediate" candidate; its orbit-closure structure connects to group theory and to practical isomorphism testing in chemistry and circuit design.
key_works: L. Babai, "Graph isomorphism in quasipolynomial time", STOC 2016 (arXiv:1512.03547); J. Köbler, U. Schöning, J. Torán, "The Graph Isomorphism Problem: Its Structural Complexity", Birkhäuser 1993

title: Optimal PCP length
open: How small can a probabilistically checkable proof be? More precisely, can we simultaneously achieve constant query complexity and near-linear proof length with optimal parameters?
status: Open. Dinur's PCP (JACM 2007) gives constant-query, polynomial-length proofs via gap amplification; short PCPs of near-linear length exist (Dinur–Harsha, SIAM J. Computing 2013, arXiv:1206.6432) but with worse parameters. The tradeoff frontier among query complexity, length, and alphabet is actively open.
solved_when: A PCP construction achieves constant queries and near-linear proof length with optimal parameters on the query-versus-length-versus-alphabet tradeoff frontier.
why: PCP parameters control inapproximability reductions, and tight PCPs would settle hardness-of-approximation constants.
key_works: I. Dinur, "The PCP theorem by gap amplification", JACM 2007; I. Dinur, P. Harsha, "Composition of low-error 2-query PCPs using decodable PCPs", SIAM J. Computing 2013 (arXiv:1206.6432)

title: Frege system lower bounds
open: Is there a family of natural tautologies whose shortest Frege proofs are superpolynomially long? More generally, the same question is open for bounded-depth Frege and for Extended Frege systems.
status: Open. No superpolynomial Frege lower bound is known for any explicit tautology. Resolution, by contrast, is well understood: Haken (1985) proved the pigeonhole principle hard for resolution, and Chvátal–Szemerédi established lower bounds for all tautologies. Key works: A. Haken, "The intractability of resolution", TCS 1985; P. Beame, T. Pitassi, "Propositional proof complexity: past, present, and future", Bull. EATCS 1998.
solved_when: An explicit tautology family is exhibited and proved to require superpolynomial-length proofs in Frege — ideally extended to bounded-depth Frege or Extended Frege.
why: Frege lower bounds cap the power of SAT solvers in the idealized limit, and lower bounds for Extended Frege would imply major circuit lower bounds, namely P/poly separations.
key_works: A. Haken, "The intractability of resolution", TCS 1985; P. Beame, T. Pitassi, "Propositional proof complexity: past, present, and future", Bull. EATCS 1998

title: Dynamic connectivity lower bound
open: Can a fully dynamic graph undergoing edge insertions and deletions be maintained under connectivity queries in less than polylogarithmic amortized time per operation? More precisely, is there a cell-probe lower bound matching the known upper bounds, separating dynamic connectivity from the easier dynamic trees problem?
status: Open. The best upper bound is the O(log^2 n) deterministic algorithm of Holm–de Lichtenberg–Thorup (JACM 2001), with a randomized improvement to O(log n (log log n)^2) by Wulff-Nilsen (2023, unverified). On the lower-bound side, cell-probe lower bounds of Ω(log n) follow from the partial sums results of Pătraşcu–Demaine (SIAM J. Computing 2006, arXiv:cs/0502041), but tight bounds remain open.
solved_when: A lower bound (or faster algorithm) resolving the exact complexity of fully dynamic connectivity is established — specifically, a cell-probe lower bound matching the O(log^2 n) deterministic upper bound up to lower-order factors, or an algorithm beating polylogarithmic amortized time.
why: Dynamic connectivity is the flagship dynamic data structure problem; its exact complexity gates a whole family of dynamic graph algorithms, including MST and subgraph connectivity.
key_works: J. Holm, K. de Lichtenberg, M. Thorup, "Poly-logarithmic deterministic fully-dynamic algorithms for connectivity, minimum spanning tree, 2-edge, and biconnectivity", JACM 2001; M. Pătraşcu, E. Demaine, "Logarithmic lower bounds in the cell-probe model", SIAM J. Computing 2006 (arXiv:cs/0502041)

title: Cell-probe lower bounds for static data structures
open: Can we prove optimal cell-probe query-time lower bounds of order Ω(log² n / log w) for natural static data structure problems — such as 3SUM indexing, adjacency listing in graphs with o(n²) nonzero edges, or predecessor search — when the structure is allowed polynomial space? More precisely, the question is to establish such bounds in the cell-probe model with space polynomial in n.
status: Open. For predecessor, the best lower bound is Ω(log n / log(w/n)) (Pătraşcu–Thorup 2006, "Time-space trade-offs for predecessor search", STOC 2006), matching van Emde Boas-type upper bounds, but for many listing/reporting problems only log^Ω(1) bounds exist. Larsen's cell-sampling technique ("The cell probe complexity of dynamic range counting", STOC 2012, arXiv:1203.5135) gives Ω(log² n / log(Sw/n)) for some range problems (2012).
solved_when: A lower bound of t_q = Ω(log² n / log w) is proved in the cell-probe model, with polynomial space, for one of the named natural static problems (3SUM indexing, adjacency in graphs with nnz = o(n²), or predecessor).
why: A query-time lower bound beyond log² n for any explicit problem would be a breakthrough comparable to circuit lower bounds.
key_works: K. Green Larsen, "The cell probe complexity of dynamic range counting", STOC 2012 (arXiv:1203.5135); M. Pătraşcu, M. Thorup, "Time-space trade-offs for predecessor search", STOC 2006

title: MCSP complexity
open: What is the computational complexity of the Minimum Circuit Size Problem — given the truth table of a Boolean function and a size parameter s, decide whether the function is computable by a circuit of size at most s? In particular, is MCSP NP-complete under standard reductions?
status: Open since the 1950s (Kolmogorov). MCSP is known to be in NP but is not known to be complete; hardness is known under plausible reductions to many problems, and there are strong connections to one-way functions and learning (Carmosino–Impagliazzo–Kabanets–Kolokolova 2016). See E. Allender, "The new complexity landscape around circuit minimization", Current Trends in TCS 2021 (arXiv:2010.10613), and I. Carmosino, R. Impagliazzo, V. Kabanets, A. Kolokolova, "Learning algorithms from natural proofs", CCC 2016 (arXiv:1601.01272).
solved_when: The complexity of MCSP is pinned down — most notably by a proof (or refutation) of NP-completeness, or by an unconditional classification placing it in P or establishing it is not NP-complete.
why: MCSP sits at the center of meta-complexity, currently the most promising lens on P vs NP, and its hardness would connect circuit complexity, learning theory, and cryptography in one stroke.
key_works: E. Allender, "The new complexity landscape around circuit minimization", Current Trends in TCS 2021 (arXiv:2010.10613); I. Carmosino, R. Impagliazzo, V. Kabanets, A. Kolokolova, "Learning algorithms from natural proofs", CCC 2016 (arXiv:1601.01272)

title: P versus PSPACE
open: Prove or refute that every polynomial-space computation can be performed in polynomial time. Equivalently, determine whether P = PSPACE.
status: Open since the 1970s. The time- and space-hierarchy theorems separate other resource levels but do not separate P from PSPACE. Key works include Stockmeyer and Meyer (1973), *Word Problems Requiring Exponential Time*, and Arora and Barak (2009), *Computational Complexity*.
solved_when: A proof that P = PSPACE, or a proof that P ≠ PSPACE, is established.
why: It determines whether polynomially bounded memory can support fundamentally more computation than polynomially bounded time, with direct consequences for the tractability of temporal-logic model checking in formal verification and efficient solution of succinct games in game theory.
key_works: Stockmeyer and Meyer (1973), *Word Problems Requiring Exponential Time*; Arora and Barak (2009), *Computational Complexity*.

title: L versus NL
open: Can directed graph reachability be decided by a deterministic algorithm using only \(O(\log n)\) workspace? Formally, this asks whether L = NL.
status: Open since the 1960s–1970s. Savitch gives deterministic \(O(\log^2 n)\) space; Reingold solved undirected connectivity in logarithmic space, not directed reachability. Key works: Savitch (1970), *Relationships between Nondeterministic and Deterministic Tape Complexities*, DOI: 10.1016/S0022-0000(70)80006-X; Reingold (2008), *Undirected Connectivity in Log-Space*, DOI: 10.1145/1391289.1391291.
solved_when: A deterministic \(O(\log n)\)-space algorithm for directed reachability is given, or a proof that no such algorithm exists.
why: It would identify the value of nondeterminism under severe memory constraints, and its techniques would bear on small-memory reachability certification in formal verification and memory-limited routing in communication networks.
key_works: Savitch (1970), *Relationships between Nondeterministic and Deterministic Tape Complexities*, DOI: 10.1016/S0022-0000(70)80006-X; Reingold (2008), *Undirected Connectivity in Log-Space*, DOI: 10.1145/1391289.1391291.

title: Uniform NC¹ versus L
open: Does every language decidable by a deterministic Turing machine using logarithmic space admit uniform circuits of logarithmic depth and polynomial size with bounded fan-in? Equivalently, is deterministic logspace contained in uniform NC¹?
status: Open for decades. Barrington's theorem characterizes nonuniform NC¹ via constant-width branching programs of polynomial size, but it does not collapse logarithmic-space computation to NC¹ (Barrington 1989, *Bounded-Width Polynomial-Size Branching Programs Recognize Exactly Those Languages in NC¹*; see also Arora and Barak 2009, *Computational Complexity*).
solved_when: A proof (or refutation) that every deterministic logarithmic-space computation can be realized by polynomial-size, bounded-fan-in circuits of logarithmic depth under a uniformity condition.
why: It determines whether long, memory-efficient sequential computations can always be compressed into very shallow parallel ones, placing a sharp boundary on the power of shallow parallelism.
key_works: Barrington (1989), *Bounded-Width Polynomial-Size Branching Programs Recognize Exactly Those Languages in NC¹*; Arora and Barak (2009), *Computational Complexity*.

title: Infinitude of the polynomial hierarchy
open: Does the polynomial hierarchy truly have infinitely many distinct levels — that is, does each additional alternation of quantifiers buy new computational power? Formally, prove that \(\Sigma_k^P \ne \Sigma_{k+1}^P\) for every fixed \(k\), or else show that the hierarchy collapses at some finite level.
status: Open since Stockmeyer's 1976 formulation. Oracle worlds exhibit both collapses and infinite hierarchies, demonstrating the limits of relativizing arguments (Baker, Gill, and Solovay, 1975).
solved_when: For every fixed \(k\), a proof that \(\Sigma_k^P \ne \Sigma_{k+1}^P\) is established; alternatively, the problem is resolved by exhibiting a collapse — a proof that \(\Sigma_k^P = \Sigma_{k+1}^P\) for some fixed \(k\) (equivalently, a collapse of PH to some finite level).
why: It determines whether each additional alternation of existential and universal certification genuinely increases computational power, or whether finite alternation suffices for all polynomial-time verifiable reasoning.
key_works: Stockmeyer (1976), *The Polynomial-Time Hierarchy*, DOI: 10.1016/0304-3975(76)90061-X; Baker, Gill, and Solovay (1975), *Relativizations of the P =? NP Question*.

title: NP versus polynomial-size circuits
open: Is there a problem verifiable in polynomial time that no small circuit family can solve — that is, prove NP ⊄ P/poly?
status: Open since the 1970s. Karp–Lipton shows that containment would collapse the polynomial hierarchy, but this consequence is not a contradiction. Razborov and Rudich's Natural Proofs barrier and Viola's *Selected Challenges in Computational Lower Bounds* frame the difficulty.
solved_when: A language in NP is exhibited whose Boolean circuit complexity is superpolynomial in the input length.
why: It rules out even nonuniform, input-length-specific efficient solutions to all NP problems, and underpins nonuniform security of one-way functions and pseudorandom generators.
key_works: Karp and Lipton (1980), *Some Connections Between Nonuniform and Uniform Complexity Classes*; Razborov and Rudich (1997), *Natural Proofs*; Viola (2017), *Selected Challenges in Computational Lower Bounds*.

title: Graph isomorphism in polynomial time
open: Is there a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that decides whether two arbitrary finite graphs are isomorphic?
status: The problem has been studied for more than five decades. Babai’s quasipolynomial-time algorithm (Babai 2016, *Graph Isomorphism in Quasipolynomial Time*, arXiv:1512.03547, DOI: 10.1145/2897518.2897542) is a major general breakthrough, but polynomial time remains unresolved.
solved_when: Such an algorithm is given and proved correct, running in polynomial time on all pairs of finite graphs.
why: It would settle a central natural problem that is not known to be either NP-complete or polynomial-time solvable, a long-standing gap in complexity theory.
key_works: Babai (2016), *Graph Isomorphism in Quasipolynomial Time*, arXiv:1512.03547, DOI: 10.1145/2897518.2897542.

title: Berman–Hartmanis isomorphism conjecture
open: Are all NP-complete languages, under polynomial-time many-one reductions, the same problem up to efficient relabeling — that is, is every pair of them related by a polynomial-time computable bijection with a polynomial-time computable inverse?
status: Proposed by Berman and Hartmanis in 1977 (see *On Isomorphisms and Density of NP and Other Complete Sets*, DOI: 10.1137/0206023). Large families of natural complete sets are known to satisfy the conjectured isomorphism structure, but no general proof or counterexample is known.
solved_when: A proof that every pair of NP-complete languages (under polynomial-time many-one reductions) is polynomial-time isomorphic, or an explicit counterexample pair that is not.
why: A positive answer would show that NP-completeness is a single structural object rather than a family of superficially different problems; a counterexample would reveal a fundamental structural divide among complete sets.
key_works: Berman and Hartmanis (1977), *On Isomorphisms and Density of NP and Other Complete Sets*, DOI: 10.1137/0206023.

title: NP versus UP
open: Does every language in NP admit an unambiguous polynomial-time verifier — one where each input has at most one accepting witness?
status: Open since the 1970s. Valiant and Vazirani (1986), *NP Is as Easy as Detecting Unique Solutions*, DOI: 10.1016/0304-3975(86)90135-0, give randomized isolation into unique-solution promise problems, which is not an unconditional equality of NP and UP.
solved_when: NP = UP is proved, or a language in NP is exhibited that has no unambiguous polynomial-time verifier.
why: It settles whether ambiguity — the possibility of many witnesses — is an essential source of computational difficulty, separating search from verification even within nondeterminism.
key_works: Valiant and Vazirani (1986), *NP Is as Easy as Detecting Unique Solutions*, DOI: 10.1016/0304-3975(86)90135-0.

title: Complete problems for NP ∩ coNP
open: Does NP ∩ coNP contain a single problem that is hardest for the whole class under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions — that is, does the class have a complete language?
status: This is a longstanding structural question; no natural member of NP ∩ coNP is known to be complete for it, and oracle results — e.g., Dose (2019), *P-Optimal Proof Systems for Each NP-Set but No Complete Disjoint NP-Pairs Relative to an Oracle*, DOI: 10.4230/LIPIcs.MFCS.2019.47 — show that standard relativizing approaches face obstacles.
solved_when: A complete language for NP ∩ coNP under polynomial-time many-one reductions is exhibited, or such a language is proven not to exist.
why: It answers whether the class of problems admitting short certificates for both yes- and no-instances has a universal representative, shaping how we understand and communicate the structure of this class.
key_works: Dose (2019), *P-Optimal Proof Systems for Each NP-Set but No Complete Disjoint NP-Pairs Relative to an Oracle*, DOI: 10.4230/LIPIcs.MFCS.2019.47.

title: Superlinear unrestricted Boolean circuit lower bounds
open: Is there an explicitly computable Boolean function that cannot be built with circuits of linear size? Formally, exhibit a polynomial-time computable Boolean function requiring \(\omega(n)\) gates in unrestricted bounded-fan-in Boolean circuits.
status: Open for decades despite strong lower bounds for restricted circuit models. Counting arguments (Shannon) show that most functions require exponentially many gates, but this does not yield efficiently computable explicit examples; see Shannon (1949), *The Synthesis of Two-Terminal Switching Circuits*, and Viola (2017), *Selected Challenges in Computational Lower Bounds*.
solved_when: An explicit polynomial-time computable Boolean function is proven to require \(\omega(n)\) gates in unrestricted bounded-fan-in Boolean circuits.
why: Crossing superlinear size for unrestricted circuits would break a basic barrier on the path to general circuit lower bounds, with consequences for provable limits of circuit compression in hardware design and explicit hard functions for cryptography.
key_works: Shannon (1949), *The Synthesis of Two-Terminal Switching Circuits*; Viola (2017), *Selected Challenges in Computational Lower Bounds*.

title: Superpolynomial general formula lower bounds
open: Is there an explicitly constructible function, computable in polynomial time, that cannot be computed by Boolean formulas of polynomial size? In other words, exhibit an explicit function in P requiring superpolynomial-size unrestricted Boolean formulas.
status: Open for decades. Strong polynomial lower bounds and exponential bounds for restricted formula models are known, but unrestricted superpolynomial bounds remain elusive. Key works include Håstad (1998), *The Shrinkage Exponent of de Morgan Formulas Is 2*, and Hoza (2024), circuit-complexity course materials.
solved_when: An explicit function in P is proved to require superpolynomial-size unrestricted Boolean formulas.
why: It would prove that reusing intermediate computations (sharing, as in circuits) can provide more than a polynomial advantage over tree-like formula expansions.
key_works: Håstad (1998), *The Shrinkage Exponent of de Morgan Formulas Is 2*; Hoza (2024), circuit-complexity course materials.

title: NP outside ACC⁰
open: Does NP require superpolynomial-size circuits even when AND, OR, NOT, and MOD_m gates are allowed at constant depth? Formally, prove that NP ⊄ ACC⁰, i.e., NP is not contained in polynomial-size constant-depth circuits over the AND/OR/NOT/MOD gate basis.
status: Williams (2011, *Non-uniform ACC Circuit Lower Bounds*) proved that NEXP is not contained in ACC⁰, but bringing the hard language down from NEXP to NP remains unresolved; Hoza (2024) provides supporting circuit-complexity materials.
solved_when: A proof that there exists a language in NP that does not admit polynomial-size constant-depth circuits with AND, OR, NOT, and modular counting gates — equivalently, NP ⊄ ACC⁰.
why: It would extend the algorithm-to-lower-bound technique to a dramatically weaker complexity class, giving strong, unconditional average-case-relevant hardness of NP against modular arithmetic circuits and sharpening the boundary of where nonconstructive circuit lower bounds can reach.
key_works: Williams (2011), *Non-uniform ACC Circuit Lower Bounds*; Hoza (2024), circuit-complexity materials.

title: Majority outside ACC⁰
open: Can the majority function be computed by polynomial-size ACC⁰ circuits of fixed depth and any fixed modulus? The goal is to prove that it cannot — that majority lies outside ACC⁰ for every fixed modulus and fixed depth.
status: Majority is known to lie outside AC⁰, but its separation from ACC⁰ remains unresolved. The problem is a concrete function-specific target rather than a class-separation formulation. Relevant background includes Razborov and Smolensky's 1980s modular-circuit lower bounds; Williams (2011), *Non-uniform ACC Circuit Lower Bounds*; and Hoza's course.
solved_when: A proof that no polynomial-size ACC⁰ circuit, of any fixed depth and over any fixed modulus, computes majority.
why: It would separate approximate counting power from constant-depth modular computation, settling a concrete function-specific lower bound rather than a class separation.
key_works: Razborov and Smolensky’s 1980s modular-circuit lower bounds; Williams (2011), *Non-uniform ACC Circuit Lower Bounds*; Hoza’s course.

title: Valiant’s explicit matrix rigidity problem
open: Can we explicitly construct a family of n×n matrices over a fixed field that cannot be approximated by sparse matrices? Formally, construct an explicit family with rigidity \(R_A(\varepsilon n)\ge n^{1+\delta}\) for constants \(\varepsilon,\delta>0\).
status: Proposed in 1977. Random matrices are highly rigid; achieving the needed parameters explicitly remains open, and several once-promising structured matrices have turned out insufficiently rigid. Key works: Valiant (1977), *Graph-Theoretic Arguments in Low-Level Complexity*; Ramya (2020), *Recent Progress on Matrix Rigidity—A Survey*, arXiv:2009.09460.
solved_when: An explicit family of \(n\times n\) matrices over a specified fixed field is exhibited with rigidity \(R_A(\varepsilon n)\ge n^{1+\delta}\) for some constants \(\varepsilon,\delta>0\).
why: Strong explicit rigidity would yield lower bounds for important classes of linear circuits.
key_works: Valiant (1977), *Graph-Theoretic Arguments in Low-Level Complexity*; Ramya (2020), *Recent Progress on Matrix Rigidity—A Survey*, arXiv:2009.09460.

title: VP versus VNP
subfield: Algebraic complexity and polynomial identity testing
open: Do all polynomial families whose coefficients are efficiently computable as exponential sums admit polynomial-size arithmetic circuits? Over characteristic zero, it suffices to separate the permanent from VP.
status: Valiant introduced the classes in 1979. Restricted circuit lower bounds are extensive, but the general separation remains open. Key works: Valiant (1979), *Completeness Classes in Algebra*; Shpilka and Yehudayoff (2010), *Arithmetic Circuits: A Survey of Recent Results and Open Questions*, DOI: 10.1561/0400000039.
solved_when: Either every VNP family is shown to have polynomial-size arithmetic circuits, or a VNP family (e.g., the permanent, over characteristic zero) is proved to require super-polynomial-size circuits.
why: This is the algebraic analogue of P versus NP, contrasting efficient computation with efficient exponential summation; resolving it would anchor our understanding of algebraic proof and circuit lower bounds.
key_works: Valiant (1979), *Completeness Classes in Algebra*; Shpilka and Yehudayoff (2010), *Arithmetic Circuits: A Survey of Recent Results and Open Questions*, DOI: 10.1561/0400000039.

title: Arithmetic circuits versus branching programs
subfield: Algebraic complexity and polynomial identity testing
open: Can every polynomial-family computed by polynomial-size, polynomial-degree arithmetic circuits also be computed by polynomial-size algebraic branching programs — that is, is VP = VBP?
status: Open for decades. Quasipolynomial simulations and strong results for restricted models are known, but these do not establish polynomial equivalence. Key works: Valiant, Skyum, Berkowitz, and Rackoff (1983), *Fast Parallel Computation of Polynomials Using Few Processors*; the Shpilka–Yehudayoff survey.
solved_when: A polynomial-size simulation of polynomial-size, polynomial-degree arithmetic circuits by algebraic branching programs is exhibited, or the classes VP and VBP are proved equal (or a separation refuting it).
why: It measures whether general arithmetic circuit structure — arbitrary wiring of gates — offers real computational power beyond iterated linear-algebraic computation, which branching programs capture.
key_works: Valiant, Skyum, Berkowitz, and Rackoff (1983), *Fast Parallel Computation of Polynomials Using Few Processors*; Shpilka–Yehudayoff survey.

title: Arithmetic formulas versus branching programs
subfield: Algebraic complexity and polynomial identity testing
open: Do polynomial-size arithmetic formulas and polynomial-size algebraic branching programs compute exactly the same polynomial families? Equivalently, is every polynomial family with polynomial-size algebraic branching programs also computable by polynomial-size formulas?
status: Open in the unrestricted commutative setting. Formula lower bounds for the determinant or iterated matrix multiplication strong enough to separate these classes remain unavailable. Key works include Valiant et al. (1983), *Fast Parallel Computation of Polynomials Using Few Processors*, and Shpilka–Yehudayoff (2010).
solved_when: A proof that any polynomial-size algebraic branching program can be converted to a polynomial-size arithmetic formula for the same polynomial, or a separation exhibiting a polynomial family computable by polynomial-size branching programs but requiring superpolynomial-size formulas.
why: It determines how much arithmetic computation benefits from sharing subcomputations across different paths — whether the DAG structure of branching programs is genuinely more powerful than the tree structure of formulas.
key_works: Valiant et al. (1983), *Fast Parallel Computation of Polynomials Using Few Processors*; Shpilka–Yehudayoff (2010).

title: Deterministic polynomial-time white-box PIT
subfield: Algebraic complexity and polynomial identity testing
open: Given an arithmetic circuit of polynomially bounded degree over a specified effective field, is there a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that decides whether it computes the zero polynomial?
status: Randomized polynomial-time identity testing has been available for decades (Schwartz, 1980; Zippel, 1979). General deterministic polynomial-time testing remains open despite many restricted-model algorithms, including recent progress by Hu, van Melkebeek, and Morgan (2024, DOI: 10.4086/toc.2024.v020a001); Kabanets and Impagliazzo (2004) established that derandomizing PIT entails proving circuit lower bounds.
solved_when: A deterministic algorithm exists that, on any such circuit, correctly decides identity in time polynomial in the circuit size.
why: It would derandomize a fundamental primitive in symbolic algebra and, via known connections, imply significant circuit lower bounds.
key_works: Schwartz (1980); Zippel (1979); Kabanets and Impagliazzo (2004), *Derandomizing Polynomial Identity Tests Means Proving Circuit Lower Bounds*; Hu, van Melkebeek, and Morgan (2024), DOI: 10.4086/toc.2024.v020a001.

title: Matrix multiplication exponent two
subfield: Algebraic complexity and polynomial identity testing
open: Is the algebraic complexity of matrix multiplication essentially quadratic: does the exponent \(\omega\) equal 2, i.e. can two \(n\times n\) matrices be multiplied in \(O(n^{2+\varepsilon})\) arithmetic operations for every \(\varepsilon>0\)?
status: Open since Strassen's 1969 breakthrough showing Gaussian elimination is not optimal. The best verified benchmark, from 2025, is \(\omega<2.371339\); the lower bound remains 2. Key works: Strassen (1969), *Gaussian Elimination Is Not Optimal*; Alman et al. (2025), *More Asymmetry Yields Faster Matrix Multiplication*, DOI: 10.1137/1.9781611978322.63.
solved_when: An algorithm is given that, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), multiplies two \(n\times n\) matrices over a field using \(O(n^{2+\varepsilon})\) arithmetic operations; equivalently, \(\omega=2\) is established.
why: A positive answer would accelerate a large family of algebraic, graph, and scientific computations whose best running times are currently tethered to \(\omega>2\).
key_works: Strassen (1969), *Gaussian Elimination Is Not Optimal*; Alman et al. (2025), *More Asymmetry Yields Faster Matrix Multiplication*, DOI: 10.1137/1.9781611978322.63.

title: Shub–Smale integer-root τ conjecture
subfield: Algebraic complexity and polynomial identity testing
open: Can the number of integer roots of an integer polynomial be polynomially bounded by the length of the shortest constant-free straight-line program computing it? Formally, prove that a nonzero integer polynomial computed by such a program of length \(\tau\) has at most \((\tau+1)^C\) integer roots for some universal constant \(C\).
status: The conjecture was proposed in the 1990s, originating with Shub and Smale (1995), *On the Intractability of Hilbert’s Nullstellensatz and an Algebraic Version of NP ≠ P*; general polynomial root-count bounds in terms of straight-line complexity remain unavailable. Bürgisser's work connects τ-type conjectures to complexity.
solved_when: There exists a universal constant \(C\) such that every nonzero integer polynomial computed by a constant-free arithmetic straight-line program of length \(\tau\) has at most \((\tau+1)^C\) integer roots.
why: A proof would tie arithmetic circuit size directly to Diophantine complexity, and the conjecture is connected to major algebraic lower-bound questions; without it, no general root-count bound in terms of straight-line complexity is available.
key_works: Shub and Smale (1995), *On the Intractability of Hilbert’s Nullstellensatz and an Algebraic Version of NP ≠ P*; Bürgisser’s work connecting τ-type conjectures to complexity.

title: Real τ conjecture for sums of products of sparse polynomials
subfield: Algebraic complexity and polynomial identity testing
open: Can the number of distinct real roots of a polynomial \(P=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\prod_{j=1}^{m} f_{ij}\), where each \(f_{ij}\) has at most \(t\) monomials, be bounded by a polynomial in \(k\), \(m\), and \(t\)? Formally, one asks for a bound on the real root count of any nonzero polynomial of this structured form that is polynomial in the sparsity parameters and the depth of the sum–product expression.
status: The problem is open in this structured model. Average-case versions are known, per Briquel and Bürgisser, *The Real Tau-Conjecture Is True on Average* (arXiv:1806.00417). The analogous claim for arbitrary arithmetic circuits is false, and that is not the problem listed here; Hrubeš (2013), *On the Real τ-Conjecture and the Distribution of Complex Roots*, is a key reference.
solved_when: A proof, for all nonzero polynomials expressible as such a sum of \(k\) products of \(m\) polynomials each with at most \(t\) monomials, that the number of distinct real roots is at most \(\mathrm{poly}(k,m,t)\).
why: A solution would connect fewnomial geometry to arithmetic circuit lower bounds, providing a route from real-root counting to proving hardness results in algebraic complexity.
key_works: Hrubeš (2013), *On the Real τ-Conjecture and the Distribution of Complex Roots*; Briquel and Bürgisser, *The Real Tau-Conjecture Is True on Average*, arXiv:1806.00417.

title: Deterministic PIT for general noncommutative circuits
subfield: Algebraic complexity and polynomial identity testing
open: Give deterministic polynomial-time identity testing for general noncommutative arithmetic circuits with polynomially bounded syntactic degree.
status: Raz–Shpilka solved important formula and branching-program cases in 2005. General circuits with sharing remain a different, unresolved problem.
why: Would advance symbolic computation in free algebras and clarify the power of circuit reuse.
key_works: Raz and Shpilka (2005), *Deterministic Polynomial Identity Testing in Non-Commutative Models*; Li, Tzameret, and Wang (2015), *Non-Commutative Formulas and Frege Lower Bounds*, DOI: 10.4230/LIPIcs.CCC.2015.412.

title: BPP equals P
open: Is every problem solvable by a randomized polynomial-time algorithm with bounded error also solvable in deterministic polynomial time — that is, does BPP equal P?
status: Open for decades. Hardness-versus-randomness results show that strong circuit-hardness assumptions imply derandomization — Nisan and Wigderson (1994), *Hardness vs Randomness*, and Impagliazzo and Wigderson (1997), *P = BPP if E Requires Exponential Circuits* — but the required unconditional hardness is missing; see also Impagliazzo (2003), arXiv:cs/0304040.
solved_when: A proof that BPP = P, or a separation showing a language in BPP outside P.
why: It settles whether randomness gives an inherent polynomial-time speedup over deterministic computation, and derandomization techniques would transform how randomized algorithms across complexity theory are used.
key_works: Nisan and Wigderson (1994), *Hardness vs Randomness*; Impagliazzo and Wigderson (1997), *P = BPP if E Requires Exponential Circuits*; Impagliazzo (2003), arXiv:cs/0304040.

title: Does derandomizing PromiseZPP derandomize PromiseBPP?
open: Does derandomizing zero-error randomized algorithms already derandomize bounded-error ones? Formally, does the assumption \(\mathrm{PromiseZPP}\subseteq\mathrm P\) imply \(\mathrm{PromiseBPP}\subseteq\mathrm P\)?
status: Explicitly retained as an open problem in the 2024 Luca Trevisan memorial collection (open-problem contributions by Fortnow, Goldreich, Håstad, Vadhan, and Williamson, 2024). Known relationships between zero-error and bounded-error randomness do not settle this implication for promise problems.
solved_when: A proof or refutation of the implication \(\mathrm{PromiseZPP}\subseteq\mathrm P \Rightarrow \mathrm{PromiseBPP}\subseteq\mathrm P\) is established.
why: It determines whether eliminating one form of randomness is already sufficient to eliminate another, a basic structural question about the relationships among randomized classes.
key_works: Fortnow, Goldreich, Håstad, Vadhan, and Williamson (2024), open-problem contributions in the Luca Trevisan memorial collection.

title: Two-source extraction at the optimal leading entropy constant
open: Can randomness be explicitly extracted from two independent sources that are barely more random than a single uniform bit's worth of entropy? Formally, construct a polynomial-time explicit one-bit extractor for two independent \(n\)-bit sources of min-entropy \(\log_2 n + O(1)\), with a fixed small error such as 0.01.
status: Li's 2023 work (arXiv:2303.06802, DOI: 10.1109/FOCS57990.2023.00075) achieved \(O(\log n)\) entropy; the unresolved target is the optimal leading constant and additive gap, not merely logarithmic entropy.
solved_when: An explicit polynomial-time extractor for two independent \(n\)-bit sources with min-entropy \(\log_2 n + O(1)\) and error 0.01 (or any fixed small constant error) is given.
why: It approaches the information-theoretic limit of extracting randomness from extremely weak independent sources.
key_works: Li (2023), *Two Source Extractors for Asymptotically Optimal Entropy, and (Many) More*, arXiv:2303.06802, DOI: 10.1109/FOCS57990.2023.00075.

bib.title: Two-source extraction at the optimal leading entropy constant

title: Optimal explicit restricted-isometry matrices
open: Can we deterministically construct, in polynomial time, an \(m\times N\) matrix with a fixed restricted-isometry constant for sparsity \(k\) using only \(m=O(k\log(N/k))\) rows? In other words, can explicit constructions match the row count that random matrices achieve for the restricted isometry property?
status: Random matrices achieve the optimal \(m=O(k\log(N/k))\) order. Explicit constructions, notably Bourgain et al. (2011) and Mixon (*Explicit Matrices with the Restricted Isometry Property: Breaking the Square-Root Bottleneck*, arXiv:1403.3427), have broken some older barriers but do not match the general optimal tradeoff.
solved_when: A deterministic polynomial-time algorithm outputs an \(m\times N\) matrix with fixed restricted-isometry constant, sparsity \(k\), and \(m=O(k\log(N/k))\).
why: It would remove the need for randomness in compressed sensing and sparse recovery while improving the associated guarantees.
key_works: Bourgain et al. (2011), explicit RIP constructions; Mixon, *Explicit Matrices with the Restricted Isometry Property: Breaking the Square-Root Bottleneck*, arXiv:1403.3427.

title: Fourier entropy–influence conjecture
open: Is the Fourier spectrum of every Boolean function concentrated enough that its entropy is at most a constant multiple of its total influence? Formally, does there exist a universal constant \(C\) such that every Boolean function \(f\) satisfies \(H(\widehat f^2)\le C\,\mathrm{Inf}(f)\)?
status: The conjecture was proposed by Friedgut and Kalai in 1996, with a later author exposition by Kalai (2007), *The Entropy/Influence Conjecture*. Many special classes of functions are understood, but the universal inequality remains open.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) of the inequality \(H(\widehat f^2)\le C\,\mathrm{Inf}(f)\) for all Boolean functions, for some universal constant \(C\) independent of the function and the number of variables.
why: A proof would tightly connect a function's spectral complexity with its sensitivity to noise and its learnability, giving a quantitative bridge between Fourier analysis and these complexity measures.
key_works: Friedgut and Kalai (1996), conjecture; Kalai (2007), *The Entropy/Influence Conjecture*, author exposition.

title: Superpolynomial Frege lower bounds
open: Is there an explicit family of propositional tautologies whose shortest Frege proofs grow superpolynomially in size? Formally, exhibit a tautology family requiring Frege proofs of superpolynomial size.
status: Open since modern proof complexity began. Strong lower bounds are known for resolution and bounded-depth systems, but these techniques have not extended to unrestricted Frege. Key works: Cook and Reckhow (1979); Li, Tzameret, and Wang (2015), *Non-Commutative Formulas and Frege Lower Bounds*, DOI: 10.4230/LIPIcs.CCC.2015.412.
solved_when: An explicit tautology family is exhibited together with a proof that every Frege proof of the n-th tautology has size superpolynomial in n.
why: It would establish inherent limitations of a central model of ordinary propositional reasoning, showing that some tautologies are provable but not feasibly provable.
key_works: Cook and Reckhow (1979); Li, Tzameret, and Wang (2015), *Non-Commutative Formulas and Frege Lower Bounds*, DOI: 10.4230/LIPIcs.CCC.2015.412.

s2_matches.title: Exponential Lower Bounds for AC0-Frege Imply Superpolynomial Frege Lower Bounds

title: Superpolynomial Extended Frege lower bounds
open: Can we exhibit a family of tautologies that requires superpolynomial-size proofs in Extended Frege, the proof system that extends Frege by allowing proofs to introduce names for intermediate formulas?
status: Open for decades and strictly stronger than the corresponding Frege lower-bound target. Recent work, including Pich and Santhanam, *Towards P ≠ NP from Extended Frege Lower Bounds*, ECCC TR23-199; journal DOI: 10.1145/3801091, explores implications of such lower bounds for computational hardness.
solved_when: An explicit family of tautologies is shown to have no Extended Frege proofs of size polynomial in the formula size.
why: It would establish the first genuine size limit on a proof system powerful enough to efficiently express circuit-style reasoning, and thereby constrain proof compression through auxiliary definitions in formal verification.
key_works: Pich and Santhanam, *Towards P ≠ NP from Extended Frege Lower Bounds*, ECCC TR23-199; journal DOI: 10.1145/3801091.

title: Ideal Proof System lower bounds
open: Can we prove that some explicit family of unsatisfiable polynomial systems has no polynomial-size proofs in the Ideal Proof System? Formally, exhibit such a family for which every IPS certificate requires superpolynomial arithmetic-circuit size.
status: The Ideal Proof System was introduced in 2014 by Grochow and Pitassi (*The Ideal Proof System: Circuit Complexity, Proof Complexity, and PIT*, DOI: 10.1145/3230742). General lower bounds are known to be tightly linked to major arithmetic circuit lower bounds, which explains both the promise and the difficulty of the problem.
solved_when: An explicit family of unsatisfiable polynomial systems is exhibited for which every IPS certificate has superpolynomial arithmetic-circuit size.
why: General IPS lower bounds are tightly tied to major arithmetic circuit lower bounds, so progress here could unify algebraic complexity and proof complexity in a single lower-bound program.
key_works: Grochow and Pitassi, *The Ideal Proof System: Circuit Complexity, Proof Complexity, and PIT*, DOI: 10.1145/3230742.

title: NP-hardness of total minimum formula size
open: Is it NP-hard, unconditionally, to decide whether a Boolean function given by its full truth table has a formula of size at most a supplied bound? In other words, does the Minimum Formula Size Problem admit an unconditional NP-hardness proof, without reliance on assumptions such as ETH?
status: Strong conditional hardness is known, including ETH-based results (Ilango, *The Minimum Formula Size Problem Is (ETH) Hard*) and NP-hardness of approximating meta-complexity under related conditions (Hirahara and Ilango, 2023, *NP-Hardness of Approximating Meta-Complexity*, DOI: 10.1145/3564246.3585154). The standard unconditional NP-hardness question remains open and separate.
solved_when: A proof establishes NP-hardness of deciding, given a complete truth table and a bound s, whether the function has a Boolean formula of size at most s.
why: It pins down the exact computational cost of optimal symbolic-expression compression, the core obstacle in tasks such as symbolic regression—finding the smallest exact expression for data.
key_works: Ilango, *The Minimum Formula Size Problem Is (ETH) Hard*; Hirahara and Ilango (2023), *NP-Hardness of Approximating Meta-Complexity*, DOI: 10.1145/3564246.3585154.

bib.title: NP-hardness of total minimum formula size

title: Strong bounded-depth Frege bounds for random 3-CNF
open: How hard is it to refute a random unsatisfiable 3-CNF formula in weak proof systems? Prove superpolynomial — ideally exponential — lower bounds on refutation size in bounded-depth Frege for random unsatisfiable 3-CNF formulas with a sufficiently large constant clause-to-variable ratio.
status: A 2024 result by Gryaznov and Talebanfard (*Bounded-Depth Frege Lower Bounds for Random 3-CNFs via Deterministic Restrictions*, arXiv:2403.02275) obtains \(n^{1+\varepsilon_d}\)-type bounds for fixed proof depth \(d\); the stronger superpolynomial and exponential growth targets remain unresolved.
solved_when: A superpolynomial (ideally exponential) lower bound on bounded-depth Frege refutation size is established for random unsatisfiable 3-CNFs at some sufficiently large constant clause-to-variable ratio.
why: It would connect proof complexity to experimentally hard random satisfiability instances, and thereby link lower-bound techniques to the algorithmic barriers observed near random-SAT phase transitions.
key_works: Gryaznov and Talebanfard (2024), *Bounded-Depth Frege Lower Bounds for Random 3-CNFs via Deterministic Restrictions*, arXiv:2403.02275.

bib.title: Strong bounded-depth Frege bounds for random 3-CNF

title: Does Frege polynomially simulate Extended Frege?
open: Can every Extended Frege proof be converted into a Frege proof of the same tautology with only polynomial blow-up, computed in polynomial time? Equivalently, do the extension variables that name intermediate propositions ever give Extended Frege superpolynomial proof-length advantages over Frege?
status: Open for decades. The question compares proof-system strength directly and is not identical to proving lower bounds for either system. Key works include Cook and Reckhow (1979); Krajíček (2019), *Proof Complexity*; and Pich–Santhanam's Extended Frege work.
solved_when: A polynomial p and a polynomial-time algorithm are given that map any Extended Frege proof to a Frege proof of size at most p(n), where n is the original proof size; or such a simulation is shown impossible via a superpolynomial separation of Extended Frege from Frege.
why: A positive answer shows extension variables are mere abbreviations with no essential power; a negative answer exhibits a concrete, structural source of superpolynomial proof-shortening, which would be a major step toward separating these standard proof systems.
key_works: Cook and Reckhow (1979); Krajíček (2019), *Proof Complexity*; Pich–Santhanam’s Extended Frege work.

bib.title: Does Frege polynomially simulate Extended Frege?

title: Nondeterministic SETH
open: Does certifying unsatisfiability of sufficiently wide CNF formulas still require essentially \(2^n\) time even for nondeterministic algorithms? Formally, the question asks whether such \(2^n\) lower bounds hold for nondeterministic computation, the premise known as the Nondeterministic Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (NSETH).
status: The problem was introduced to study the limits of fine-grained reductions and is stronger in a different direction than ordinary deterministic SETH. Key work: Carmosino, Gao, Impagliazzo, Mihajlin, Paturi, and Schneider (2016), *Nondeterministic Extensions of the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis and Consequences for Non-Reducibility*.
solved_when: A proof that certifying unsatisfiability of sufficiently wide CNF formulas requires essentially \(2^n\) nondeterministic time, or a refutation showing a nondeterministic certification algorithm running substantially faster than \(2^n\) for such formulas.
why: A resolution explains why certain desired fine-grained reductions cannot exist: producing them would itself imply unexpected nondeterministic algorithmic breakthroughs.
key_works: Carmosino, Gao, Impagliazzo, Mihajlin, Paturi, and Schneider (2016), *Nondeterministic Extensions of the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis and Consequences for Non-Reducibility*.

title: Gap Exponential Time Hypothesis
open: Prove or refute exponential-time hardness of distinguishing satisfiable 3-CNF formulas from formulas in which every assignment violates a fixed positive fraction of clauses.
status: A central hypothesis in approximation and parameterized hardness. Ordinary ETH does not currently imply the standard Gap-ETH formulation. Key works include Dinur's and Manurangsi–Raghavendra's 2016 Gap-ETH formulations and Vassilevska Williams's fine-grained survey.
solved_when: Either a proof establishes the gap-exponential-time hardness of this distinguishing problem (for 3-CNF with a fixed positive fraction of violated clauses) under exponential-time lower-bound assumptions, or a refutation shows it can be done in subexponential time.
why: Gap-ETH supplies robust hardness that survives approximation-preserving transformations, whereas ordinary ETH alone does not currently yield such guarantees.
key_works: Dinur’s and Manurangsi–Raghavendra’s 2016 Gap-ETH formulations; Vassilevska Williams’s fine-grained survey.

title: Counting SETH
open: Does counting the satisfying assignments of a CNF formula require essentially \(2^{n}\) time as \(n\) grows, even when the clause width is allowed to be large? Formally, is there no algorithm running in \(2^{(1-o(1))n}\) time that counts satisfying assignments of sufficiently wide CNF formulas?
status: This is a longstanding counting analogue of SETH. It remains open in part because decision algorithms and counting algorithms need not share the same optimal exponential rate. Key works: Impagliazzo–Paturi–Zane (2001); Dell et al., *Exponential Time Complexity of the Permanent and the Tutte Polynomial* (2014).
solved_when: A proof that no \(2^{(1-o(1))n}\)-time algorithm can count satisfying assignments of sufficiently wide CNF formulas, or an algorithm achieving that running time for all such formulas.
why: The conjecture underlies fine-grained lower bounds for exact counting, partition functions, and enumeration; settling it calibrates the true exponential complexity of these tasks.
key_works: Impagliazzo–Paturi–Zane (2001); Dell et al., *Exponential Time Complexity of the Permanent and the Tutte Polynomial* (2014).

title: Truly subquadratic 3SUM
open: Can 3SUM be solved in truly subquadratic time? That is, does there exist an \(O(n^{2-\varepsilon})\)-time algorithm for some fixed \(\varepsilon>0\) in the standard real-RAM model — or can an appropriate conditional barrier ruling out such an algorithm be established?
status: Quadratic time has been improved by subpolynomial factors, but a fixed exponent improvement remains unknown. Key works include Gajentaan and Overmars (1995), *On a Class of O(n²) Problems in Computational Geometry*, and Grønlund and Pettie (2014), *Threesomes, Degenerates, and Love Triangles*.
solved_when: Either an \(O(n^{2-\varepsilon})\)-time algorithm for 3SUM is given in the standard real-RAM model for some fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), or a suitable conditional lower bound is proven showing no such algorithm exists.
why: 3SUM controls conjectured lower bounds for numerous geometric problems, so resolving it either yields faster algorithms across that class or firm evidence those problems are genuinely quadratic.
key_works: Gajentaan and Overmars (1995), *On a Class of O(n²) Problems in Computational Geometry*; Grønlund and Pettie (2014), *Threesomes, Degenerates, and Love Triangles*.

title: Truly subquadratic min-plus convolution
open: Compute \(c_k=\min_{i+j=k}(a_i+b_j)\) for two arbitrary length-\(n\) sequences in \(O(n^{2-\varepsilon})\) time.
status: Open despite faster algorithms for restricted inputs and numerous equivalence reductions.
why: Would accelerate knapsack-like dynamic programs and many optimization recurrences.
key_works: Cygan, Mucha, Węgrzycki, and Włodarczyk (2017), *On Problems Equivalent to (min,+)-Convolution*; Vassilevska Williams’s survey.

title: Orthogonal Vectors Hypothesis
open: Is there, for every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), a constant \(c\) such that detecting an orthogonal pair among \(n\) Boolean vectors of dimension \(c\log n\) requires \(n^{2-\varepsilon}\) time?
status: The conjecture is implied by standard formulations of SETH but has not been independently established; low-dimensional variants admit faster algorithms. See Williams (2005), *A New Algorithm for Optimal 2-Constraint Satisfaction and Its Implications*, and Vassilevska Williams (2018).
solved_when: Either a proof exhibits, for every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), a dimension \(c\log n\) for which orthogonal-pair detection needs \(n^{2-\varepsilon}\) time, or a faster algorithm refutes this for some \(\varepsilon\).
why: The hypothesis is a widely reusable hardness source, underpinning conditional lower bounds for similarity search and sequence problems.
key_works: Williams (2005), *A New Algorithm for Optimal 2-Constraint Satisfaction and Its Implications*; Vassilevska Williams (2018).

title: Online Matrix–Vector Multiplication conjecture
open: Can an algorithm process a sequence of n Boolean matrix–vector products, posed online against a fixed n×n matrix, in substantially less than cubic total time? Formally, the OMv conjecture asserts that answering n such queries, each before the next vector is revealed, requires n^{3-o(1)} total time, with the preprocessing convention explicitly fixed.
status: Proposed in 2015 by Henzinger, Krinninger, Nanongkai, and Saranurak (*Unifying and Strengthening Hardness for Dynamic Problems via the Online Matrix-Vector Multiplication Conjecture*, arXiv:1504.06148); each answer must precede the next vector, and it has become a major foundation of dynamic lower bounds, including in databases—incremental query maintenance.
solved_when: A proof that any algorithm (under a stated preprocessing convention) needs n^{3-o(1)} total time, or an algorithm breaking that bound.
why: The conjecture is a major foundation of dynamic lower bounds, capturing the cost of online dependence that offline matrix multiplication can avoid.
key_works: Henzinger, Krinninger, Nanongkai, and Saranurak (2015), *Unifying and Strengthening Hardness for Dynamic Problems via the Online Matrix-Vector Multiplication Conjecture*, arXiv:1504.06148.

title: Optimal exponent for fixed-size clique detection
open: For fixed clique sizes \(k\) divisible by three, is it possible to detect a \(k\)-clique faster than the matrix-multiplication-based approach by a fixed positive margin? Formally, can \(k\)-clique detection beat the exponent \(\omega k/3\) by a constant amount independent of \(k\)?
status: Matrix multiplication supplies the standard general benchmark for this problem. Its optimality is conjectural, and it should not be confused with NP-hardness when \(k\) is part of the input. Key works include Nešetřil and Poljak (1985), *On the Complexity of the Subgraph Problem*, and Vassilevska Williams (2018).
solved_when: For some fixed \(k\) divisible by three, an algorithm is exhibited whose exponent is \(\omega k/3 - \epsilon\) for a positive constant \(\epsilon\); or, conversely, the \(\omega k/3\) exponent is shown to be optimal for such \(k\).
why: It would sharpen our understanding of the fine-grained complexity of dense subgraph detection, either by breaking a long-standing algorithmic barrier or by proving it genuine.
key_works: Nešetřil and Poljak (1985), *On the Complexity of the Subgraph Problem*; Vassilevska Williams (2018).

title: Derive 3SUM hardness from SETH
open: Can a truly subquadratic algorithm for 3SUM be shown to refute the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis via a fine-grained reduction, or is there a precisely stated barrier proving such a reduction cannot exist?
status: The main fine-grained conjectures remain incompletely connected: existing nondeterministic barriers (Carmosino et al., 2016) constrain particular reduction strategies rather than every conceivable proof. See also Vassilevska Williams (2018).
solved_when: Either a fine-grained reduction is exhibited whose existence, combined with a truly subquadratic 3SUM algorithm, refutes SETH, or a barrier is proved that formally rules out such reductions.
why: It would reduce the number of independent assumptions needed to establish geometric lower bounds, unifying quadratic-barrier explanations in computational geometry under SETH alone.
key_works: Carmosino et al. (2016), nondeterministic SETH and non-reducibility; Vassilevska Williams (2018).

title: Derive APSP hardness from SETH
open: Can the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis be shown to imply that all-pairs shortest paths in general weighted graphs requires essentially cubic time? Formally, prove that a truly subcubic algorithm for general weighted APSP would yield a fixed-base improvement for sufficiently wide SAT — or establish a rigorous limitation of a specified reduction framework.
status: This remains a major missing connection among fine-grained hypotheses; see Vassilevska Williams and Williams (2018), DOI: 10.1145/3186893, and Carmosino et al. (2016).
solved_when: A proof is given that any truly subcubic general weighted APSP algorithm implies a fixed-base speedup for k-SAT on sufficiently wide formulas, or a rigorous barrier is established for a specified class of reductions attempting this connection.
why: It would unify many conditional lower bounds that currently rest on distinct, incomparable fine-grained hypotheses under a single assumption.
key_works: Vassilevska Williams and Williams (2018), DOI: 10.1145/3186893; Carmosino et al. (2016).

title: Existence of a dynamically optimal online binary search tree
subfield: Communication complexity and adaptive data structures
open: Is there an online binary search tree that, on every access sequence, is dynamically optimal — that is, costs only a constant factor more than the best offline BST execution of that sequence, up to the standard additive initialization term?
status: Open since the 1980s (Sleator and Tarjan, 1985, *Self-Adjusting Binary Search Trees*). The best known result is the tango tree of Demaine, Harmon, Iacono, and Pătraşcu (2007, *Dynamic Optimality—Almost*), which achieves \(O(\log\log n)\)-competitiveness; constant competitiveness remains unknown.
solved_when: An explicit online BST algorithm is constructed and proven constant-competitive against the optimal offline BST on every access sequence, allowing the standard additive initialization term.
why: It would establish a universally adaptive comparison-search structure — a single self-adjusting tree that automatically exploits any access-pattern locality as well as any offline algorithm could.
key_works: Sleator and Tarjan (1985), *Self-Adjusting Binary Search Trees*; Demaine, Harmon, Iacono, and Pătraşcu (2007), *Dynamic Optimality—Almost*.

bib.title: Existence of a dynamically optimal online binary search tree

title: Splay-tree deque conjecture
subfield: Communication complexity and adaptive data structures
open: Does a splay tree executing any sequence of deque operations — push and pop at either end — take total time linear in the length of the sequence, up to the cost of initialization?
status: Open since the 1980s; only very slowly growing overhead bounds are known (Pettie, 2008, *Splay Trees, Davenport–Schinzel Sequences, and the Deque Conjecture*, building on Tarjan's deque conjecture), and the exact linear target remains unresolved.
solved_when: A proof that the amortized total time for any deque operation sequence on splay trees is O(n), excluding initialization.
why: It tests whether splaying by itself achieves optimal performance for the most basic restricted access discipline, without any tailored balancing machinery.
key_works: Tarjan’s deque conjecture; Pettie (2008), *Splay Trees, Davenport–Schinzel Sequences, and the Deque Conjecture*.

title: Linear-time integer sorting for unrestricted word length
subfield: Communication complexity and adaptive data structures
open: Can \(n\) word-sized integers be sorted in linear time on a standard word RAM when the word length \(w\) is unrestricted (any \(w \ge \log n\)), with all operations charged honestly? That is, does an \(O(n)\)-time integer-sorting algorithm exist for arbitrary word length, without recourse to unbounded-cost operations?
status: The problem is decades old. For \(w = O(\log n)\), radix-based methods already give linear sorting; the unrestricted-word case is a different target and remains unresolved. The best known results are Han and Thorup (2002), *Integer Sorting in O(n√log log n) Expected Time and Linear Space*, and Han (2004), *Deterministic Sorting in O(n log log n) Time and Linear Space*.
solved_when: A deterministic or randomized algorithm sorts \(n\) integers of word length \(w \ge \log n\) in \(O(n)\) time on the word RAM, with no operation exceeding unit cost in the model.
why: It would close the gap between comparison sorting and the apparent power of integer operations, showing word-level arithmetic suffices for fully linear sorting.
key_works: Han and Thorup (2002), *Integer Sorting in O(n√log log n) Expected Time and Linear Space*; Han (2004), *Deterministic Sorting in O(n log log n) Time and Linear Space*.

title: Dynamically optimal external-memory search trees
subfield: Communication complexity and adaptive data structures
open: Is there an online external-memory search tree (B-tree) that is constant-competitive against an offline adversary in a well-defined model of block access and restructuring? In other words, can dynamic optimality be achieved in external memory, and what is the right comparison model in which to pose the question?
status: Existing models and the Belga B-tree results of Demaine, Iacono, Koumoutsos, and Langerman (*What Does Dynamic Optimality Mean in External Memory?*) provide nonconstant competitive guarantees; both the optimal algorithm and the most useful comparison model remain open questions.
solved_when: A dynamically optimal (constant-competitive) online external-memory search structure is constructed, together with a precisely defined offline block-access and restructuring model relative to which the competitive guarantee holds.
why: It would extend adaptivity guarantees from internal-memory search trees to databases and storage systems, where block transfers rather than comparisons dominate the cost of every operation.
key_works: Demaine, Iacono, Koumoutsos, and Langerman, Belga B-tree work; *What Does Dynamic Optimality Mean in External Memory?*

title: FPT versus W[1]
subfield: Parameterized algorithms, kernelization, and structural graph algorithms
open: Does the Clique problem, parameterized by the size \(k\) of the desired clique, admit an algorithm running in \(f(k) \cdot n^{O(1)}\) time — that is, fixed-parameter tractable — or is W[1]-hardness a true barrier?
status: The question has been central since the development of parameterized complexity in the 1990s; extensive W[1]-hardness theory rests on the unproved separation (Downey and Fellows (1999), *Parameterized Complexity*, DOI: 10.1007/978-1-4612-0515-9; Cygan et al. (2015), *Parameterized Algorithms*).
solved_when: Either an \(f(k)n^{O(1)}\)-time algorithm for parameterized Clique is given, or the separation FPT \(\neq\) W[1] is proved.
why: It decides whether the combinatorial explosion in this broad class of problems can always be confined to a parameter-dependent factor, underpinning the validity of W[1]-hardness as evidence of intractability.
key_works: Downey and Fellows (1999), *Parameterized Complexity*, DOI: 10.1007/978-1-4612-0515-9; Cygan et al. (2015), *Parameterized Algorithms*.

title: Polynomial kernel for Directed Feedback Vertex Set
subfield: Parameterized algorithms, kernelization, and structural graph algorithms
open: Does Directed Feedback Vertex Set admit a polynomial kernel? That is, can every instance with parameter \(k\) be reduced, in polynomial time, to an equivalent instance of size polynomial in \(k\)?
status: The problem is known to be fixed-parameter tractable, but no general polynomial kernel is known; partial progress comes from restricted graph classes and structural approaches, including Bergougnoux, Eiben, Ganian, Ordyniak, and Ramanujan (2021), *Towards a Polynomial Kernel for Directed Feedback Vertex Set*, DOI: 10.1007/s00453-020-00777-5.
solved_when: A polynomial-time algorithm outputs, for any instance with parameter \(k\), an equivalent instance whose size is bounded by a polynomial in \(k\).
why: It would turn the problem's parameterized tractability into strong, reusable preprocessing, with applications to network control such as compressing feedback-removal instances.
key_works: Bergougnoux, Eiben, Ganian, Ordyniak, and Ramanujan (2021), *Towards a Polynomial Kernel for Directed Feedback Vertex Set*, DOI: 10.1007/s00453-020-00777-5.

title: Deterministic polynomial kernel for Odd Cycle Transversal
subfield: Parameterized algorithms, kernelization, and structural graph algorithms
open: Can the randomized polynomial kernelization for Odd Cycle Transversal be made deterministic — that is, is there a polynomial-time deterministic algorithm that reduces any instance to an equivalent instance of polynomial size in the parameter?
status: Randomized algebraic compression via matroids is known (Kratsch and Wahlström, 2012, *Compression via Matroids: A Randomized Polynomial Kernel for Odd Cycle Transversal*; Cygan et al., 2015). Eliminating randomness without sacrificing polynomial size remains unresolved in the general setting.
solved_when: A deterministic algorithm produces, in polynomial time, an equivalent instance of Odd Cycle Transversal whose size is bounded polynomially in the parameter, matching the size guarantees of the known randomized kernel.
why: It would make powerful graph preprocessing reproducible and failure-free, removing the error probability that currently limits practical and theoretical use of the compression.
key_works: Kratsch and Wahlström (2012), *Compression via Matroids: A Randomized Polynomial Kernel for Odd Cycle Transversal*; Cygan et al. (2015).

title: Graph isomorphism FPT in maximum degree
subfield: Parameterized algorithms, kernelization, and structural graph algorithms
open: Can graph isomorphism be decided by an algorithm whose running time is fixed-parameter tractable in the maximum degree \(d\) — that is, \(f(d)\,n^{O(1)}\) for some computable \(f\)? In other words, can all dependence on the degree be confined to a multiplicative prefactor, leaving only polynomial dependence on the number of vertices?
status: Algorithms with \(n^{\mathrm{polylog}(d)}\)-type running time are known, but moving all degree dependence out of the exponent of \(n\) remains open. Key works include Luks (1982), *Isomorphism of Graphs of Bounded Valence Can Be Tested in Polynomial Time*, and Grohe, Neuen, and Schweitzer, *A Faster Isomorphism Test for Graphs of Small Degree* (arXiv:1802.04659, DOI: 10.1137/19M1245293).
solved_when: An algorithm testing isomorphism of \(n\)-vertex graphs of maximum degree \(d\) in time \(f(d)\,n^{O(1)}\) is given, with all degree dependence removed from the exponent of \(n\).
why: It would give substantially stronger guarantees for bounded-valence structures, such as the molecular comparisons arising in chemical informatics.
key_works: Luks (1982), *Isomorphism of Graphs of Bounded Valence Can Be Tested in Polynomial Time*; Grohe, Neuen, and Schweitzer, *A Faster Isomorphism Test for Graphs of Small Degree*, arXiv:1802.04659, DOI: 10.1137/19M1245293.

title: Single-exponential MWIS by clique-width without an expression
subfield: Parameterized algorithms, kernelization, and structural graph algorithms
open: Can Maximum Weight Independent Set be solved in single-exponential time parameterized by clique-width when no clique-width expression is given? Formally, is there an algorithm running in \(2^{O(k)}n^{O(1)}\) time on graphs of clique-width \(k\), without requiring a decomposition as part of the input?
status: The best known benchmark is a \(2^{O(k\log k)}n^{O(1)}\)-time algorithm (Oum, Sæther, and Vatshelle, *Faster Algorithms for Vertex Partitioning Problems Parameterized by Clique-Width*, arXiv:1311.0224). Obtaining and exploiting the needed structure at single-exponential cost remains open.
solved_when: An algorithm solves MWIS on graphs of clique-width \(k\) in \(2^{O(k)}n^{O(1)}\) time, taking only the graph as input.
why: It removes the common but unrealistic assumption that the decomposition an algorithm needs is handed to it for free, making single-exponential structural algorithms actually usable in practice.
key_works: Oum, Sæther, and Vatshelle, *Faster Algorithms for Vertex Partitioning Problems Parameterized by Clique-Width*, arXiv:1311.0224.
