title: Automatically discover near-optimal MWIS dynamic programs
subfield: Parameterized algorithms, kernelization, and structural graph algorithms
open: Can a near-optimal dynamic program for Maximum Weight Independent Set be discovered automatically, rather than designed by hand? Formally, given a graph \(G\), construct and execute a correct max-plus circuit for MWIS in time polynomial or quasipolynomial in \(n+\tau(G)\), where \(\tau(G)\) is the size of the smallest such circuit.
status: The problem was explicitly posed in Korhonen's open-problem program. Lower bounds on dynamic-programming circuits are known (Korhonen (2021), *Lower Bounds on Dynamic Programming for Maximum Weight Independent Set*, arXiv:2102.06901), but a general near-optimal synthesis algorithm is not.
solved_when: An algorithm exists that, given any graph \(G\), constructs and executes a correct max-plus circuit for MWIS in time polynomial or quasipolynomial in \(n+\tau(G)\).
why: It would automate the choice of a good decomposition or dynamic program, replacing ad hoc hand-designed DP schemas with automatic algorithm discovery.
key_works: Korhonen (2021), *Lower Bounds on Dynamic Programming for Maximum Weight Independent Set*, arXiv:2102.06901.

title: Small-Set Expansion Hypothesis
open: Is there a polynomial-time algorithm that distinguishes graphs containing a small poorly expanding set from graphs in which all sets of the specified small size expand almost maximally, or is the problem computationally hard?
status: The hypothesis was formulated around 2010, notably by Raghavendra and Steurer (2010) in *Graph Expansion and the Unique Games Conjecture*. Its connections to Unique Games and graph partitioning are extensive, but the standard hardness hypothesis remains unproved.
solved_when: The complexity of this gap problem is resolved, either by an algorithm distinguishing graphs with a small non-expanding set from graphs where all small sets expand almost maximally, or by a proof that no such efficient algorithm exists.
why: It would explain the observed barriers for graph partitioning, layout, and expansion optimization, and clarify the reach of the Unique Games Conjecture, to which it is closely tied.
key_works: Raghavendra and Steurer (2010), *Graph Expansion and the Unique Games Conjecture*.

title: Sliding Scale Conjecture
open: Can we construct PCPs whose soundness and answer length both slide together, achieving the full conjectured tradeoff for arbitrarily small soundness, rather than only at some fixed constant soundness?
status: The conjecture was proposed in the early 1990s, with the original formulation due to Bellare, Goldwasser, Lund, and Russell (1993); Moshkovitz (2019), *The Sliding Scale Conjecture*, surveys the problem. Many parameter regimes are known, but the full tradeoff remains open. Related questions arise in coding theory, specifically local testing at tiny error probabilities.
solved_when: A PCP construction is given that attains the conjectured sliding-scale tradeoff between soundness and answer (alphabet) length across the full range of parameters, including the regime of very small soundness.
why: It would yield sharper approximation-hardness results while keeping proof size and alphabet size under control, tightening inapproximability from qualitative to quantitative.
key_works: Bellare, Goldwasser, Lund, and Russell (1993), original formulation; Moshkovitz (2019), *The Sliding Scale Conjecture*.

title: Projection Games Conjecture
open: Can every NP language be reduced, via a reduction of near-linear size, to a projection game whose soundness is inverse-polynomial and whose alphabet size is polynomial in the inverse soundness? Equivalently, the conjecture asks for near-linear-size PCP reductions to label cover that simultaneously achieve inverse-polynomial soundness error with only polynomially large alphabets.
status: Open in the full parameter regime. Bafna–Minzer–Vyas's 2025 HDX-based PCP work (arXiv:2407.12762, DOI: 10.1145/3717823.3718197) achieves strong small-constant-soundness results, which do not automatically yield the full inverse-polynomial target; the conjecture was formulated by Moshkovitz (2015), *The Projection Games Conjecture and the NP-Hardness of ln n-Approximating Set-Cover*.
solved_when: A construction of near-linear-size reductions to projection games is given that achieves inverse-polynomial soundness with alphabet size polynomial in the inverse soundness.
why: It would sharpen hardness results for set cover and for the large family of label-cover-based reductions that underpin many inapproximability theorems.
key_works: Moshkovitz (2015), *The Projection Games Conjecture and the NP-Hardness of ln n-Approximating Set-Cover*; Bafna, Minzer, and Vyas, arXiv:2407.12762, DOI: 10.1145/3717823.3718197.

title: A 4/3 approximation for metric TSP
open: Is there a polynomial-time algorithm achieving a 4/3-approximation for the symmetric metric Traveling Salesperson Problem? Formally, find a polynomial-time algorithm whose tour cost is at most 4/3 times the optimal tour cost on any metric instance.
status: Christofides' 3/2 barrier was slightly beaten by Karlin–Klein–Oveis Gharan; the much stronger 4/3 target remains open. See also Traub and Vygen (2024), *Approximation Algorithms for Traveling Salesman Problems*, DOI: 10.1017/9781009445436.
solved_when: A polynomial-time algorithm is given, with proof, that on every symmetric metric TSP instance outputs a tour of cost at most \(4/3 \cdot \mathrm{OPT}\).
why: It would substantially improve the central guarantee for metric routing, directly impacting operations research settings such as vehicle routing under metric costs.
key_works: Christofides (1976); Karlin, Klein, and Oveis Gharan, *A (Slightly) Improved Approximation Algorithm for Metric TSP*; Traub and Vygen (2024), *Approximation Algorithms for Traveling Salesman Problems*, DOI: 10.1017/9781009445436.

title: A factor-two approximation for asymmetric TSP
open: Is there a polynomial-time algorithm that always produces a tour of cost at most twice the optimum for the asymmetric traveling salesman problem on general metrics? Formally: a factor-2 approximation for general metric ATSP.
status: The existence of a constant-factor approximation is settled — Svensson, Tarnawski, and Végh (2018), *A Constant-Factor Approximation Algorithm for the Asymmetric Traveling Salesman Problem* — but factor two remains open. Traub and Vygen's verified general benchmark is \(22+\varepsilon\), not \(2+\varepsilon\).
solved_when: A polynomial-time algorithm for general metric ATSP is exhibited and proved to return tours of cost at most \(2\cdot\mathrm{OPT}\) (or \(2+\varepsilon\) times OPT).
why: It would sharply improve routing on networks with asymmetric travel costs, such as directed transportation and logistics networks.
key_works: Svensson, Tarnawski, and Végh (2018), *A Constant-Factor Approximation Algorithm for the Asymmetric Traveling Salesman Problem*; Traub and Vygen, *An Improved Approximation Algorithm for ATSP*, arXiv:1912.00670.

title: A 3/2 approximation for Steiner Forest
open: Can minimum-cost Steiner Forest be approximated within a factor of 3/2 in polynomial time? Formally, is there a polynomial-time algorithm whose output forest cost is at most 3/2 times the optimum?
status: The longstanding factor-two barrier was broken in 2025 (Ahmadi et al., 2025, better-than-two Steiner Forest work); the stronger 3/2 target remains open. Gupta and Traub (2026), *Steiner Forest: A Simplified Better-Than-2 Approximation* (arXiv:2511.18460, DOI: 10.1145/3798129.3800808), simplifies the better-than-two approximation.
solved_when: A polynomial-time algorithm for Steiner Forest achieving an approximation ratio of 3/2 (or better) is given and proved correct.
why: It would improve multi-pair network connection costs, allowing many demand pairs to be connected while sharing infrastructure.
key_works: Ahmadi et al. (2025), better-than-two Steiner Forest work; Gupta and Traub (2026), *Steiner Forest: A Simplified Better-Than-2 Approximation*, arXiv:2511.18460, DOI: 10.1145/3798129.3800808.

title: A 4/3 approximation for Steiner Tree
open: Can the Steiner Tree problem on general undirected graphs be approximated within a factor of 4/3 in polynomial time, or does some clearly stated hardness assumption forbid this ratio?
status: The best known benchmark is a \(\ln 4 + \varepsilon\) approximation, due to Byrka, Grandoni, Rothvoß, and Sanità (2013, *Steiner Tree Approximation via Iterative Randomized Rounding*; see also Williamson and Shmoys, 2011, *The Design of Approximation Algorithms*), which comes close to but does not reach 4/3; known hardness results do not close the gap.
solved_when: A polynomial-time algorithm achieving approximation ratio 4/3 for general undirected Steiner Tree is given, or a hardness result under an explicit assumption rules out a 4/3-approximation.
why: Steiner Tree is a basic building block of infrastructure and interconnection optimization, including VLSI interconnection length minimization; closing the 4/3 gap directly improves these applications.
key_works: Byrka, Grandoni, Rothvoß, and Sanità (2013), *Steiner Tree Approximation via Iterative Randomized Rounding*; Williamson and Shmoys (2011), *The Design of Approximation Algorithms*.

title: Vertex Cover below factor two
open: Can general Vertex Cover be approximated in polynomial time strictly better than factor two? Formally, is there a polynomial-time (2−ε)-approximation for some fixed ε > 0, or can hardness below two be derived from an assumption weaker than the Unique Games Conjecture?
status: The elementary factor-two algorithm remains a central benchmark. UGC implies hardness below two, but UGC is unresolved.
solved_when: Either a polynomial-time (2−ε)-approximation for Vertex Cover is given for some fixed ε > 0, or impossibility of such an approximation is proved under an assumption strictly weaker than UGC.
why: It would settle one of the clearest gaps between known approximation algorithms and unconditional hardness for a central problem.
key_works: Dinur and Safra (2005), *On the Hardness of Approximating Minimum Vertex Cover*; Khot and Regev (2008), *Vertex Cover Might Be Hard to Approximate to Within 2−ε*.

title: Constant-factor Directed Feedback Vertex Set
open: Does the general Directed Feedback Vertex Set problem admit a polynomial-time approximation algorithm with a constant approximation factor? Formally, is there a polynomial-time algorithm that always returns a feedback vertex set of size at most C·OPT for some absolute constant C?
status: Polylogarithmic approximation algorithms are known; a constant factor remains unresolved. Key works include Even, Naor, Schieber, and Sudan (1998), *Approximating Minimum Feedback Sets and Multicuts in Directed Graphs*, and Chen et al.'s exact parameterized work.
solved_when: A polynomial-time algorithm achieves a constant-factor approximation for Directed Feedback Vertex Set on general directed graphs.
why: It would yield principled, provably near-optimal cycle elimination in directed dependency networks, with applications such as feedback intervention in systems biology and dependency-cycle removal in database design.
key_works: Even, Naor, Schieber, and Sudan (1998), *Approximating Minimum Feedback Sets and Multicuts in Directed Graphs*; Chen et al.’s exact parameterized work.

title: Polynomial-time polylogarithmic Directed Steiner Tree
open: Can Directed Steiner Tree be approximated within a factor polylogarithmic in the number of terminals by a polynomial-time algorithm? Formally, is there a poly(n)-time algorithm whose approximation ratio is polylog(k), where k is the number of terminals?
status: Quasipolynomial-time algorithms achieve substantially better approximation ratios than known polynomial-time algorithms, but removing the quasipolynomial running time remains a major gap. Key works include Charikar et al. (1999), *Approximation Algorithms for Directed Steiner Problems*, and Chekuri and Pál (2005), recursive-greedy directed network design.
solved_when: A polynomial-time algorithm for Directed Steiner Tree achieves an approximation ratio polylogarithmic in the number of terminals.
why: It would improve directed multicast and the design of reachability infrastructure in communication networks.
key_works: Charikar et al. (1999), *Approximation Algorithms for Directed Steiner Problems*; Chekuri and Pál (2005), recursive-greedy directed network design.

title: Constant-factor general Sparsest Cut
open: Is there a polynomial-time algorithm that approximates general-demand Sparsest Cut within a constant factor, or is there a fundamental obstruction ruling this out?
status: Semidefinite methods provide nonconstant guarantees; constant-factor approximability remains tied to deep metric-embedding questions, notably embedding negative-type metrics into \(L_1\). Key works: Arora, Rao, and Vazirani (2009), *Expander Flows, Geometric Embeddings and Graph Partitioning*; Arora, Lee, and Naor (2008), *Euclidean Distortion and the Sparsest Cut*.
solved_when: A polynomial-time algorithm achieving a constant-factor approximation for general-demand Sparsest Cut is given, or a matching hardness/obstruction result is proved showing no such algorithm exists.
why: A solution would improve graph partitioning and divide-and-conquer algorithms across many domains; an obstruction would clarify the limits of semidefinite and metric-embedding techniques.
key_works: Arora, Rao, and Vazirani (2009), *Expander Flows, Geometric Embeddings and Graph Partitioning*; Arora, Lee, and Naor (2008), *Euclidean Distortion and the Sparsest Cut*.

title: Improve the Densest-k-Subgraph exponent
open: Can Densest k-Subgraph be approximated within a factor \(n^{1/4-\delta}\) in polynomial time, for some fixed \(\delta>0\)? In other words, is there a polynomial-time algorithm beating the \(n^{1/4}\)-approximation barrier by a fixed power of \(n\)?
status: The \(n^{1/4+\varepsilon}\)-type benchmark has resisted a fixed exponent improvement; the best known result is the \(O(n^{1/4})\)-approximation of Bhaskara, Charikar, Chlamtac, Feige, and Vijayaraghavan (2010), *Detecting High Log-Densities: An O(n^{1/4}) Approximation for Densest k-Subgraph*. Hardness results remain far from a complete characterization.
solved_when: A polynomial-time algorithm achieves an \(n^{1/4-\delta}\)-approximation for Densest k-Subgraph for some fixed constant \(\delta>0\).
why: It would advance dense-community discovery and push approximation techniques beyond standard LP/SDP templates, for a problem that has resisted them.
key_works: Bhaskara, Charikar, Chlamtac, Feige, and Vijayaraghavan (2010), *Detecting High Log-Densities: An O(n^{1/4}) Approximation for Densest k-Subgraph*.

title: Constant-coloring of 3-colorable graphs
open: Given a graph promised to be 3-colorable, can we find, in polynomial time, a proper coloring that uses only some fixed constant number of colors — a bound independent of the graph's size?
status: Open for decades. Known algorithms use a number of colors growing with \(n\), notably the line of work from Wigderson (1983), *Improving the Performance Guarantee for Approximate Graph Coloring*, and Karger, Motwani, and Sudan (1998), *Approximate Graph Coloring by Semidefinite Programming*. Hardness results rule out various restricted constant targets, but they do not settle every constant.
solved_when: A polynomial-time algorithm is exhibited that, on every 3-colorable graph on \(n\) vertices, outputs a proper coloring with at most \(C\) colors for a constant \(C\) independent of \(n\).
why: It would close a conspicuous gap between the guaranteed existence of a tiny (3-color) coloring and our ability to efficiently find any bounded coloring.
key_works: Wigderson (1983), *Improving the Performance Guarantee for Approximate Graph Coloring*; Karger, Motwani, and Sudan (1998), *Approximate Graph Coloring by Semidefinite Programming*.

title: Constant approximation for unrestricted Santa Claus allocation
open: Can indivisible items with arbitrary nonnegative agent-item values be allocated so that the minimum agent utility is within a universal constant factor of the optimal max-min value? Formally, is there a constant-factor approximation algorithm for the unrestricted Santa Claus (max-min fair allocation) problem?
status: Constant-factor results exist only for restricted variants of the problem, and these do not settle the unrestricted case. Key works include Bansal and Sviridenko (2006), *The Santa Claus Problem*, and Asadpur and Saberi (2010), *An Approximation Algorithm for Max-Min Fair Allocation of Indivisible Goods*.
solved_when: A polynomial-time algorithm produces an allocation whose minimum agent utility is at least a universal constant times the optimum, for arbitrary nonnegative valuations.
why: It would give strong worst-case guarantees for max-min resource allocation, replacing the variant-specific results currently available with a guarantee that holds whenever values are unrestricted.
key_works: Bansal and Sviridenko (2006), *The Santa Claus Problem*; Asadpour and Saberi (2010), *An Approximation Algorithm for Max-Min Fair Allocation of Indivisible Goods*.

bib.title: Constant approximation for unrestricted Santa Claus allocation

title: Close the unrelated-machine makespan gap
open: Can the general unrelated-machine makespan scheduling problem be approximated strictly better than a factor of two? The goal is a constant-factor improvement over the classic 2-approximation, with \(3/2\) as the natural ultimate target suggested by hardness.
status: The classic approximation and hardness bounds of Lenstra, Shmoys, and Tardos (1990), *Approximation Algorithms for Scheduling Unrelated Parallel Machines*, leave a persistent gap between the 2-approximation and the hardness side. Stronger results exist for restricted instances, but they do not solve the general assignment model.
solved_when: A polynomial-time algorithm for unrelated-machine scheduling achieving an approximation ratio strictly below 2 for the makespan objective; achieving \(3/2\) would close the gap entirely.
why: Each job may have a different processing time on every machine, so any improvement directly yields better placement decisions in heterogeneous settings such as cloud computing and manufacturing.
key_works: Lenstra, Shmoys, and Tardos (1990), *Approximation Algorithms for Scheduling Unrelated Parallel Machines*.

title: Constant additive error for Bin Packing
open: Is there a polynomial-time algorithm that packs every Bin Packing instance into at most OPT + O(1) bins — an additive constant, independent of the instance? Formally, the goal is a constant C such that the algorithm always uses at most OPT + C bins.
status: Logarithmic additive-gap algorithms are known, from Karmarkar and Karp (1982), *An Efficient Approximation Scheme for the One-Dimensional Bin-Packing Problem*, through Hoberg and Rothvoß (2017), *A Logarithmic Additive Integrality Gap for Bin Packing*; a universal constant additive gap remains open.
solved_when: A polynomial-time algorithm exists with an additive gap bounded by a universal constant, i.e., at most OPT + C bins for some absolute C on every instance.
why: It would nearly eliminate the residual loss in packing efficiency without requiring exact optimization, directly improving container utilization in logistics.
key_works: Karmarkar and Karp (1982), *An Efficient Approximation Scheme for the One-Dimensional Bin-Packing Problem*; Hoberg and Rothvoß (2017), *A Logarithmic Additive Integrality Gap for Bin Packing*.

title: Polylogarithmic-overhead exact maximum flow
subfield: Graph algorithms, parallelism, and dynamic computation
open: Can exact maximum flow with integral capacities bounded by \(U\) be computed with only a polylogarithmic factor of overhead, i.e., in \(m\,\mathrm{polylog}(nU)\) time on polynomially encoded inputs? Formally, the goal is an exact algorithm matching near-linear time up to a fixed polylogarithmic factor rather than an \(o(1)\) exponent.
status: Almost-linear \(m^{1+o(1)}\) time algorithms are a major breakthrough, represented by Chen, Kyng, Liu, Peng, Probst Gutenberg, and Sachdeva (2022), *Maximum Flow and Minimum-Cost Flow in Almost-Linear Time*, arXiv:2203.00671, but they do not automatically yield a fixed polylogarithmic overhead.
solved_when: An algorithm computes the exact maximum flow in \(m\,\mathrm{polylog}(nU)\) time for graphs with integral capacities bounded by \(U\) and polynomial encoding.
why: It would convert asymptotic near-linearity into a stronger, quantitatively controlled primitive, giving precise overhead bounds instead of hidden \(m^{o(1)}\) factors.
key_works: Chen, Kyng, Liu, Peng, Probst Gutenberg, and Sachdeva (2022), *Maximum Flow and Minimum-Cost Flow in Almost-Linear Time*, arXiv:2203.00671.

title: Deterministic NC for general perfect matching
subfield: Graph algorithms, parallelism, and dynamic computation
open: Is there a deterministic NC algorithm that, given an arbitrary graph, finds a perfect matching or correctly reports that none exists? That is, can this be done in deterministic polylogarithmic parallel time on polynomially many processors?
status: Randomized NC for matching is classical, via Mulmuley, Vazirani, and Vazirani (1987), *Matching Is as Easy as Matrix Inversion*. Svensson and Tarnawski (2017), *The Matching Problem in General Graphs Is in Quasi-NC*, gave a deterministic quasi-NC algorithm. Full deterministic NC remains unresolved.
solved_when: A deterministic parallel algorithm for perfect matching in general graphs runs in polylogarithmic time using polynomially many processors, with a correct "no perfect matching" output when none exists.
why: It would eliminate randomness from a foundational parallel combinatorial task, giving derandomized NC algorithms where currently only randomized ones are known.
key_works: Mulmuley, Vazirani, and Vazirani (1987), *Matching Is as Easy as Matrix Inversion*; Svensson and Tarnawski (2017), *The Matching Problem in General Graphs Is in Quasi-NC*.

title: Deterministic polynomial-time Exact Matching
subfield: Graph algorithms, parallelism, and dynamic computation
open: Given a graph whose edges are colored red or blue and an integer \(q\), is there a perfect matching using exactly \(q\) red edges — and can we decide this deterministically in polynomial time? Formally, the question asks for a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for this constrained matching problem.
status: Randomized polynomial-time algorithms are known, but no deterministic polynomial-time algorithm is known in general; the deterministic case remains open. Key works include Papadimitriou and Yannakakis (1982), *The Complexity of Restricted Spanning Tree Problems*, and Mulmuley, Vazirani, and Vazirani (1987).
solved_when: A deterministic polynomial-time algorithm decides, for any red/blue edge-colored graph and integer \(q\), whether some perfect matching contains exactly \(q\) red edges.
why: It probes the power of algebraic randomization: a natural constrained matching problem where randomization is known to help, and resolving it would clarify whether that randomness is essential.
key_works: Papadimitriou and Yannakakis (1982), *The Complexity of Restricted Spanning Tree Problems*; Mulmuley, Vazirani, and Vazirani (1987).

title: Work-efficient polylog-depth directed reachability
subfield: Graph algorithms, parallelism, and dynamic computation
open: Can directed reachability be solved using near-linear total work — \(m\,\mathrm{polylog}(n)\) — while keeping the parallel depth polylogarithmic in \(n\)? In other words, can we achieve both efficiency targets simultaneously?
status: Polylogarithmic-depth algorithms exist but incur excessive work, while nearly work-efficient algorithms retain substantial depth; achieving both targets simultaneously remains open (see Ullman and Yannakakis, 1991; Spencer, 1997).
solved_when: A parallel algorithm for directed reachability is exhibited with total work \(m\,\mathrm{polylog}(n)\) and depth \(\mathrm{polylog}(n)\), with matching analysis.
why: It would make parallelism genuinely useful for large sparse directed graphs, rather than trading excessive work for shallow depth — with downstream relevance to parallel state-space exploration in formal verification.
key_works: Ullman and Yannakakis (1991), *High-Probability Parallel Transitive-Closure Algorithms*; Spencer (1997), *Time–Work Tradeoffs for Parallel Algorithms*.

title: Sublogarithmic dynamic forest orientation
subfield: Graph algorithms, parallelism, and dynamic computation
open: Can we maintain an explicit orientation of a forest that undergoes edge insertions and deletions so that every vertex keeps constant out-degree and each update is processed in \(o(\log n)\) amortized time?
status: Logarithmic-amortized approaches are established, notably via Brodal and Fagerberg (1999), *Dynamic Representations of Sparse Graphs*; the sublogarithmic target remains open on Korhodon's 2026 problem list (*Open Problems*).
solved_when: A data structure is given that, under arbitrary updates to a dynamic forest, maintains an orientation with constant maximum out-degree and answers each update in \(o(\log n)\) amortized time, with a matching proof of correctness.
why: This is a basic dynamic primitive whose solution would unlock faster dynamic algorithms for broader classes of sparse graphs.
key_works: Brodal and Fagerberg (1999), *Dynamic Representations of Sparse Graphs*; Korhonen, *Open Problems*.

title: Deterministic linear-time comparison MST
subfield: Graph algorithms, parallelism, and dynamic computation
open: Can a minimum spanning tree be computed deterministically in linear time in the comparison model? Formally, is there a deterministic comparison-based algorithm running in \(O(m+n)\) time?
status: Randomized linear-time algorithms are known. Chazelle (2000) gives an inverse-Ackermann overhead, and Pettie and Ramachandran (2002) achieve decision-tree optimality without resolving whether that optimum is linear.
solved_when: A deterministic comparison-model algorithm for minimum spanning trees is proved to run in \(O(m+n)\) time.
why: It would settle the exact comparison complexity of a basic optimization problem.
key_works: Chazelle (2000), *A Minimum Spanning Tree Algorithm with Inverse-Ackermann Type Complexity*; Pettie and Ramachandran (2002), *An Optimal Minimum Spanning Tree Algorithm*.

title: Deterministic k-server conjecture
open: Is there a deterministic online algorithm for the k-server problem that achieves a competitive ratio of exactly k on every metric space? Formally, does a deterministic k-competitive k-server algorithm exist for all metric spaces?
status: Proposed in 1988. The work-function algorithm gives the classical \(2k-1\) general guarantee, and the target of \(k\) remains open. Key works: Manasse, McGeoch, and Sleator (1990), *Competitive Algorithms for Server Problems*; Koutsoupias and Papadimitriou (1995), *On the k-Server Conjecture*.
solved_when: A deterministic algorithm is given, with proof, that is k-competitive for the k-server problem on every metric space.
why: It would resolve a central model unifying paging, movement, and online service, with direct bearing on online service dispatch and demand-responsive fleets.
key_works: Manasse, McGeoch, and Sleator (1990), *Competitive Algorithms for Server Problems*; Koutsoupias and Papadimitriou (1995), *On the k-Server Conjecture*.

title: Polylogarithmic randomized k-server competitiveness
open: Is there a randomized online algorithm for the k-server problem that is polylog(k)-competitive on every metric space, with bounds independent of the metric's size or aspect ratio? Formally, the goal is a randomized algorithm achieving competitive ratio polylog(k) on arbitrary metrics.
status: The older O(log k) conjecture is false: Bubeck–Coester–Rabani prove an Ω(log² k) lower bound (arXiv:2211.05753, *The Randomized k-Server Conjecture Is False!*, 2023). A previously claimed general polylogarithmic upper-bound route was withdrawn (Lee's 2021 erratum); the broader polylogarithmic target remains open.
solved_when: A randomized algorithm is exhibited whose competitive ratio is polylog(k) on every metric, with no dependence on the number of points or the aspect ratio of the metric.
why: It would identify the true power of randomization for online movement problems, resolving how much randomization helps beyond the Ω(log² k) barrier.
key_works: Bubeck, Coester, and Rabani (2023), *The Randomized k-Server Conjecture Is False!*, arXiv:2211.05753; Lee’s 2021 erratum.

title: An FPRAS for #BIS
subfield: Approximate counting, sampling, and average-case complexity
open: Does there exist a fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme for counting independent sets in bipartite graphs? More precisely, is #BIS — the problem of counting independent sets in a bipartite graph — efficiently approximable in the FPRAS sense, or is it intrinsically hard?
status: A central open approximate-counting problem since the 1990s–2000s. It organizes a large family of problems not known to be either efficiently approximable or as hard as #SAT; key works include Dyer, Goldberg, Greenhill, and Jerrum (2004), *The Relative Complexity of Approximate Counting Problems*, DOI: 10.1007/S00453-003-1073-Y, and Curticapean et al., arXiv:1702.05543. It also connects to statistical mechanics via hard-core partition functions.
solved_when: An FPRAS for #BIS is given, or the problem is shown to be as hard as #SAT to approximate, thereby closing the intermediate classification.
why: #BIS organizes a large family of approximate-counting problems between efficient approximability and #SAT-hardness; settling it would classify this major intermediate region of approximate counting.
key_works: Dyer, Goldberg, Greenhill, and Jerrum (2004), *The Relative Complexity of Approximate Counting Problems*, DOI: 10.1007/S00453-003-1073-Y; Curticapean et al., arXiv:1702.05543.

title: Deterministic FPTAS for the nonnegative permanent
subfield: Approximate counting, sampling, and average-case complexity
open: Can the permanent of a nonnegative matrix be approximated deterministically within relative error \(\varepsilon\) in time polynomial in the input size and \(1/\varepsilon\) — that is, does a deterministic FPTAS exist for the nonnegative permanent?
status: Jerrum, Sinclair, and Vigoda (2004), *A Polynomial-Time Approximation Algorithm for the Permanent of a Matrix with Nonnegative Entries*, supplied a randomized approximation scheme. A comparable deterministic approximation remains open.
solved_when: A deterministic algorithm approximates the permanent of any nonnegative matrix within relative error \(\varepsilon\) in time polynomial in the input size and \(1/\varepsilon\).
why: It would derandomize a landmark counting algorithm, removing the randomness from one of the most celebrated results in approximate counting.
key_works: Jerrum, Sinclair, and Vigoda (2004), *A Polynomial-Time Approximation Algorithm for the Permanent of a Matrix with Nonnegative Entries*.

title: Exact random 3-SAT threshold
subfield: Approximate counting, sampling, and average-case complexity
open: What is the exact limiting satisfiability threshold for random 3-SAT? In particular, is the statistical-physics prediction near 4.267 clauses per variable the true threshold, and can this be proven rigorously?
status: Threshold results for sufficiently large clause width do not settle width three. The exact 3-SAT constant remains unresolved. Key works include Mézard, Parisi, and Zecchina (2002), *Analytic and Algorithmic Solution of Random Satisfiability Problems*, and Ding, Sly, and Sun, *Proof of the Satisfiability Conjecture for Large k* (arXiv:1411.0650).
solved_when: A theorem identifies the precise constant limiting the satisfiability threshold density for random 3-SAT at clause-to-variable ratio near 4.267, confirming or correcting the predicted value.
why: It serves as a benchmark for understanding random constraint systems and phase transitions, and would settle the most important case left open by large-k results.
key_works: Mézard, Parisi, and Zecchina (2002), *Analytic and Algorithmic Solution of Random Satisfiability Problems*; Ding, Sly, and Sun, *Proof of the Satisfiability Conjecture for Large k*, arXiv:1411.0650.

title: Polynomial-time refutation of linear-density random 3-SAT
subfield: Approximate counting, sampling, and average-case complexity
open: Is there a constant \(C\) such that a random 3-CNF formula with \(Cn\) clauses can be certified unsatisfiable in polynomial time, with high probability over the draw of the formula? In other words, can we efficiently refute linear-density random 3-SAT for some sufficiently large fixed constant \(C\)?
status: Efficient refutation is known at much larger densities; statistical unsatisfiability alone does not provide an efficient certificate. Key works: Feige (2002), *Relations Between Average Case Complexity and Approximation Complexity*; Allen, O'Donnell, and Witmer (2015), *How to Refute a Random CSP*, arXiv:1505.04383.
solved_when: For some fixed sufficiently large constant \(C\), an algorithm certifies unsatisfiability of a random 3-CNF with \(Cn\) clauses in polynomial time, succeeding with high probability.
why: It separates recognizing typical impossibility from merely proving that it is overwhelmingly likely, i.e., turning statistical knowledge of unsatisfiability into an efficiently checkable certificate.
key_works: Feige (2002), *Relations Between Average Case Complexity and Approximation Complexity*; Allen, O’Donnell, and Witmer (2015), *How to Refute a Random CSP*, arXiv:1505.04383.

title: Polynomial-time planted-clique recovery below square root
subfield: Approximate counting, sampling, and average-case complexity
open: Can a clique of size \(n^{1/2-\varepsilon}\) planted in \(G(n,1/2)\) be recovered in polynomial time for some fixed \(\varepsilon>0\)? In other words, is there a polynomial-time algorithm that finds a planted clique noticeably smaller than the square-root barrier?
status: The square-root scale is the central algorithmic benchmark. Lower bounds for restricted methods provide evidence, not an unconditional polynomial-time barrier. Key works include Alon, Krivelevich, and Sudakov (1998), *Finding a Large Hidden Clique in a Random Graph*, and Barak et al. (2016), *A Nearly Tight Sum-of-Squares Lower Bound for the Planted Clique Problem*, arXiv:1604.03084.
solved_when: A polynomial-time algorithm exists that, for some fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), recovers a planted clique of size \(n^{1/2-\varepsilon}\) in \(G(n,1/2)\).
why: The problem is a canonical model of statistical–computational gaps, so a resolution either way would sharpen our understanding of when inference is information-theoretically possible but computationally infeasible.
key_works: Alon, Krivelevich, and Sudakov (1998), *Finding a Large Hidden Clique in a Random Graph*; Barak et al. (2016), *A Nearly Tight Sum-of-Squares Lower Bound for the Planted Clique Problem*, arXiv:1604.03084.

title: Tight bounds on planar k-sets
open: What is the maximum number of k-sets an n-point set in the plane can determine? A complete asymptotic answer should settle the halving-line regime as well.
status: A classical problem with a substantial upper–lower gap: Dey's O(nk^{1/3}) upper bound remains a key benchmark against much smaller known lower bounds. Key works include Dey (1998), *Improved Bounds on Planar k-Sets and Related Problems*; Tóth (2000), *Point Sets with Many k-Sets*; and TOPP Problem 7.
solved_when: The maximum number of k-sets is determined up to constant factors, closing the gap between the best upper and lower bounds.
why: The k-set count governs the complexity of levels in arrangements of lines and thereby the running time of many geometric algorithms.
key_works: Dey (1998), *Improved Bounds on Planar k-Sets and Related Problems*; Tóth (2000), *Point Sets with Many k-Sets*; TOPP Problem 7.

title: Simultaneously small and balanced planar BSPs
open: Can every set of \(n\) disjoint line segments in the plane admit a binary space partition that is simultaneously near-optimal in size and balanced in height — concretely, achieving \(O(n\log n/\log\log n)\) size together with \(O(\log n)\) height?
status: BSPs of optimal size \(O(n\log n/\log\log n)\) are known when the balancing requirement is dropped (Tóth's optimal-size work, building on Paterson and Yao 1990, *Efficient Binary Space Partitions for Hidden-Surface Removal and Solid Modeling*; see TOPP Problem 14). Achieving the size and height targets simultaneously remains open.
solved_when: A construction is given for disjoint planar line segments producing BSPs of size \(O(n\log n/\log\log n)\) and height \(O(\log n)\) at the same time, ideally with a matching lower bound showing both are optimal.
why: Small partitions keep the structure memory-efficient, while balanced height guarantees fast query descent; graphics applications such as visibility acceleration need both at once.
key_works: Paterson and Yao (1990), *Efficient Binary Space Partitions for Hidden-Surface Removal and Solid Modeling*; Tóth’s optimal-size work; TOPP Problem 14.

title: Optimal output-sensitive high-dimensional convex hulls
open: For fixed dimension, can we compute the convex hull of \(n\) points in \(O(n\log f + f)\) time, where \(f\) is the number of facets in the output? That is, an algorithm achieving the optimal output-sensitive bound for arbitrary fixed dimension.
status: Optimal bounds are known in low dimensions, but higher-dimensional output sensitivity retains gaps. Key references: Chan (1996), *Output-Sensitive Results on Convex Hulls, Extreme Points, and Related Problems*; TOPP Problem 15.
solved_when: An algorithm computes the convex hull in \(O(n\log f + f)\) time for fixed dimension, with \(f\) the number of output facets.
why: It avoids paying for worst-case hull complexity when the actual output is small, which matters since hull size can dominate running time in high dimension.
key_works: Chan (1996), *Output-Sensitive Results on Convex Hulls, Extreme Points, and Related Problems*; TOPP Problem 15.

title: Logarithmic dynamic planar nearest neighbors
open: Can we maintain a set of planar points under insertions and deletions so that exact Euclidean nearest-neighbor queries, updates, or both run in logarithmic time per operation? Formally, achieve \(O(\log n)\) amortized cost per operation with near-linear space, improving known polylogarithmic dynamic bounds.
status: Polylogarithmic dynamic bounds are known (Chan, 2006, *A Dynamic Data Structure for 3-D Convex Hulls and 2-D Nearest Neighbor Queries*; see also TOPP Problem 63). The sharper logarithmic target remains open; it is not the old, already solved question of obtaining any polylogarithmic bound.
solved_when: A dynamic data structure supporting exact Euclidean nearest-neighbor queries under point insertions and deletions with \(O(\log n)\) amortized operation costs and near-linear space exists, with a proof of correctness and the stated bounds.
why: It would match static-query efficiency while supporting continuous updates, which matters for applications such as dynamic proximity queries in robotics.
key_works: Chan (2006), *A Dynamic Data Structure for 3-D Convex Hulls and 2-D Nearest Neighbor Queries*; TOPP Problem 63.

title: Linear-space logarithmic-query 3D point location
open: Can a general three-dimensional polyhedral subdivision of total complexity \(n\) be preprocessed into a data structure of linear space that answers point-location queries in logarithmic time? Formally, achieve \(O(n)\) space with \(O(\log n)\)-time queries.
status: The planar analogue is well understood, but the general 3D linear-space target remains open; the problem is surveyed in Snoeyink (1997), *Point Location*, and listed as TOPP Problem 13.
solved_when: A preprocessing scheme for any 3D polyhedral subdivision of complexity \(n\) using \(O(n)\) space and answering point-location queries in \(O(\log n)\) time, or a proof that no such scheme exists.
why: It would enable fast navigation and queries in volumetric geometric models, such as volumetric meshes arising in scientific visualization.
key_works: Snoeyink (1997), *Point Location*; TOPP Problem 13.

title: Dürer’s edge-unfolding conjecture
open: Can every convex polyhedron be cut along its edges so that the surface unfolds into a single flat polygon with no overlap? Equivalently, prove the edge-unfolding conjecture for all convex polyhedra, or produce a convex polyhedron admitting no nonoverlapping edge net.
status: Rooted in Dürer's 1525 work *Underweysung der Messung*; the modern universal conjecture, posed in the era of Shephard (1975), *Convex Polytopes with Convex Nets*, remains open despite many special classes having been settled. It appears as TOPP Problem 9.
solved_when: Either a proof that every convex polyhedron has a nonoverlapping edge unfolding, or an explicit convex polyhedron for which no such unfolding exists.
why: A resolution either way would clarify the fundamental link between polyhedral geometry and single-sheet fabrication, with direct consequences for manufacturing and foldable structures.
key_works: Dürer (1525), *Underweysung der Messung*; Shephard (1975), *Convex Polytopes with Convex Nets*; TOPP Problem 9.

title: Universal zipper unfolding of convex polyhedra
open: Does every convex polyhedron have a nonoverlapping unfolding produced by cutting along a single suitable path, where the path may cross faces?
status: Special cases and variants are understood, but the general path-cut question remains open; edge-only versions are distinct and must not be conflated with it. See Demaine, Demaine, Lubiw, Arlo Shallit, and Jonah Shallit (2010), *Zipper Unfoldings of Polyhedral Complexes*, and TOPP Problem 77.
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) establishing whether every convex polyhedron admits a nonoverlapping single-path unfolding with face-crossing cuts permitted.
why: A positive answer would let physical objects be fabricated or deployed from one continuous seam, a key requirement in origami-inspired engineering and deployable structures.
key_works: Demaine, Demaine, Lubiw, Arlo Shallit, and Jonah Shallit (2010), *Zipper Unfoldings of Polyhedral Complexes*; TOPP Problem 77.

title: Subquadratic universal point sets for planar graphs
open: Does every $n$-vertex planar graph admit a crossing-free straight-line drawing on some universal point set of subquadratic size? Formally, construct $o(n^2)$ points in the plane such that every $n$-vertex planar graph has a crossing-free straight-line drawing using a subset of those points.
status: Quadratic-size constructions are known, as are superlinear lower bounds; the asymptotic gap between them remains large.
solved_when: An explicit construction of $o(n^2)$ points is given that supports a crossing-free straight-line drawing of every $n$-vertex planar graph, or a matching quadratic lower bound closes the question negatively.
why: A solution would reveal how much geometric flexibility universal planar drawings actually require, separating the known quadratic upper bound from the superlinear lower bound.
key_works: Chrobak and Karloff (1989), *A Lower Bound on the Size of Universal Sets for Planar Graphs*; de Fraysseix, Pach, and Pollack (1990); TOPP Problem 45.

title: Sorting X + Y in quadratic time
open: Can the sorted list of all \(n^2\) pairwise sums \(x_i+y_j\) be produced in \(O(n^2)\) total time on a real RAM? That is, we seek a uniform quadratic-time algorithm that actually outputs the sums in order, not merely a comparison-count bound.
status: Quadratic comparison bounds are known — Fredman (1976), *How Good Is the Information Theory Bound in Sorting?*, and Lambert (1992), *Sorting Sums … in O(n²) Comparisons* (see also TOPP Problem 41) — but they do not automatically produce a uniform quadratic-time algorithm.
solved_when: An algorithm running in \(O(n^2)\) time on the real-RAM model correctly sorts all \(n^2\) sums \(x_i+y_j\).
why: It separates comparison information from the cost of finding and organizing those comparisons: knowing quadratic comparisons suffice does not by itself yield a quadratic-time procedure, and closing this gap would clarify the true computational cost of ordering structured sumsets.
key_works: Fredman (1976), *How Good Is the Information Theory Bound in Sorting?*; Lambert (1992), *Sorting Sums … in O(n²) Comparisons*; TOPP Problem 41.

title: Sum-of-square-roots comparison in NP
open: Given a sum of square roots of integers with integer coefficients, can its sign be decided with a polynomially bounded certificate — that is, does this comparison problem belong to NP? Alternatively, establish a sharper complexity classification for the problem.
status: Open since the early 1980s. General algebraic-number techniques and counting-hierarchy containments do not establish NP membership. Key works: O'Rourke (1981), *Advanced Problem 6369*; Allender, Bürgisser, Kjeldgaard-Pedersen, and Miltersen (2009), *On the Complexity of Numerical Analysis*; TOPP Problem 33.
solved_when: A proof that deciding the sign of such a sum lies in NP, or a refined classification (e.g., containment in or hardness for a smaller class) that settles its exact complexity status.
why: Exact Euclidean optimization problems — for instance, comparing lengths of polygonal paths — reduce to deciding the sign of such sums, so an NP membership would place those problems in NP as well.
key_works: O’Rourke (1981), *Advanced Problem 6369*; Allender, Bürgisser, Kjeldgaard-Pedersen, and Miltersen (2009), *On the Complexity of Numerical Analysis*; TOPP Problem 33.

title: Polynomial-bit separation for sums of square roots
open: How small can a nonzero signed sum of \(k\) square roots of integers at most \(N\) actually be? Prove an inverse-exponential lower bound \(2^{-\mathrm{poly}(k,\log N)}\) on the absolute value of any such sum.
status: Known general separation bounds, such as those of Burnikel, Fleischer, Mehlhorn, and Schirra (2000) on radical separation bounds, can require much more precision than the proposed polynomial-bit bound; Cheng, Meng, Sun, and Chen (2009), *Bounding Sum of Square Roots via Lattice Reduction* (arXiv:0905.4487), study the problem but the polynomial-bit bound remains unproven.
solved_when: A proof shows that every nonzero signed sum of \(k\) square roots of integers bounded by \(N\) has absolute value at least \(2^{-\mathrm{poly}(k,\log N)}\).
why: It would convert exact symbolic comparison of such sums into polynomial-precision numerical computation, settling important exact-comparison questions.
key_works: Burnikel, Fleischer, Mehlhorn, and Schirra (2000), radical separation bounds; Cheng, Meng, Sun, and Chen (2009), *Bounding Sum of Square Roots via Lattice Reduction*, arXiv:0905.4487.

title: Near-quadratic complexity of 3D line Voronoi diagrams
open: Is the Euclidean Voronoi diagram of \(n\) lines in three dimensions always of near-quadratic size? Formally, prove an \(O(n^{2+\varepsilon})\) bound on its combinatorial complexity for every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), or exhibit a superquadratic counterexample.
status: Quadratic lower bounds and substantially larger upper bounds leave a longstanding gap; the problem is recorded as TOPP Problem 3, and the sharpest upper-bound technique is Sharir (1994), *Almost Tight Upper Bounds for Lower Envelopes in Higher Dimensions*.
solved_when: A proof that the complexity is \(O(n^{2+\varepsilon})\) for every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), or an explicit family of inputs whose Voronoi diagrams have superquadratic complexity.
why: It settles the feasible output complexity of spatial proximity among linear features, which underlies proximity questions in robotics such as distance to edges and axes.
key_works: Sharir (1994), *Almost Tight Upper Bounds for Lower Envelopes in Higher Dimensions*; TOPP Problem 3.

bib.title: Near-quadratic complexity of 3D line Voronoi diagrams

title: Near-linear exact Euclidean minimum-weight perfect matching
open: Can an exact minimum-weight perfect matching on planar point sets be computed in near-linear time? A satisfactory answer must specify the exact-arithmetic model (e.g., how distance comparisons are performed) under which the bound is proved.
status: Known exact algorithms are substantially slower than near-linear. Approximation is easier, but approximate solutions do not resolve the target. Relevant references include Varadarajan (1998), *A Divide and Conquer Algorithm for Min-Cost Perfect Matching in the Plane*, and TOPP Problem 6.
solved_when: A deterministic or randomized algorithm computes an exact Euclidean minimum-weight perfect matching of n planar points in near-linear time (i.e., within constant or polylogarithmic factors of linear), with its exact-arithmetic model explicitly stated and its complexity bound proved in that model.
why: It would make exact geometric assignment and pairing practical at scale, where current exact methods are too slow and approximation does not guarantee optimality.
key_works: Varadarajan (1998), *A Divide and Conquer Algorithm for Min-Cost Perfect Matching in the Plane*; TOPP Problem 6.

bib.title: Near-linear exact Euclidean minimum-weight perfect matching

title: Near-linear exact Euclidean MST in higher fixed dimension
open: Can an exact Euclidean minimum spanning tree be computed in near-linear time when points lie in any fixed dimension \(d\ge3\)? Formally, is there an algorithm running in \(O(n\,\mathrm{polylog}n)\) time for every fixed \(d\ge3\)?
status: The planar case is easier, but higher-dimensional algorithms and closest-pair machinery leave a longstanding gap from near-linearity. Key works include Callahan and Kosaraju (1995) on well-separated pair decomposition, and TOPP Problem 5.
solved_when: An algorithm computes the exact Euclidean MST on \(n\) points in any fixed dimension \(d\ge3\) in \(O(n\,\mathrm{polylog}n)\) time.
why: It would accelerate geometric clustering and network construction while avoiding any approximation.
key_works: Callahan and Kosaraju (1995), well-separated pair decomposition work; TOPP Problem 5.

title: Strongly polynomial linear programming
open: Is there an algorithm that solves an arbitrary rational linear program using a number of arithmetic operations bounded by a polynomial in the number of variables and constraints alone, independent of the bit lengths of the input numbers?
status: Open since polynomial-time LP algorithms appeared. Ellipsoid and interior-point methods achieve polynomial time in the encoding length (Khachiyan, 1979; Karmarkar, 1984), but not strongly polynomial time; Tardos (1986) obtained strongly polynomial algorithms for important restricted classes of coefficient structure, including combinatorial linear programs.
solved_when: A strongly polynomial algorithm for general rational linear programs is given: the arithmetic operation count is polynomial only in the numbers of variables and constraints, and the intermediate numbers computed have bit lengths polynomially bounded.
why: It would make linear programming complexity independent of numerical scaling in the strongest standard sense, removing bit-length dependence that current polynomial-time methods retain.
key_works: Khachiyan (1979); Karmarkar (1984); Tardos (1986), *A Strongly Polynomial Algorithm to Solve Combinatorial Linear Programs*.

s2_matches.title: A New Approach to Strongly Polynomial Linear Programming

title: Polynomial diameter of polytopes
open: Is there a polynomial upper bound, in the dimension and number of facets, on the graph diameter of every polytope? Formally, does there exist a polynomial p(d, n) such that every d-dimensional polytope with n facets has graph diameter at most p(d, n)?
status: The linear Hirsch conjecture is false, but its polynomial replacement remains open. Quasipolynomial upper bounds are known, notably via Kalai and Kleitman (1992), *A Quasi-Polynomial Bound for the Diameter of Graphs of Polyhedra*; the Hirsch conjecture was refuted by Santos (2012), *A Counterexample to the Hirsch Conjecture*.
solved_when: An explicit polynomial function of dimension and number of facets is proven to bound the graph diameter of every polytope.
why: It would bound the number of edge moves needed to connect feasible LP vertices, i.e., the combinatorial cost of vertex-to-vertex traversal in linear optimization.
key_works: Kalai and Kleitman (1992), *A Quasi-Polynomial Bound for the Diameter of Graphs of Polyhedra*; Santos (2012), *A Counterexample to the Hirsch Conjecture*.

title: A polynomial pivot rule for the simplex method
open: Does there exist a pivot rule for the simplex method whose number of pivots is polynomially bounded on every linear program? A complete answer must include an initialization procedure whose cost is also polynomially controlled.
status: Many natural pivot rules have exponential examples (Klee and Minty (1972), *How Good Is the Simplex Algorithm?*). Known work includes randomized pivoting (Kalai, 1992) and smoothed analysis (Spielman and Teng, 2004). Even a polynomial bound on polytope diameter alone would not supply an efficiently computable rule.
solved_when: A concrete pivot rule is specified, together with a polynomially bounded initialization procedure, and it is proved that on every linear program the rule terminates after polynomially many pivots.
why: It would give the simplex method a worst-case theory matching its practical success, replacing the current gap between exponential counterexamples and observed efficient behavior.
key_works: Klee and Minty (1972), *How Good Is the Simplex Algorithm?*; Kalai (1992), randomized pivoting; Spielman and Teng (2004), smoothed analysis.

bib.title: A polynomial pivot rule for the simplex method

title: Output-polynomial hypergraph dualization
open: Can every minimal transversal of a hypergraph be enumerated in time polynomial in the combined size of the input and the output? Equivalently, is there an output-polynomial algorithm for hypergraph dualization?
status: Quasipolynomial dualization has been known since the 1990s, following Fredman and Khachiyan (1996), *On the Complexity of Dualization of Monotone Disjunctive Forms*, with further results in Eiter, Gottlob, and Makino (2003), *New Results on Monotone Dualization and Generating Hypergraph Transversals*. General output-polynomial enumeration remains open.
solved_when: An algorithm exists that enumerates all minimal transversals of any hypergraph in time polynomial in the input size plus the total output size, with the current best bound being quasipolynomial.
why: It is a foundational enumeration problem that underlies tasks such as computing minimal keys in databases and minimal sufficient explanations in explainable AI.
key_works: Fredman and Khachiyan (1996), *On the Complexity of Dualization of Monotone Disjunctive Normal Forms*; Eiter, Gottlob, and Makino (2003), *New Results on Monotone Dualization and Generating Hypergraph Transversals*.

title: Polynomial-delay minimal-transversal enumeration
open: Can all minimal transversals of a hypergraph be enumerated with only polynomial preprocessing time and polynomial delay between consecutive outputs? This strengthens the requirement of output-polynomial total time, which itself remains unresolved in general.
status: The problem is stronger than output-polynomial total time and is also unresolved in general; numerous restricted hypergraph classes are tractable, per Eiter, Gottlob, and Makino (2003), *New Results on Monotone Dualization and Generating Hypergraph Transversals*.
solved_when: An algorithm exists that, given any hypergraph, performs polynomial preprocessing and then outputs each minimal transversal with at most polynomial time between consecutive outputs.
why: It would make enumeration practical when the full output is enormous and users need early answers, as in interactive enumeration of minimal patterns in knowledge discovery.
key_works: Eiter, Gottlob, and Makino (2003), *New Results on Monotone Dualization and Generating Hypergraph Transversals*.

title: Constant approximation for the smallest grammar
open: Given an input string, can we construct a context-free straight-line grammar that generates exactly that string and whose size is within a universal constant factor of the smallest such grammar?
status: Logarithmic approximation guarantees are known; constant-factor approximation remains open. (Charikar et al. 2005, *The Smallest Grammar Problem*; Bannai et al., *The Smallest Grammar Problem Revisited*, DOI: 10.1109/TIT.2020.3038147.)
solved_when: A polynomial-time algorithm is exhibited that, for every input string, outputs a straight-line grammar generating that string of size at most C times the optimum grammar size, for a universal constant C independent of the input.
why: It would yield provably near-optimal compression for repetitive data and near-minimal symbolic representations, closing the gap between practical grammar-based compressors and the theoretical optimum.
key_works: Charikar et al. (2005), *The Smallest Grammar Problem*; Bannai et al., *The Smallest Grammar Problem Revisited*, DOI: 10.1109/TIT.2020.3038147.

title: Fixed-factor edit-distance approximation in n polylog n time
open: Can edit distance be approximated to within a fixed universal constant factor in \(O(n\,\mathrm{polylog} n)\) time? That is, does there exist an algorithm with a constant approximation ratio, independent of the input, achieving a running time of \(n\) times a polylogarithmic factor?
status: Andoni–Nosatzki achieve a constant-factor approximation in \(n^{1+\varepsilon}\) time for fixed \(\varepsilon\) (arXiv:2005.07678, DOI: 10.1137/21M1392322). This does not automatically give the stated running time with a fixed approximation factor.
solved_when: An algorithm returns an estimate within a fixed universal constant factor of the true edit distance and runs in \(O(n\,\mathrm{polylog} n)\) time.
why: It would support fast sequence alignment with robust worst-case guarantees, rather than relying on heuristics or near-linear time only at the cost of running time \(n^{1+\varepsilon}\).
key_works: Andoni and Nosatzki, *Edit Distance in Near-Linear Time: It’s a Constant Factor*, arXiv:2005.07678, DOI: 10.1137/21M1392322.

title: Parity games in polynomial time
open: Is there a polynomial-time algorithm that decides the winner and computes winning strategies in arbitrary finite parity games?
status: Quasipolynomial-time algorithms were a major 2017 breakthrough (Calude, Jain, Khoussainov, Li, and Stephan, 2017, *Deciding Parity Games in Quasipolynomial Time*), but whether parity games are decidable in polynomial time remains unresolved.
solved_when: An algorithm decides the winner, and computes winning strategies, for every finite parity game in time polynomial in the size of the game.
why: A polynomial-time algorithm would give fast synthesis and model checking for expressive temporal logics such as the modal μ-calculus, replacing today's quasipolynomial methods in practical verification.
key_works: Calude, Jain, Khoussainov, Li, and Stephan (2017), *Deciding Parity Games in Quasipolynomial Time*.

title: Mean-payoff games in polynomial time
open: Is there a polynomial-time algorithm for finite two-player mean-payoff games? That is, can the winner be determined in time polynomial in the size of the graph and the length of the binary weight encoding?
status: Only pseudopolynomial algorithms are known, whose running times depend on the numerical magnitudes of the weights; the decision problem lies in NP ∩ coNP, yet that dependence on numerical magnitudes remains the central obstacle to a polynomial-time solution (Zwick and Paterson, 1996, *The Complexity of Mean Payoff Games on Graphs*).
solved_when: An algorithm decides the winner (and the value) of any finite two-player mean-payoff game in time polynomial in both the number of vertices/edges and the bit-length of the weights.
why: A polynomial algorithm would settle a canonical open problem at the border of P and NP ∩ coNP and enable optimal long-run average-cost control against an adversary without blowup from weight magnitudes.
key_works: Zwick and Paterson (1996), *The Complexity of Mean Payoff Games on Graphs*.

title: Simple stochastic games in polynomial time
open: Is there a polynomial-time algorithm that computes the values of simple stochastic games, or decides whether a given threshold on the value is met? Equivalently, can the decision version be solved in P?
status: Open since Condon's 1992 formulation (Condon, *The Complexity of Stochastic Games*). The problem is known to lie in NP ∩ coNP, and subexponential algorithms exist, but neither establishes polynomial time.
solved_when: A polynomial-time algorithm is given that, for any simple stochastic game, computes its value or decides a given threshold query.
why: These games are a minimal setting where adversarial choice and random transitions interact; polynomial-time solvability would settle a natural complexity boundary between P and NP ∩ coNP.
key_works: Condon (1992), *The Complexity of Stochastic Games*.

title: Černý’s synchronizing-word conjecture
open: Is every synchronizing deterministic automaton on \(n\) states reset by a word of length at most \((n-1)^2\)? In other words, does the quadratic Černý bound always hold, and is it tight?
status: Proposed in 1964. Matching quadratic examples exist, while general upper bounds remain cubic in order; see Szykuła (2018), *Improving the Upper Bound on the Length of the Shortest Reset Word*, DOI: 10.4230/LIPIcs.STACS.2018.56.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof with counterexample) that every synchronizing deterministic automaton with \(n\) states admits a reset word of length at most \((n-1)^2\) is given.
why: It would establish the optimal worst-case reset complexity of finite-state systems, settling the fundamental limit on how long a synchronizing sequence must be.
key_works: Černý (1964); Szykuła (2018), *Improving the Upper Bound on the Length of the Shortest Reset Word*, DOI: 10.4230/LIPIcs.STACS.2018.56.

title: Sakoda–Sipser two-way automata problem
open: Does nondeterminism ever require a superpolynomial price in state complexity for two-way finite automata? Formally, determine whether every n-state two-way nondeterministic finite automaton has an equivalent two-way deterministic automaton with only polynomially many states.
status: Open since 1978, when posed by Sakoda and Sipser (*Nondeterminism and the Size of Two Way Finite Automata*, DOI: 10.1145/800133.804357). Partial results exist for restricted alphabets and restricted automaton classes (see Pighizzini 2013, DOI: 10.3233/FI-2013-879), but the general state-complexity question remains unresolved.
solved_when: A proof (or refutation) that for every n-state 2NFA there exists an equivalent 2DFA with polynomially many states — i.e., either a polynomial upper bound on the deterministic state count or a superpolynomial lower bound.
why: It isolates the power of nondeterminism in a very small computational model, making it a clean test case for whether nondeterminism can be cheap.
key_works: Sakoda and Sipser (1978), *Nondeterminism and the Size of Two Way Finite Automata*, DOI: 10.1145/800133.804357; Pighizzini (2013), DOI: 10.3233/FI-2013-879.
