title: Generalized star height greater than one
open: Does there exist a regular language that cannot be expressed by a regular expression using complementation and at most one level of nesting of the star operation? Equivalently, is there a regular language of generalized star height greater than one, or does every regular language have generalized star height at most one?
status: A longstanding automata-theoretic problem. Ordinary star-height hierarchies do not resolve the complement-allowing version. Pin (1992), *Some Results on the Generalized Star-Height Problem*, HAL: hal-00019978.
solved_when: Either a specific regular language is exhibited and proven to have generalized star height strictly greater than one, or it is proven that every regular language has generalized star height at most one.
why: It determines the irreducible nesting complexity of regular-language descriptions when complementation is freely available, settling how succinct such expressions can fundamentally be.
key_works: Pin (1992), *Some Results on the Generalized Star-Height Problem*, HAL: hal-00019978.

title: General Skolem problem
open: Does a given linear recurrence sequence over the integers or rationals ever take the value zero? Equivalently, is there an algorithm that, for any such sequence, decides whether some term vanishes?
status: Open since the 1930s. Low-order cases and important restricted families are decidable; the general problem remains unresolved. Key works include Bilu et al. (2022), *Skolem Meets Schanuel* (arXiv:2204.13417, DOI: 10.4230/LIPIcs.MFCS.2022.20) and the Skolem tool project.
solved_when: A decision procedure (or a proof of undecidability) for the general problem: given an arbitrary integer or rational linear recurrence sequence, determine whether zero appears among its terms.
why: The problem sits at the boundary between number theory and program verification; deciding zeros of recurrence sequences is directly tied to termination questions for linear loops, so a resolution would clarify what is decidable in a basic class of programs.
key_works: Bilu et al. (2022), *Skolem Meets Schanuel*, arXiv:2204.13417, DOI: 10.4230/LIPIcs.MFCS.2022.20; the Skolem tool project.

title: Skolem problem at order five
open: Given an integer linear recurrence sequence of order five, can we decide whether it contains a zero term? Formally: is there an algorithm that, for every order-five linear recurrence sequence, determines whether some term equals zero?
status: The problem is decidable for orders up to four, and order five is the first unresolved general order. Conditional transcendence-based results (Lipton et al. (2022), *On the Skolem Problem and the Skolem Conjecture*, DOI: 10.1145/3531130.3533328; Bilu et al. (2022)) do not supply an unconditional decision algorithm.
solved_when: An unconditional decision algorithm exists that, for every linear recurrence sequence of order five, correctly determines whether zero occurs among its terms.
why: Order five is the first unresolved general case, so it is a sharply bounded test case for the general decidability of the Skolem problem.
key_works: Lipton et al. (2022), *On the Skolem Problem and the Skolem Conjecture*, DOI: 10.1145/3531130.3533328; Bilu et al. (2022).

title: Positivity of arbitrary linear recurrences
open: Given a linear recurrence sequence with rational coefficients and initial values, decide whether every term of the sequence is nonnegative. Is this unrestricted positivity problem decidable?
status: The problem is decidable for several low-order and structurally restricted classes, notably via work of Ouaknine and Worrell (2014), *Positivity Problems for Low-Order Linear Recurrence Sequences*, and *On the Positivity Problem for Simple Linear Recurrence Sequences*, arXiv:1309.1550; the unrestricted problem remains open.
solved_when: An algorithm is provided that, for any rational linear recurrence sequence, decides in finitely many steps whether all its terms are nonnegative.
why: It captures invariant checking and safety verification of linear dynamical systems, so a decision procedure would give a general tool for proving such systems safe.
key_works: Ouaknine and Worrell (2014), *Positivity Problems for Low-Order Linear Recurrence Sequences*; *On the Positivity Problem for Simple Linear Recurrence Sequences*, arXiv:1309.1550.

title: Ultimate positivity with repeated characteristic roots
open: Is there an algorithm that decides whether an arbitrary linear recurrence sequence is eventually nonnegative, when the characteristic polynomial may have repeated roots? In other words, decide ultimate positivity in full generality, beyond the simple-root case.
status: Ultimate positivity is decidable for simple recurrences of all orders (Ouaknine and Worrell, 2014, *Ultimate Positivity Is Decidable for Simple Linear Recurrence Sequences*; see also their positivity survey and related papers). The unrestricted repeated-root case remains a distinct open problem.
solved_when: A decision procedure (or a proof of undecidability) is established for ultimate positivity of linear recurrence sequences of arbitrary order whose characteristic polynomials have repeated roots.
why: A solution would complete the decidability picture for long-run sign behavior of linear recurrences, which underpins eventual safety verification of linear dynamical systems.
key_works: Ouaknine and Worrell (2014), *Ultimate Positivity Is Decidable for Simple Linear Recurrence Sequences*; their positivity survey and related papers.

title: Continuous Skolem problem
open: Given a continuous linear dynamical system specified by rational matrices \(A, x, c\), does the orbit \(e^{At}x\) ever meet the hyperplane \(c^\top y = 0\) at some positive time \(t > 0\)? Formally, decide whether \(c^\top e^{At}x = 0\) for some \(t > 0\), treating identically zero cases separately.
status: General decidability remains open; bounded-dimensional and spectral restrictions admit partial results, notably Chonev, Ouaknine, and Worrell (2016), *On the Skolem Problem for Continuous Linear Dynamical Systems*.
solved_when: An algorithm is given that, for any rational \(A, x, c\), decides in finite time whether \(c^\top e^{At}x = 0\) for some \(t > 0\), or a proof is provided that no such algorithm exists.
why: It is the continuous-time counterpart of detecting a zero in a linear recurrence, so a decidability result would extend the reachability toolkit for hybrid and continuous systems; undecidability would show a fundamental limit on verifying linear flows.
key_works: Chonev, Ouaknine, and Worrell (2016), *On the Skolem Problem for Continuous Linear Dynamical Systems* (identifier verify).

title: EFX existence for additive goods
open: Does every finite set of indivisible goods, with additive nonnegative valuations, admit a complete allocation that is envy-free up to any good? Formally, prove EFX existence in full generality, or construct a counterexample.
status: Open since the modern EFX formulation. Existence is known for three agents (Chaudhury, Garg, and Mehlhorn, 2020, *EFX Exists for Three Agents*); the case of arbitrarily many agents remains unresolved. See also Caragiannis et al., *The Unreasonable Fairness of Maximum Nash Welfare*, and the Dagstuhl fair-division report.
solved_when: Either a proof that all instances with any number of agents and additive nonnegative valuations admit a complete EFX allocation, or an explicit counterexample instance.
why: It would establish the strongest known fairness guarantee for indivisible goods without discarding resources, resolving the central existence question in discrete fair division.
key_works: Caragiannis et al., *The Unreasonable Fairness of Maximum Nash Welfare*; Chaudhury, Garg, and Mehlhorn (2020), *EFX Exists for Three Agents*; Dagstuhl fair-division report.

title: EFX existence for four additive agents
open: Does a complete EFX allocation always exist when four agents with additive valuations divide indivisible goods — or is there a four-agent instance where none exists?
status: This is the smallest unresolved general agent count beyond the three-agent theorem (Chaudhury, Garg, and Mehlhorn, 2020, *EFX Exists for Three Agents*). Restricted valuation classes and partial allocations are known, but these do not settle existence of complete EFX allocations for arbitrary additive valuations; a 2025 Dagstuhl fair-division report surveys the state of the area.
solved_when: Either a proof that every four-agent additive-goods instance admits a complete EFX allocation, or an explicit four-agent additive counterexample with no such allocation.
why: Four agents is the smallest unresolved general case beyond the three-agent theorem, so its resolution is likely to reveal whether the general EFX existence conjecture is plausible at all.
key_works: Chaudhury, Garg, and Mehlhorn (2020), *EFX Exists for Three Agents*; 2025 Dagstuhl fair-division report.

title: Optimal universal maximin-share approximation
open: What is the largest fraction of the maximin share that can be guaranteed to every agent when indivisible goods are allocated among agents with additive valuations, and can that guarantee be computed efficiently?
status: Exact MMS allocations need not exist; a line of successively improved positive approximation guarantees remains below the best known impossibility examples, leaving the optimal constant open (Kurokawa, Procaccia, and Wang, 2018, *Fair Enough: Guaranteeing Approximate Maximin Shares*; subsequent MMS approximation literature surveyed by Dagstuhl).
solved_when: The optimal constant \(\alpha\) is identified (matching the best impossibility examples) together with a determination of whether an \(\alpha\)-MMS allocation can be found efficiently for every additive-goods instance.
why: It would settle the strongest universal form of a major fairness benchmark, pinning down exactly what proportionality-like guarantee is possible without interpersonal utility comparison.
key_works: Kurokawa, Procaccia, and Wang (2018), *Fair Enough: Guaranteeing Approximate Maximin Shares*; subsequent MMS approximation literature surveyed by Dagstuhl.

title: BQP versus BPP
subfield: Quantum complexity and locally decodable codes
open: Does every problem solvable efficiently by a quantum computer also admit an efficient classical randomized algorithm, or is there a genuine unconditional separation? Formally, prove that BQP ≠ BPP, or establish BQP = BPP.
status: Quantum algorithms and oracle separations provide strong evidence of advantage, but they do not prove the unrelativized class separation. Foundational references include Bernstein and Vazirani (1997), *Quantum Complexity Theory*, and Watrous (2008), *Quantum Computational Complexity*, arXiv:0804.3401.
solved_when: A rigorous, unconditional proof either separating BQP from BPP or showing their equality, with no oracle relativization assumptions.
why: It determines whether quantum computation fundamentally extends efficient classical computation, or whether apparent quantum speedups are artifacts of our proof limitations.
key_works: Bernstein and Vazirani (1997), *Quantum Complexity Theory*; Watrous (2008), *Quantum Computational Complexity*, arXiv:0804.3401.

title: Can quantum computers solve all NP problems efficiently?
subfield: Quantum complexity and locally decodable codes
open: Can a quantum computer solve every problem in NP efficiently — that is, is NP contained in BQP? A formal answer would settle whether polynomial-time quantum algorithms exist for general NP-complete problems.
status: No polynomial-time quantum algorithm for general NP-complete problems is known. Black-box search lower bounds (Bennett, Bernstein, Brassard, and Vazirani, 1997, *Strengths and Weaknesses of Quantum Computing*; Watrous, 2008, arXiv:0804.3401) do not establish the desired unrelativized exclusion.
solved_when: A proof that NP ⊆ BQP (exhibiting polynomial-time quantum algorithms for an NP-complete problem), or a proof that NP ⊄ BQP (a separation in the unrelativized setting).
why: It defines the ultimate limits of quantum acceleration for combinatorial search and optimization, determining whether quantum computing can deliver broad speedups on NP-hard problems or only on structured ones.
key_works: Bennett, Bernstein, Brassard, and Vazirani (1997), *Strengths and Weaknesses of Quantum Computing*; Watrous (2008), arXiv:0804.3401.

title: QMA versus QCMA
subfield: Quantum complexity and locally decodable codes
open: Do polynomial-size quantum witnesses give a quantum verifier more power than polynomial-size classical witnesses? Formally, is QMA strictly larger than QCMA?
status: Oracle separations between QMA and QCMA are known, but the unrelativized equality or separation remains open. Key works: Aharonov and Naveh (2002), *Quantum NP—A Survey*; Watrous (2008), arXiv:0804.3401.
solved_when: A proof, or a refutation, of QMA ≠ QCMA in the unrelativized setting.
why: It settles whether quantum information itself is essential in efficiently verifiable certificates, beyond what a classical description can convey.
key_works: Aharonov and Naveh (2002), *Quantum NP—A Survey*; Watrous (2008), arXiv:0804.3401.

title: QMA versus QMA(2)
subfield: Quantum complexity and locally decodable codes
open: Does allowing a verifier to receive two unentangled quantum witnesses — a promise that the witnesses are product states — yield more computational power than a single quantum witness? Formally, is QMA(2) strictly more powerful than QMA?
status: Harrow and Montanaro (*Testing Product States, Quantum Merlin–Arthur Games and Tensor Optimization*, arXiv:1001.0017, DOI: 10.1145/2432622.2432625) showed that constant numbers of unentangled witnesses can be reduced to two in important formulations, but whether QMA(2) equals QMA remains open.
solved_when: QMA is proved equal to (or strictly separated from) QMA(2).
why: It isolates exactly what an unentanglement promise is worth computationally, a basic structural question about entanglement as a resource in proof verification.
key_works: Harrow and Montanaro, *Testing Product States, Quantum Merlin–Arthur Games and Tensor Optimization*, arXiv:1001.0017, DOI: 10.1145/2432622.2432625.

title: Quantum PCP conjecture for local Hamiltonians
subfield: Quantum complexity and locally decodable codes
open: Is it quantum-computationally hard, even in principle, to estimate the energy of a many-body system's ground state to within any fixed constant accuracy? Formally: prove QMA-hardness of approximating the ground-state energy to a fixed positive fraction of the number of bounded-norm local terms.
status: Open since the 2000s. Progress on nonlocal games, NLTS, and good quantum LDPC codes does not by itself resolve this local-Hamiltonian formulation. See Aharonov, Arad, and Vidick (2013), *The Quantum PCP Conjecture*, arXiv:1309.7495, DOI: 10.1145/2491533.2491549.
solved_when: A proof is given that approximating the ground-state energy of a local Hamiltonian to within a fixed positive fraction of the number of bounded-norm local terms is QMA-hard.
why: A resolution would show that even coarse estimates of many-body ground energies can be quantum-computationally intractable, placing a fundamental limit on simulation of low-energy physics.
key_works: Aharonov, Arad, and Vidick (2013), *The Quantum PCP Conjecture*, arXiv:1309.7495, DOI: 10.1145/2491533.2491549.

title: Asymptotically good quantum locally testable codes
subfield: Quantum complexity and locally decodable codes
open: Do there exist quantum error-correcting code families that are simultaneously good and locally testable — combining constant rate, linear distance, constant-size checks, and constant soundness under a standard quantum local-testability definition?
status: Good quantum LDPC codes — with constant rate and linear distance — are known, but adding constant local-testability soundness remains a stronger, unresolved goal; see Aharonov and Eldar (2015), *Quantum Locally Testable Codes*, and quantum PCP workshop materials.
solved_when: An explicit construction of quantum codes achieving, simultaneously, constant rate, linear minimum distance, checks of constant size, and constant soundness parameter under an accepted quantum local-testability definition — or a proof that no such family exists.
why: Such codes would tie together robust quantum error correction, locally checkable entanglement, and Hamiltonian complexity, potentially informing fault-tolerant quantum memory and the structure of low-energy states.
key_works: Aharonov and Eldar (2015), *Quantum Locally Testable Codes*; quantum PCP workshop materials.

title: Polynomial-length constant-query locally decodable codes
subfield: Quantum complexity and locally decodable codes
open: Do there exist locally decodable codes with a constant-size alphabet and constant query complexity, polynomial block length, and constant tolerance to adversarial errors, for some fixed number of queries at least three?
status: Two-query codes require exponential length; constant-query constructions with much larger length, together with strong lower bounds, leave the general polynomial-length possibility unresolved. Key works include Yekhanin (2007), DOI: 10.1145/1250790.1250830, and Efremenko (2009), *3-Query Locally Decodable Codes of Subexponential Length*.
solved_when: An explicit construction of constant-alphabet, constant-query (at least three queries) locally decodable codes is given whose block length is polynomial in the message length and which tolerates a constant adversarial error rate.
why: Such codes would allow recovery of any individual data symbol with tiny access cost and only modest redundancy, directly serving local error correction and private information retrieval.
key_works: Yekhanin (2007), DOI: 10.1145/1250790.1250830; Efremenko (2009), *3-Query Locally Decodable Codes of Subexponential Length*.

title: Efficient uniform-distribution DNF learning from examples alone
open: Can polynomial-size DNF formulas be learned efficiently over the uniform distribution using only random labeled examples, without access to membership queries?
status: Quasipolynomial Fourier-based learning is known via Linial, Mansour, and Nissen (1993), *Constant Depth Circuits, Fourier Transform, and Learnability*. Jackson’s polynomial-time Harmonic Sieve algorithm (1997, *An Efficient Membership-Query Algorithm for Learning DNF with Respect to the Uniform Distribution*) relies on membership queries and therefore does not solve this version.
solved_when: A learning algorithm exists whose running time is polynomial in the dimension, the DNF size, and the inverse error, and which uses only randomly drawn labeled examples.
why: A solution would separate passive data access from active query access for a basic expressive concept class, clarifying the power of membership queries in learning.
key_works: Linial, Mansour, and Nisan (1993), *Constant Depth Circuits, Fourier Transform, and Learnability*; Jackson (1997), *An Efficient Membership-Query Algorithm for Learning DNF with Respect to the Uniform Distribution*.

title: Efficient distribution-free PAC learning of DNF
open: Can polynomial-size DNF formulas be PAC-learned in polynomial time from random examples drawn from an arbitrary distribution, with no restriction on the hypothesis representation? Equivalently, is the class of polynomial-size DNF formulas efficiently and improperly learnable in the distribution-free PAC model?
status: Open since the early PAC-learning era. Known results cover restricted DNF classes, stronger query access, and conditional hardness results, but none settle the general distribution-free formulation. Key works include Valiant (1984), *A Theory of the Learnable*; Klivans and Servedio (2004), *Learning DNF in Time 2^{Õ(n^{1/3})}*; and Jackson's uniform-query work.
solved_when: A polynomial-time algorithm outputs, for any target DNF of polynomial size, any distribution over examples, and any accuracy and confidence parameters, a hypothesis (of arbitrary form) whose error is at most the specified accuracy with the specified confidence.
why: It is a foundational test of whether a simple, natural symbolic class is efficiently learnable from unrestricted random examples; settling it in either direction would clarify the reach of the PAC model itself.
key_works: Valiant (1984), *A Theory of the Learnable*; Klivans and Servedio (2004), *Learning DNF in Time 2^{Õ(n^{1/3})}*; Jackson’s uniform-query work.

title: Polynomial-time Learning Parity with Noise
open: Can an unknown binary parity be learned from polynomially many randomly sampled examples corrupted by a fixed noise rate below one half, in polynomial time? Formally, is there a polynomial-time algorithm that, given noisy labeled samples of a parity function, recovers the underlying parity with high probability?
status: Subexponential-time algorithms are known, notably via Blum, Kalai, and Wasserman (2003), *Noise-Tolerant Learning, the Parity Problem, and the Statistical Query Model*; general polynomial-time learning remains open and is widely used as a hardness assumption.
solved_when: A polynomial-time algorithm is exhibited that recovers the unknown parity from polynomially many random samples corrupted by any fixed noise rate below one half.
why: LPN is a minimal noisy learning problem whose solvability or hardness underpins cryptographic primitives; a polynomial-time learner would break LPN-based cryptography, while a hardness proof would ground it as a foundational assumption.
key_works: Blum, Kalai, and Wasserman (2003), *Noise-Tolerant Learning, the Parity Problem, and the Statistical Query Model*.

title: Existence of one-way functions
open: Does a one-way function exist — a function easy to compute in polynomial time yet impossible to invert in probabilistic polynomial time? Formally, prove that some polynomial-time computable function is hard to invert on a nonnegligible fraction of its outputs for every probabilistic polynomial-time adversary.
status: Open since the foundations of modern cryptography. Candidate constructions exist but depend on unproved hardness assumptions. Key works: Diffie and Hellman (1976), *New Directions in Cryptography*; Goldreich (2001), *Foundations of Cryptography, Volume 1*; Håstad et al. (1999).
solved_when: An explicit polynomial-time computable function is exhibited, together with a proof that no probabilistic polynomial-time adversary inverts it on more than a negligible fraction of inputs.
why: One-way functions underlie pseudorandomness, commitments, digital signatures, and much of symmetric cryptography; without them, the standard foundations of provable computational security collapse.
key_works: Diffie and Hellman (1976), *New Directions in Cryptography*; Goldreich (2001), *Foundations of Cryptography, Volume 1*; Håstad et al. (1999).

title: Does P ≠ NP imply one-way functions?
open: Does the worst-case separation P ≠ NP alone force the existence of functions that are hard to invert on average? Equivalently, can average-case inversion hardness be derived from P ≠ NP, or is there a precise obstruction ruling out any such derivation?
status: Worst-case hardness is not currently known to imply the needed average-case hardness, and oracle and black-box barriers constrain the possible routes to such a derivation.
solved_when: Either a proof that P ≠ NP implies one-way functions is given, or a formal barrier (e.g., a black-box or relativization-style obstruction) is established showing that no such derivation is possible.
why: A positive answer would connect the central complexity-theoretic separation directly to the foundations of cryptographic possibility; a precise obstruction would clarify why current techniques fail and chart what new methods are needed.
key_works: Impagliazzo (1995), *A Personal View of Average-Case Complexity*; Goldreich (2001), *Foundations of Cryptography*.

title: Public-key encryption from one-way functions
open: Can public-key encryption be constructed from nothing more than the existence of arbitrary one-way functions, if we allow unrestricted and possibly non-black-box techniques — or is there a fundamental barrier showing this is impossible?
status: Fully black-box constructions are ruled out by the Impagliazzo–Rudich barrier (Impagliazzo and Rudich, 1989, *Limits on the Provable Consequences of One-Way Permutations*), but that barrier does not rule out every non-black-box construction; further limits on the power of random oracles in this setting are given by Mahmoody, Maji, and Prabhakaran (2012), *Limits of Random Oracles in Secure Computation*, arXiv:1205.3554.
solved_when: Either a construction of public-key encryption from arbitrary one-way functions is given (with no black-box restriction on the technique), or an impossibility theorem is proved that rules out such constructions beyond the existing black-box barrier.
why: A positive answer would collapse a major distinction between basic private-key hardness and public-key cryptography, showing one-wayness alone suffices for public-key primitives.
key_works: Impagliazzo and Rudich (1989), *Limits on the Provable Consequences of One-Way Permutations*; Mahmoody, Maji, and Prabhakaran (2012), *Limits of Random Oracles in Secure Computation*, arXiv:1205.3554.

title: Classical polynomial-time integer factorization
subfield: Computational number theory, lattices, and topology
open: Is there a classical algorithm that factors arbitrary integers in time polynomial in their bit length, whether deterministic or randomized?
status: General classical factoring algorithms are subexponential rather than polynomial in the bit length. Shor's polynomial-time quantum algorithm (Shor, 1997, *Polynomial-Time Algorithms for Prime Factorization and Discrete Logarithms on a Quantum Computer*, arXiv:quant-ph/9508027) does not settle the classical question; the number field sieve lineage is documented in Lenstra and Lenstra, eds. (1993), *The Development of the Number Field Sieve*.
solved_when: An explicit classical (deterministic or randomized) algorithm is given whose running time is bounded by a polynomial in the bit length of the input integer, with a proof of correctness for all integers.
why: A solution would transform computational number theory and invalidate major cryptographic assumptions, including those underlying RSA.
key_works: Lenstra and Lenstra, eds. (1993), *The Development of the Number Field Sieve*; Shor (1997), *Polynomial-Time Algorithms for Prime Factorization and Discrete Logarithms on a Quantum Computer*, arXiv:quant-ph/9508027.

title: Classical polynomial-time prime-field discrete logarithms
subfield: Computational number theory, lattices, and topology
open: Is there a classical algorithm that computes discrete logarithms in the multiplicative group of an arbitrary prime field in time polynomial in \(\log p\)? Equivalently, can the exponent in the running time be reduced from the known subexponential bounds to a constant?
status: General-purpose classical subexponential methods are known, dating to Adleman (1979), *A Subexponential Algorithm for the Discrete Logarithm Problem with Applications to Cryptography*, and refined by Gordon's (1993) number-field-sieve discrete logarithms. Special-field algorithms and quantum algorithms exist, but neither resolves arbitrary prime fields classically.
solved_when: A deterministic or randomized classical algorithm is exhibited that, for every prime \(p\) and every generator \(g\) and target \(h\) in \(\mathbb{F}_p^*\), outputs \(x\) with \(g^x = h\) in time polynomial in \(\log p\).
why: It would settle the computational foundation of major finite-field cryptosystems, since it determines definitively whether problems like Diffie–Hellman key exchange rest on genuine super-polynomial hardness.
key_works: Adleman (1979), *A Subexponential Algorithm for the Discrete Logarithm Problem with Applications to Cryptography*; Gordon (1993), number-field-sieve discrete logarithms.

title: Deterministic polynomial-time finite-field polynomial factorization
subfield: Computational number theory, lattices, and topology
open: Can every univariate polynomial over a finite field be factored deterministically in polynomial time? That is, is there a deterministic algorithm running in time polynomial in the degree and \(\log q\) that requires no unproved number-theoretic assumptions?
status: Randomized polynomial-time factorization algorithms are classical, due to Berlekamp (1967), *Factoring Polynomials over Finite Fields*, and Cantor and Zassenhaus (1981), *A New Algorithm for Factoring Polynomials over Finite Fields*; general unconditional deterministic polynomial time remains open.
solved_when: An unconditional deterministic algorithm factors arbitrary univariate polynomials over \(\mathbb{F}_q\) in time polynomial in the degree and \(\log q\).
why: It would derandomize a basic operation used throughout algebra and coding theory, making a fundamental algebraic primitive reliably deterministic.
key_works: Berlekamp (1967), *Factoring Polynomials over Finite Fields*; Cantor and Zassenhaus (1981), *A New Algorithm for Factoring Polynomials over Finite Fields*.

title: Single-exponential, polynomial-space exact SVP
subfield: Computational number theory, lattices, and topology
open: Can the exact Shortest Vector Problem in Euclidean lattices be solved in single-exponential time while using only polynomial space? Formally: is there an algorithm running in \(2^{O(n)}\) time and polynomial space that finds a shortest nonzero vector in a rank-\(n\) lattice?
status: Known single-exponential time algorithms generally use exponential space (e.g., the deterministic Voronoi-cell approach of Micciancio and Voulgaris, 2013), while polynomial-space enumeration methods incur \(n^{O(n)}\)-type running time; closing this gap is listed on Micciancio's SVP open-problem page.
solved_when: A (deterministic or randomized) algorithm computes an exact shortest nonzero vector in \(2^{O(n)}\) time using space polynomial in \(n\).
why: Memory, not time, is a major practical bottleneck in lattice computation, so such an algorithm would make exact SVP tractable at dimensions where current methods exhaust available memory.
key_works: Micciancio and Voulgaris (2013), *A Deterministic Single Exponential Time Algorithm for Most Lattice Problems Based on Voronoi Cell Computations*; Micciancio’s SVP open-problem page.

title: Decidability of 4-sphere recognition
subfield: Computational number theory, lattices, and topology
open: Given a triangulated closed four-manifold, is there an algorithm that decides whether it is homeomorphic to \(S^4\) — or is the problem undecidable, with no such algorithm existing?
status: Three-sphere recognition is decidable; sphere recognition in sufficiently high dimensions is undecidable. Dimension four remains exceptional and unresolved. Key works: Novikov’s sphere-recognition undecidability work; Poonen, *Undecidable Problems: A Sampler*; recent computational-topology discussions.
solved_when: Either a decision algorithm for 4-sphere recognition is produced, or a proof of undecidability is given.
why: It locates a fundamental computability boundary in low-dimensional topology, settling whether dimension four behaves like the decidable case of dimension three or the undecidable high-dimensional case.
key_works: Novikov’s sphere-recognition undecidability work; Poonen, *Undecidable Problems: A Sampler*; recent computational-topology discussions.

title: Hilbert’s tenth problem over the rationals
subfield: Computational number theory, lattices, and topology
open: Is there an algorithm that, given an arbitrary multivariate polynomial with integer coefficients, decides whether it has a solution in rational numbers — or is this decision problem undecidable?
status: The integer version was resolved negatively in 1970 (Matiyasevich–Robinson–Davis–Putnam). The rational version remains open despite substantial work on subrings of Q and Diophantine definability; see Poonen (2003), *Hilbert’s Tenth Problem and Mazur’s Conjecture for Large Subrings of Q*, and Poonen, *Undecidability in Number Theory*.
solved_when: Either an algorithm is given that decides rational solvability for every such polynomial, or a proof of undecidability is established.
why: It would settle a foundational boundary of algorithmic number theory: whether rational numbers, unlike the integers, admit an effective Diophantine decision procedure.
key_works: Poonen (2003), *Hilbert’s Tenth Problem and Mazur’s Conjecture for Large Subrings of Q*; Poonen, *Undecidability in Number Theory*.

title: Skolem problem
open: Is there an algorithm that, given an algebraic linear recurrence sequence, decides whether some term of the sequence equals zero? Equivalently, is the Skolem problem decidable for linear recurrence sequences?
status: The problem is listed as unsolved on Wikipedia as of 2026-10-07.
solved_when: An algorithm is given that, for any algebraic linear recurrence sequence, terminates with a correct yes/no answer as to whether the sequence contains a zero; alternatively, a proof that no such algorithm exists.
key_works: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List%20of%20unsolved%20problems%20in%20computer%20science

title: Gilbert–Pollak conjecture
open: Is the Steiner ratio of the Euclidean plane — the worst-case ratio between the length of a minimum Steiner tree and that of a minimum spanning tree — exactly 2/√3?
status: The problem appears on Wikipedia's list of unsolved problems in computer science (as of 2026-10-07); no resolution is recorded there.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that the Steiner ratio of the Euclidean plane equals 2/√3, resolving the Gilbert–Pollak conjecture.
key_works: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List%20of%20unsolved%20problems%20in%20computer%20science

title: Barendregt–Geuvers–Klop conjecture
open: Is every weakly normalizing pure type system also strongly normalizing? In formal terms, does the existence of a reduction sequence terminating in a normal form imply that all reduction sequences terminate, uniformly across all pure type systems?
status: The problem, known as the Barendregt–Geuvers–Klop conjecture, is listed as unsolved on Wikipedia as of 2026-10-07 (see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List%20of%20unsolved%20problems%20in%20computer%20science).
solved_when: A proof (or refuting counterexample) settling whether weak normalization implies strong normalization for every pure type system.
key_works: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List%20of%20unsolved%20problems%20in%20computer%20science

title: Černý conjecture
open: Must every n-state deterministic finite automaton that admits a synchronizing word have one of length at most (n − 1)²? Formally, the conjecture asserts a cubic-in-n bound never arises: the synchronizing word length is always at most the square (n − 1)², matching the extremal automata constructed by Černý.
status: The problem is listed as unsolved on Wikipedia (as of 2026-10-07).
solved_when: A proof (or a counterexample) resolves the conjecture: either every synchronizing n-state DFA admits a synchronizing word of length at most (n − 1)², or an automaton is exhibited requiring a longer one.
key_works: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List%20of%20unsolved%20problems%20in%20computer%20science

title: Separating words problem
open: How many states are needed in a deterministic finite automaton that behaves differently on two given strings of length n? More precisely, what is the growth rate, as a function of n, of the size of the smallest DFA separating two length-n words?
status: The problem is listed as unsolved on Wikipedia as of 2026-10-07 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List%20of%20unsolved%20problems%20in%20computer%20science).
solved_when: An exact answer or tight asymptotic bounds are determined for the minimum number of DFA states sufficient to separate any two distinct strings of length n.
key_works: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List%20of%20unsolved%20problems%20in%20computer%20science

title: Superpolynomial determinantal complexity of the permanent
subfield: Algebraic complexity and polynomial identity testing
open: How large must a matrix of affine-linear forms be for its determinant to equal the \(n\times n\) permanent? Prove that any such expression requires superpolynomial matrix dimension.
status: Open since Valiant's work. Quadratic-scale lower bounds are known: Mignon and Ressayre (2004), *A Quadratic Bound for the Determinant and Permanent Problem*, and a 2026 Kumar–Volk preprint (*A Quadratic Lower Bound on Determinantal Complexity*, ECCC TR26-218) develops further quadratic lower-bound results — still far from superpolynomial growth.
solved_when: A proof that every representation of the \(n\times n\) permanent as the determinant of a matrix whose entries are affine-linear forms uses matrix dimension growing faster than any polynomial in \(n\).
why: It would give a concrete route toward separating algebraic complexity classes, vindicating the determinantal-complexity approach that underlies geometric complexity theory.
key_works: Mignon and Ressayre (2004), *A Quadratic Bound for the Determinant and Permanent Problem*; Kumar and Volk (2026), *A Quadratic Lower Bound on Determinantal Complexity*, ECCC TR26-218.

title: Polynomial-size explicit hitting sets for general circuits
subfield: Algebraic complexity and polynomial identity testing
open: Can we explicitly construct, in polynomial time, a hitting set of polynomial size for all arithmetic circuits of size \(s\) and degree polynomial in \(s\)? This is the black-box derandomization of polynomial identity testing for general circuits.
status: Open in the general model. This asks for black-box derandomization, a stronger access restriction than white-box PIT. Key works: Heintz and Schnorr (1980), *Testing Polynomials Which Are Easy to Compute*; Shpilka–Yehudayoff (2010); Hu–van Melkebeek–Morgan (2024).
solved_when: An explicit family of hitting sets, each of size polynomial in \(s\) and constructible in polynomial time, is exhibited that intersects every nonzero polynomial computed by an arithmetic circuit of size \(s\) and degree polynomial in \(s\).
why: It would allow deterministic verification of polynomial computations that are accessible only through evaluations, derandomizing PIT in the black-box model.
key_works: Heintz and Schnorr (1980), *Testing Polynomials Which Are Easy to Compute*; Shpilka–Yehudayoff (2010); Hu–van Melkebeek–Morgan (2024).

title: EFX for arbitrarily many agents with bi-valued chores
open: When agents have additive costs over indivisible chores and each agent's costs take only two possible values, must a complete EFX allocation always exist — for any number of agents?
status: General additive-chores EFX was shown false in 2026. He–Tao (*EFX for Additive Chores: Nonexistence, Pareto Incompatibility, and Bi-Valued Existence*, arXiv:2606.08872) establish EFX existence for four agents in the bi-valued setting, leaving the unrestricted agent-count question open.
solved_when: A proof (or algorithm producing) a complete EFX allocation for every bi-valued additive chore instance with an unbounded number of agents; or a counterexample instance of this form with no complete EFX allocation.
why: It maps the boundary of fair chore division: general additive chores admit no EFX, so identifying which structure restores existence separates impossible fairness from tractable positive results.
key_works: He and Tao (2026), *EFX for Additive Chores: Nonexistence, Pareto Incompatibility, and Bi-Valued Existence*, arXiv:2606.08872.

title: EFX plus Pareto optimality for personalized bi-valued goods
open: Does every instance of indivisible goods with additive, personalized bi-valued utilities — where each agent has its own two positive utility levels — admit an allocation that is simultaneously envy-free up to any good (EFX) and Pareto optimal?
status: A restricted but unresolved efficiency–fairness compatibility problem. Negative 2026 results exist for bi-valued chores, but these must not be transferred to goods. Key works: Jin and Tao (2025), *On Pareto-Optimal and Fair Allocations with Personalized Bi-Valued Utilities*, WINE; He–Tao's 2026 comparison discussion.
solved_when: A proof that such an allocation always exists (with an algorithm to construct it), or an explicit counterexample instance with personalized bi-valued utilities admitting no EFX and Pareto-optimal allocation.
why: It probes whether fairness and efficiency are compatible without any avoidable welfare loss in a structured utility class general enough to be nontrivial yet restricted enough that existence may be tractable.
key_works: Jin and Tao (2025), *On Pareto-Optimal and Fair Allocations with Personalized Bi-Valued Utilities*, WINE; He–Tao’s 2026 comparison discussion.

title: Efficient sampling near the graph-coloring uniqueness threshold
subfield: Approximate counting, sampling, and average-case complexity
open: Can we sample approximately uniformly from the proper \(q\)-colorings of every graph of maximum degree \(\Delta\) in polynomial time when \(q \ge \Delta+2\)? In other words, is there a polynomial-time sampler that works uniformly over all such graphs at and just above this palette size?
status: Current algorithms handle substantially larger palettes; the cited 2026 literature (Kuchukova, Perkins, and Povill, 2026, *Sampling Colorings with Fixed Color Class Sizes*, arXiv:2603.08259) discusses an approximately \(1.809\Delta\) benchmark for unconstrained colorings, building on earlier work such as Vigoda (2000), *Improved Bounds for Sampling Colorings*.
solved_when: A polynomial-time algorithm exists that, for every graph of maximum degree \(\Delta\), outputs an approximately uniform proper \(q\)-coloring whenever \(q \ge \Delta+2\).
why: It would connect algorithmic sampling to the natural uniqueness threshold suggested by statistical mechanics for antiferromagnetic Potts models, closing the gap between where physics predicts a phase transition and where algorithms provably work.
key_works: Vigoda (2000), *Improved Bounds for Sampling Colorings*; Kuchukova, Perkins, and Povill (2026), *Sampling Colorings with Fixed Color Class Sizes*, arXiv:2603.08259.

bib.title: Efficient sampling near the graph-coloring uniqueness threshold

title: Sampling equitable colorings near q = Δ
subfield: Approximate counting, sampling, and average-case complexity
open: Can we approximately uniformly sample proper graph colorings in which each color class has a prescribed, balanced size, when the number of colors is only slightly above the maximum degree, \(q \ge (1+\varepsilon)\Delta\) for fixed \(\varepsilon > 0\)? Formally, this asks for a polynomial-time sampler for equitable colorings with fixed color-class sizes in the near-\(q = \Delta\) regime.
status: Kuchukova–Perkins–Povill's 2026 work (*Sampling Colorings with Fixed Color Class Sizes*, arXiv:2603.08259) gives polynomial-time sampling in a regime above \(2\Delta\); closing the palette gap between that regime and \((1+\varepsilon)\Delta\) remains open.
solved_when: A polynomial-time algorithm approximately uniformly samples proper colorings with prescribed balanced color-class sizes for all \(q \ge (1+\varepsilon)\Delta\) with fixed \(\varepsilon > 0\).
why: It forces samplers to handle global conservation constraints — fixed species counts — that ordinary coloring samplers ignore, connecting algorithmic sampling to canonical ensembles in statistical mechanics.
key_works: Kuchukova, Perkins, and Povill (2026), *Sampling Colorings with Fixed Color Class Sizes*, arXiv:2603.08259.

title: Superpolynomial depth-two threshold lower bounds
open: Is there an explicit, polynomial-time computable Boolean function that cannot be computed by a depth-two threshold circuit (THR∘THR) with polynomially many gates? Formally, exhibit \(f \in \mathrm{FP}\) such that any \(\mathrm{THR}\circ\mathrm{THR}\) circuit computing \(f\) requires a superpolynomial number of gates.
status: The problem remains open despite substantial lower bounds for restricted threshold architectures and stronger depth restrictions; general polynomial-size depth-two threshold circuits are still poorly understood. See Hajnal, Maass, Pudlák, Szegedy, and Turán (1993), *Threshold Circuits of Bounded Depth*; Viola (2017), lower-bound challenges.
solved_when: An explicit polynomial-time computable function is proven to require superpolynomially many gates in any THR∘THR circuit.
why: It establishes the computational limitations of a simple but expressive neural-style architecture, directly informing depth-separation and representation-complexity questions in machine learning theory.
key_works: Hajnal, Maass, Pudlák, Szegedy, and Turán (1993), *Threshold Circuits of Bounded Depth*; Viola (2017), lower-bound challenges.

title: Superlinear explicit XOR-circuit lower bounds
open: Is there an explicitly constructible binary matrix whose associated linear transformation cannot be computed with a linear number of two-input XOR gates? Formally, construct an explicit matrix requiring \(\omega(n)\) XOR gates in an unrestricted linear circuit.
status: Counting arguments give large lower bounds for most matrices, but known lower bounds for explicit matrices in the unrestricted linear-circuit model remain weak; restricted models such as cancellation-free circuits are better understood.
solved_when: An explicit family of binary matrices is exhibited, with a proof that its linear transformation requires more than \(c \cdot n\) two-input XOR gates for every constant \(c\), i.e. superlinear gate count in the unrestricted linear-circuit model.
why: It would establish that certain explicit linear transforms used in computation and communication have unavoidable cost, pinning down a basic gap between what exists abundantly and what we can prove.
key_works: Valiant (1977), *Graph-Theoretic Arguments in Low-Level Complexity*; Ramya’s rigidity survey and associated bibliography.

title: Dynamic optimality of splay trees
subfield: Communication complexity and adaptive data structures
open: Is the splay tree dynamically optimal — that is, does it serve every access sequence within a constant factor of the best offline binary search tree? Formally, is the splay-tree algorithm constant-competitive with the offline optimal BST?
status: Conjectured by Sleator and Tarjan (1985), DOI: 10.1145/3828.3835. A July 2026 preprint by Chmel et al. (2026), *Splay Trees Are Almost Dynamically Optimal*, arXiv:2607.18498, reports \(O(\log\log n(\log\log\log n)^2)\)-competitiveness — a major advance, but not constant competitiveness.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that splay trees are constant-competitive with the offline optimal BST on every access sequence.
why: It would justify a particularly simple, widely studied self-adjusting structure as universally optimal.
key_works: Sleator and Tarjan (1985), DOI: 10.1145/3828.3835; Chmel et al. (2026), *Splay Trees Are Almost Dynamically Optimal*, arXiv:2607.18498.

title: Dynamic optimality of Greedy BST
subfield: Communication complexity and adaptive data structures
open: Is the online Greedy binary search tree algorithm constant-competitive — that is, does its total cost on every access sequence remain within a constant factor of the offline optimal BST serving the same sequence?
status: Constant competitiveness has long been conjectured. Guo, Pettie, Skora, and Wan's August 2026 preprint (*The Greedy Binary Search Tree Is Non-trivially Competitive*, arXiv:2608.04410) proves competitiveness \(2^{O(\sqrt{\log\log n})}\), which is not constant. The greedy-BST proposals originate with Lucas and Munro.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that Greedy BST's cost on any access sequence is within an absolute constant factor of the dynamic optimal BST's cost; quantitative progress toward that end counts only as partial, as with the current \(2^{O(\sqrt{\log\log n})}\) bound.
why: A positive answer would validate a geometrically motivated alternative route to optimal adaptive search, establishing Greedy as a concrete dynamically optimal BST.
key_works: Lucas and Munro’s greedy-BST proposals; Guo et al. (2026), *The Greedy Binary Search Tree Is Non-trivially Competitive*, arXiv:2608.04410.

title: Recognizing polygon vertex-visibility graphs
open: Given a graph together with a proposed cyclic order on its vertices, is it the vertex-visibility graph of a simple polygon — and if so, can we draw the polygon realizing it?
status: This is a longstanding open recognition problem. Results for point visibility, polygons with holes, and pseudovisibility do not settle recognition in this exact model. Key works: O'Rourke (1993), computational geometry column on visibility recognition; O'Rourke and Streinu's pseudovisibility work; TOPP Problem 17.
solved_when: An algorithm decides, for any graph with a cyclic boundary order, whether it is the vertex-visibility graph of a simple polygon, and constructs a realizing polygon when one exists.
why: A solution would let one reconstruct the geometry of a polygon purely from line-of-sight information about its vertices, a basic inverse problem in shape reconstruction.
key_works: O’Rourke (1993), computational geometry column on visibility recognition; O’Rourke and Streinu’s pseudovisibility work; TOPP Problem 17.

title: Deterministically construct an n-bit prime in polynomial time
subfield: Computational number theory, lattices, and topology
open: Is there a deterministic algorithm that, given n, outputs an n-bit prime in time polynomial in n?
status: Primality testing is deterministic polynomial time, and randomized construction of primes is easy. Polynomial-time pseudodeterministic construction is known — Tao, Croot, and Helfgott (2012), *Deterministic Methods to Find Primes*, DOI: 10.1090/S0025-5718-2011-02542-1; and Chen et al. (2023), *Polynomial-Time Pseudodeterministic Construction of Primes*, ECCC TR23-076 — but full deterministic construction remains open.
solved_when: An explicit deterministic algorithm is given that, for every input n, outputs an n-bit prime in poly(n) time, with a proof of correctness.
why: It would separate recognizing a mathematical object from explicitly finding one, showing determinism can match randomness even for explicit construction of primes.
key_works: Tao, Croot, and Helfgott (2012), *Deterministic Methods to Find Primes*, DOI: 10.1090/S0025-5718-2011-02542-1; Chen et al. (2023), *Polynomial-Time Pseudodeterministic Construction of Primes*, ECCC TR23-076.

title: Single-exponential, polynomial-space exact CVP
subfield: Computational number theory, lattices, and topology
open: Can the exact Euclidean Closest Vector Problem be solved in single-exponential time using only polynomial space, with polynomial dependence on the input bit length? In other words, is there an algorithm achieving \(2^{O(n)}\) time and polynomial space simultaneously?
status: Single-exponential-time and polynomial-space algorithms are each known, but with incompatible resource bounds; achieving both simultaneously remains open.
solved_when: An algorithm is given that solves exact Euclidean CVP in \(2^{O(n)}\) time and polynomial space, where the dependence on the input bit length is polynomial.
why: It would make exact lattice decoding and optimization practical under realistic memory constraints, where current single-exponential-time methods cannot run.
key_works: Micciancio and Voulgaris (2013); Blömer and Naewe, *Solving the Closest Vector Problem with Respect to ℓp Norms*, arXiv:1104.3720.

title: Polynomial-time unknot recognition
subfield: Computational number theory, lattices, and topology
open: Is there a polynomial-time algorithm that decides whether a given knot diagram represents the unknot? Formally, given a diagram with n crossings, decide unknottedness in time polynomial in n.
status: The problem is decidable, and short certificates are known on both sides through major results in low-dimensional topology — notably Hass, Lagarias, and Pippenger (1999), *The Computational Complexity of Knot and Link Problems*, and Lackenby (2021), *The Efficient Certification of Knottedness and Thurston Norm*. Polynomial time remains unresolved.
solved_when: An algorithm is exhibited that decides, for every knot diagram, whether it represents the unknot, in time polynomial in the number of crossings.
why: It is a central test of the algorithmic accessibility of three-dimensional topology; a resolution would clarify which knot problems are genuinely tractable and enable efficient knot detection in applications such as DNA knot identification in molecular biology.
key_works: Hass, Lagarias, and Pippenger (1999), *The Computational Complexity of Knot and Link Problems*; Lackenby (2021), *The Efficient Certification of Knottedness and Thurston Norm*.

title: Logarithmic-round deterministic network decomposition

solved_when: A deterministic LOCAL-model algorithm produces a network decomposition with \(O(\log n)\) colors and \(O(\log n)\) weak diameter in \(O(\log n)\) rounds.
why: Network decomposition serves as a general derandomization engine for distributed algorithms, so a logarithmic-round construction would sharpen the foundation for fast deterministic distributed computing.
key_works: Rozhoň and Ghaffari (2020), *Polylogarithmic-Time Deterministic Network Decomposition and Distributed Derandomization*; Chang and Dolatabadi (2026), arXiv:2609.10044.

title: Near-log-squared deterministic list edge coloring with 1+ε palettes

title: Nearly locally balanced cuts in polylogarithmic rounds

solved_when: A distributed algorithm computes a cut in which every vertex has at least a \(1/2-\varepsilon\) fraction of its neighbors across the cut, in polylogarithmic rounds independent of \(\Delta\).
why: It would pin down the distributed complexity of finding approximate local optima, and it connects to game-theoretic questions of distributed convergence to approximate equilibria.

title: Tenfold faster exact maximum flow on a frozen diverse corpus
subfield: Experimental algorithms, benchmarks, infrastructure, and funding
open: Can exact maximum-flow solvers be made an order of magnitude faster in practice, not just in asymptotic theory? The goal is at least a tenfold geometric-mean end-to-end speedup over a declared baseline on a preregistered diverse corpus, with parsing and certificate verification included, exactness preserved, and a stated memory budget respected.

why: It would convert recent asymptotic breakthroughs into measurable value on real optimization workloads, closing the gap between theory and deployed implementations.
key_works: Chen et al. (2022), *Maximum Flow and Minimum-Cost Flow in Almost-Linear Time*, arXiv:2203.00671; Goldberg and Tarjan’s push–relabel work.

title: Truly subcubic weighted APSP
open: Can we compute all-pairs shortest paths on arbitrary weighted directed graphs in truly subcubic time? Formally, is there an \(O(n^{3-\varepsilon})\)-time algorithm for some fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), under standard weight and arithmetic conventions?
status: Subcubic-by-subpolynomial-factor algorithms are known, but a fixed exponent improvement remains a central open problem; see Vassilevska Williams and Williams (2018), *Subcubic Equivalences Between Path, Matrix, and Triangle Problems*, DOI: 10.1145/3186893.
solved_when: An algorithm is given that computes weighted directed APSP in \(O(n^{3-\varepsilon})\) time for a fixed constant \(\varepsilon>0\).
why: A fixed-exponent improvement would yield faster algorithms for a large equivalence class of path, matrix, and optimization problems, with concrete impact on large-scale shortest-path computation in transportation optimization.
key_works: Vassilevska Williams and Williams (2018), *Subcubic Equivalences Between Path, Matrix, and Triangle Problems*, DOI: 10.1145/3186893.

title: Linear-time directed nonnegative shortest paths
subfield: Graph algorithms, parallelism, and dynamic computation
open: Can single-source shortest paths in directed graphs with nonnegative real edge weights be computed deterministically in linear time in the comparison-addition model? Formally, is an \(O(m+n)\) deterministic comparison-addition-time algorithm achievable?

why: It would remove a fundamental overhead from a ubiquitous graph primitive, including large-scale routing in transportation systems.

title: Deterministic worst-case polylogarithmic dynamic maximal matching
subfield: Graph algorithms, parallelism, and dynamic computation
open: Can a maximal matching be maintained deterministically under adversarial edge insertions and deletions with worst-case polylogarithmic update time per operation? That is, no randomness, no amortization, and no expensive deferred updates — a polylogarithmic bound on every single update.

solved_when: A deterministic dynamic algorithm exists that maintains a maximal matching under adversarial insertions and deletions with worst-case update time polylogarithmic in the number of vertices per operation.
why: It supplies predictable latency per update without randomization or deferred expensive updates, which is what real-time systems with worst-case scheduling guarantees actually need.

why: It tests whether randomness in edge order is a real resource saving in streaming approximation, and directly informs limited-memory graph analytics in network measurement, where beating the trivial approximation under tight memory budgets matters.

title: Single-exponential exact treewidth
subfield: Parameterized algorithms, kernelization, and structural graph algorithms
open: Can we decide whether an \(n\)-vertex graph has treewidth at most \(k\), and produce an optimal-width tree decomposition when it does, in \(2^{O(k)}n\) time?
status: Fixed-parameter algorithms and single-exponential approximation algorithms for treewidth are known (building on work such as Bodlaender (1996), *A Linear-Time Algorithm for Finding Tree-Decompositions of Small Treewidth*), but the exact single-exponential linear-input target remains explicitly open in Korhendon's *Open Problems* list (September 2026).

solved_when: A deterministic algorithm computes an optimal directed feedback vertex set of size \(k\) in \(2^{O(k)}n^{O(1)}\) time.
why: It would sharpen exact cycle-breaking algorithms for directed networks, including feedback-loop intervention in systems biology.

title: Unconditional NP-hardness of total MCSP
open: Is the Minimum Circuit Size Problem for complete (total) truth tables NP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions?
status: Open since the 1950s–1970s origins of circuit minimization. Partial-function MCSP hardness (Hirahara, 2022) and conditional hardness results (Hirahara and Ilango, 2025, *NP-Hardness of the Minimum Circuit Size Problem from Well-Studied Assumptions*, DOI: 10.1109/FOCS63196.2025.00087) do not settle total MCSP under this reduction.

why: It would explain the apparent intractability of recognizing computational structure in explicit data, with connections to machine learning's task of distinguishing structure from randomness.

title: BPL equals L
open: Can every bounded-error randomized computation using \(O(\log n)\) space be simulated deterministically with the same \(O(\log n)\) space bound — that is, does BPL equal L?
status: Open for decades. General space-bounded generators and simulations incur additional space; recent work sharpens equivalences between logspace derandomization and hardness (Nisan 1992, *Pseudorandom Generators for Space-Bounded Computation*; Shalunov 2024, *Leakage-Resilient Hardness Equivalence to Logspace Derandomization*, arXiv:2312.14023, DOI: 10.4230/LIPIcs.MFCS.2024.83).
solved_when: A deterministic simulation of any BPL machine using at most \(O(\log n)\) workspace is exhibited, proving BPL = L.
why: It would make randomized streaming-style computations deterministic without increasing their memory order.
key_works: Nisan (1992), *Pseudorandom Generators for Space-Bounded Computation*; Shalunov (2024), *Leakage-Resilient Hardness Equivalence to Logspace Derandomization*, arXiv:2312.14023, DOI: 10.4230/LIPIcs.MFCS.2024.83.

title: Optimal-seed generators for general branching programs
open: Is there an explicit pseudorandom generator, with seed length O(log n), that fools polynomial-length, polynomial-width read-once branching programs to inverse-polynomial error?
status: This is a longstanding target that lies beyond currently available general seed-length bounds; even proving BPL = L would not automatically yield this particular black-box generator. Key works: Nisan (1992); Tal (2020), *Derandomizing Space-Bounded Computation* workshop materials; Shalunov (2024).
solved_when: An explicit generator with O(log n) seed length is constructed and proved to fool polynomial-length, polynomial-width read-once branching programs up to inverse-polynomial error.
why: It would supply reusable, randomness-efficient simulation rather than problem-specific derandomization, with applications such as streaming systems needing small-state reproducible randomization.
key_works: Nisan (1992); Tal (2020), *Derandomizing Space-Bounded Computation* workshop materials; Shalunov (2024).

title: Strongly explicit optimal Ramsey graphs
open: Can we explicitly construct graphs on \(N\) vertices with no clique or independent set larger than \(O(\log N)\), while keeping adjacency computable in time polynomial in \(\log N\)? In other words, can the Ramsey behavior of random graphs be matched by a strongly explicit construction?
status: Random graphs achieve the desired bound (Erdős, 1947, probabilistic Ramsey lower bound). Explicit constructions remain weaker: Li's 2023 extractor advances (arXiv:2303.06802) yield polylogarithmic Ramsey bounds, not the optimal logarithmic bound.
solved_when: An explicit construction exists of graphs on \(N\) vertices with neither clique nor independent set exceeding \(O(\log N)\), with adjacency computable in time polynomial in \(\log N\).
why: It would make probabilistic extremal-combinatorial behavior efficiently explicit, turning an existence argument into a usable deterministic object.

title: Subquadratic three-query relaxed locally decodable codes
subfield: Quantum complexity and locally decodable codes
open: Can a three-query relaxed locally decodable code over a constant alphabet encode messages of length \(k\) using codewords of length \(O(k^{2-\varepsilon})\) for some fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), or is near-quadratic length essentially forced once only three queries are allowed?
status: Gur–Minzer–Weissenberg–Zheng's December 2025 construction (arXiv:2512.12960) achieves length \(\widetilde O(k^2)\); general lower bounds do not settle the exact exponent. Related work appears in Goldberg, Gur, and Saraogi (2025), arXiv:2511.21659.
solved_when: Either a constant-alphabet three-query relaxed LDC construction of length \(O(k^{2-\varepsilon})\) for some fixed \(\varepsilon>0\) is given, or a lower bound is proved showing that such codes require near-quadratic length.

title: A factor-two approximation for shortest common superstring
open: Does there exist a polynomial-time algorithm that, given any set of strings, produces a common superstring of length at most twice the optimum? Equivalently, is a factor-two approximation for the shortest common superstring problem achievable in polynomial time?
status: General approximation remains above two in the cited literature. Shibata's September 2026 preprint, *Disproving the Greedy Superstring Conjecture* (arXiv:2609.01365), reports that the classical greedy algorithm can have ratio at least \(9/4\); this defeats that proposed route, not the general factor-two target. Other key work: Nikolaev (2024), arXiv:2407.20422.
solved_when: A polynomial-time algorithm is given, with proof, whose output superstring has length at most \(2\cdot\mathrm{OPT}\) for every input instance.
why: The shortest common superstring is the central overlap-based model of sequence assembly, so a factor-two algorithm would directly improve the guaranteed quality of genome assembly in bioinformatics.
key_works: Nikolaev (2024), arXiv:2407.20422; Shibata (2026), *Disproving the Greedy Superstring Conjecture*, arXiv:2609.01365.

title: Factor-two superstring approximation with reverse complements
open: Can the shortest common superstring problem be approximated within factor two when each input string may be embedded in either its original orientation or its reverse-complement orientation? Formally, the goal is a polynomial-time algorithm achieving an approximation ratio of 2 for the shortest common superstring with reverse complements.
status: Yamano and Shibuya (2026) give an \(8/3\)-approximation and prove hardness beyond exact optimization (*Improved Approximation Algorithms and Hardness Results for Shortest Common Superstring with Reverse Complements*, DOI: 10.4230/LIPIcs.WABI.2026.2); a large gap remains between \(8/3\) and the target factor of two.
solved_when: A polynomial-time algorithm produces a superstring whose length is at most twice the optimum for the reverse-complement variant, for arbitrary input strings.
why: It captures the orientation ambiguity of double-stranded DNA, which ordinary superstring formulations ignore, so progress here directly improves models of sequence assembly from double-stranded biological data.
key_works: Yamano and Shibuya (2026), *Improved Approximation Algorithms and Hardness Results for Shortest Common Superstring with Reverse Complements*, DOI: 10.4230/LIPIcs.WABI.2026.2.

title: P versus uniform NC
open: Does every problem solvable in polynomial time admit uniform Boolean circuits of polynomial size and polylogarithmic depth — that is, can polynomial-time computation always be parallelized efficiently? Formally, the question asks whether P equals (some reasonable uniform version of) NC.
status: Open since the development of P-completeness and parallel complexity theory. Numerous natural problems are known to be P-complete (e.g., the circuit value problem, per Ladner (1975), *The Circuit Value Problem Is Log Space Complete for P*), so they would be inherently sequential if the classes differ, but this presumed sequentiality remains conditional. Standard references include Greenlaw, Hoover, and Ruzzo (1995), *Limits to Parallel Computation: P-Completeness Theory*, and the Arora–Barak textbook.
solved_when: A proof that P ⊆ uniform NC, or a separation showing some polynomial-time language has no polynomial-size, polylogarithmic-depth uniform circuit family.
why: It draws the line between computations that parallel hardware can dramatically accelerate and those that are genuinely sequential, directly informing the parallelization limits of simulation and iterative scientific computing.
key_works: Ladner (1975), *The Circuit Value Problem Is Log Space Complete for P*; Greenlaw, Hoover, and Ruzzo (1995), *Limits to Parallel Computation: P-Completeness Theory*; Arora–Barak textbook.

title: Matrix multiplication exponent ω
open: What is the true value of ω, the smallest exponent for which n×n matrix multiplication can be done in n^{ω+ε} time? In particular, is ω = 2?
status: Open since Strassen (1969, ω ≤ 2.81). The current record is ω < 2.371866 (Duan–Wu–Zhou 2025), improving Alman–Vassilevska Williams 2021's bound of 2.3728596. Group-theoretic approaches (Cohn–Umans) have stalled at the same barriers.
solved_when: A proof that ω = 2, or more generally any improved bound on ω together with a determination of its exact value.
why: Fast matrix multiplication underlies nearly all of numerical algebra, and the value of ω sets complexity limits across combinatorial and scientific computing.
key_works: V. Strassen, "Gaussian elimination is not optimal", Numer. Math. 1969; J. Alman, V. Vassilevska Williams, "A refined laser method and faster matrix multiplication", SODA 2021 (arXiv:2010.05846); R. Duan, H. Wu, R. Zhou, "Faster matrix multiplication via asymmetric hashing", FOCS 2025 (verify)
