title: Near-linear seed length in generic OWF-to-PRG constructions
open: Can every one-way function on \(n\)-bit inputs be converted, by a generic black-box construction, into a pseudorandom generator with seed length only \(n^{1+o(1)}\)? Formally, the goal is a secure pseudorandom generator built from an arbitrary one-way function under a clearly specified black-box security-preserving reduction.
status: Generic constructions incur substantial overhead; stronger results are available for special classes such as regular one-way functions. The unrestricted near-linear target remains open in the cited problem formulation. Key references include Håstad, Impagliazzo, Levin, and Luby (1999), *A Pseudorandom Generator from Any One-Way Function*, and the Trevisan memorial collection (2024).
solved_when: A construction from any one-way function on \(n\)-bit inputs yields a secure pseudorandom generator with seed length \(n^{1+o(1)}\), together with a clearly specified black-box security-preserving reduction.
why: It would make foundational cryptographic reductions quantitatively useful, so that the generic OWF-to-PRG transformation could be applied without prohibitive overhead in seed length.
key_works: Håstad, Impagliazzo, Levin, and Luby (1999), *A Pseudorandom Generator from Any One-Way Function*; Trevisan memorial collection (2024).

title: Fourier min-entropy–influence conjecture
open: Does every Boolean function have a Fourier coefficient carrying a nontrivial share of its spectral mass, in an amount controlled by its total influence? Formally, is there a universal constant \(C\) such that \(-\log_2 \max_S \widehat{f}(S)^2 \le C\,\mathrm{Inf}(f)\) for every Boolean function \(f\)?
status: The conjecture remains open; it is a weaker but still unresolved relative of the Fourier entropy–influence (FEI) conjecture. Recent work has improved the necessary lower bounds on the constant (*A Lower Bound on the Constant in the Fourier Min-Entropy/Influence Conjecture*, 2025, DOI: 10.1016/j.dam.2024.12.011) rather than establishing the general inequality.
solved_when: The inequality \(-\log_2 \max_S \widehat{f}(S)^2 \le C\,\mathrm{Inf}(f)\) is proved for all Boolean functions with a single universal constant \(C\).
why: It would guarantee that any function of small total influence has a substantially large Fourier coefficient, tying spectral concentration directly to influence.
key_works: *A Lower Bound on the Constant in the Fourier Min-Entropy/Influence Conjecture* (2025), DOI: 10.1016/j.dam.2024.12.011; authors (verify).

title: Mansour’s conjecture
open: Does every \(s\)-term DNF formula concentrate nearly all of its Fourier mass on a polynomially large set of coefficients, for any fixed approximation error? More precisely, Mansour conjectured that for each fixed error, all but a small fraction of the Fourier weight lies on poly(\(s\)) many Fourier coefficients.
status: The conjecture was proposed in the early 1990s, in Mansour's original Fourier-learning work. It is known to hold for random DNF formulas (Mansour's Conjecture Is True for Random DNF Formulas, 2010, ECCC TR10-023) and for restricted-parameter cases, with sharper bounds on Fourier concentration of DNFs given in arXiv:2109.04525; the general concentration statement remains unresolved.
solved_when: A proof (or refutation) is given of the general statement that an \(s\)-term DNF has nearly all its Fourier mass on polynomially many Fourier coefficients, for every fixed approximation error, with no restrictions on the DNF's parameters.
why: Fourier concentration of DNF directly controls both spectral complexity and sample/representation complexity in learning, so a proof would substantially advance efficient DNF learning and Boolean-analysis tools for pseudorandomness and derandomization.
key_works: Mansour’s original Fourier-learning work; *Mansour’s Conjecture Is True for Random DNF Formulas* (2010), ECCC TR10-023; *Sharper Bounds on Fourier Concentration of DNFs*, arXiv:2109.04525.

title: Exponential Time Hypothesis
open: Is there genuinely no way to solve 3-SAT on \(n\) variables substantially faster than brute force — specifically, is \(2^{o(n)}\) time impossible?
status: Formulated around 1999–2001 in work of Impagliazzo, Paturi, and Zane (2001), *Which Problems Have Strongly Exponential Complexity?* (DOI: 10.1006/jcss.2001.1774). Exact algorithms continue to improve the exponential bases, but neither a subexponential algorithm nor an unconditional exponential lower bound is known.
solved_when: Either a \(2^{o(n)}\)-time algorithm for 3-SAT on \(n\) variables is given, or an unconditional proof that no such algorithm exists.
why: ETH underpins quantitative lower bounds far more precise than NP-hardness, giving exact exponential trade-offs across a wide range of problems.
key_works: Impagliazzo, Paturi, and Zane (2001), *Which Problems Have Strongly Exponential Complexity?*, DOI: 10.1006/jcss.2001.1774.

title: Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis
open: Does the difficulty of SAT grow all the way to the trivial 2^n bound as clause width increases? Formally: is it true that for every ε > 0 there exists a clause width k such that k-SAT cannot be solved in O((2−ε)^n) time?
status: Open since Impagliazzo and Paturi's work (Impagliazzo and Paturi, 2001, *On the Complexity of k-SAT*; see also Vassilevska Williams, 2018, *Some Open Problems in Fine-Grained Complexity*, DOI: 10.1145/3300150.3300158). Note that refuting SETH would not necessarily refute the weaker Exponential Time Hypothesis.
solved_when: Either an ε > 0 is exhibited such that k-SAT is solvable in O((2−ε)^n) time for every clause width k (refuting the hypothesis), or a clause width k is proved to resist O((2−ε)^n)-time algorithms for every ε > 0 (confirming it).
why: SETH anchors sharp running-time lower bounds for a wide range of polynomial-time and exponential-time problems; resolving it would either unlock substantially faster SAT algorithms or firmly justify the many conditional hardness results built on it.
key_works: Impagliazzo and Paturi (2001), *On the Complexity of k-SAT*; Vassilevska Williams (2018), *Some Open Problems in Fine-Grained Complexity*, DOI: 10.1145/3300150.3300158.

title: Log-rank conjecture
subfield: Communication complexity and adaptive data structures
open: Is the deterministic two-party communication complexity of every Boolean function at most polynomial in the logarithm of the rank of its communication matrix? Formally, does D(f) ≤ poly(log rank(M_f)) hold for all f?
status: Open since the late 1970s–1980s. Known bounds depend approximately on the square root of rank, which remains far from polynomial dependence on log-rank. New equivalent formulations of the conjecture appeared in 2025–2026; see Lovász and Saks (1988) and Hambardzumyan, Lovett, and Shirley, *The Log-Rank Conjecture: New Equivalent Formulations*, arXiv:2510.02583, DOI: 10.4230/LIPIcs.CCC.2026.7.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that deterministic communication complexity is bounded by a polynomial in log(rank) of the communication matrix for all functions.
why: It would establish that algebraic simplicity (low rank of the communication matrix) forces efficient distributed communication, bridging linear algebra and communication complexity.
key_works: Lovász and Saks (1988); Hambardzumyan, Lovett, and Shirley, *The Log-Rank Conjecture: New Equivalent Formulations*, arXiv:2510.02583, DOI: 10.4230/LIPIcs.CCC.2026.7.

title: Splay-tree traversal conjecture
subfield: Communication complexity and adaptive data structures
open: Does a splay tree access the preorder traversal of a fixed BST in only linear total time, regardless of the splay tree's initial shape? Formally, the conjecture is that performing the sequence of n accesses given by a preorder traversal of an arbitrary BST, starting from an arbitrary initial splay tree on the same keys, costs O(n) total time.
status: Open since Sleator–Tarjan's original work; the known access theorems do not establish the full conjecture. Key works: Sleator and Tarjan (1985), *Self-Adjusting Binary Search Trees*, DOI: 10.1145/3828.3835; Chmel et al. (2026), arXiv:2607.18498.
solved_when: A proof (or refutation) that the total access time is O(n) for every BST and every initial splay tree configuration.
why: It would show that splay trees recover hidden tree structure in an access sequence with optimal overhead, with connections to structural compression of access sequences in information theory.
key_works: Sleator and Tarjan (1985), *Self-Adjusting Binary Search Trees*, DOI: 10.1145/3828.3835; Chmel et al. (2026), arXiv:2607.18498.

title: Minimum-color simple cycle in polynomial time
subfield: Parameterized algorithms, kernelization, and structural graph algorithms
open: Given a graph whose edges are colored, can we find in polynomial time a simple cycle that uses as few distinct colors as possible? Alternatively, give an appropriate hardness classification showing this is out of reach.
status: Quasipolynomial-time algorithms follow from work on monotone submodular cycle costs (Fomin, Golovach, Korhonen, Lokshtanov, and Stamoulis, 2022, *Shortest Cycles With Monotone Submodular Costs*, arXiv:2211.04797). A polynomial-time algorithm remains open in the cited formulation.
solved_when: A polynomial-time algorithm for computing a minimum-color simple cycle in an edge-colored graph is produced, or a hardness classification resolving the cited formulation is established.
why: It captures network cycles whose cost is determined by the number of distinct resources or failure domains involved rather than by the number of edges, a natural model in network design.
key_works: Fomin, Golovach, Korhonen, Lokshtanov, and Stamoulis (2022), *Shortest Cycles With Monotone Submodular Costs*, arXiv:2211.04797.

title: Unique Games Conjecture
open: Is it NP-hard to distinguish a system of unique-label constraints that is almost fully satisfiable from one whose optimum is arbitrarily small, with the alphabet size allowed to grow with the gap? A resolution in either direction would settle the Unique Games Conjecture.
status: Proposed by Khot in 2002 (Khot, *On the Power of Unique 2-Prover 1-Round Games*). Powerful approximation consequences and substantial partial hardness results are known — notably the integrality-ratio and hardness framework of Raghavendra (2008), *Optimal Algorithms and Inapproximability Results for Every CSP?* — but the conjecture remains unresolved. An IAS exposition (2026) surveys the area. Related lines of attack come from Gaussian noise stability in probability and from energy landscapes of constraint systems in statistical physics.
solved_when: A proof or refutation of the NP-hardness of the described almost-satisfiable versus arbitrarily-small-optimum distinction for unique-label constraint systems, where the alphabet size may depend on the gap.
why: A proof would organize many sharp approximation thresholds under one principle; a refutation would reopen the true approximability landscape for a large class of problems.
key_works: Khot (2002), *On the Power of Unique 2-Prover 1-Round Games*; Raghavendra (2008), *Optimal Algorithms and Inapproximability Results for Every CSP?*; IAS exposition (2026).

title: The 4/3 subtour-LP integrality-gap conjecture
open: Is the subtour-elimination linear programming relaxation for the metric traveling salesman problem always nearly optimal? Specifically, does every metric TSP instance admit a tour of cost at most \(4/3\) times the subtour-elimination LP optimum?
status: The conjecture has been open for decades, with continued progress on special structural cases; a 2026 result by Villa, Vercesi, Barta, and Mastrolilli proves the gap is \(4/3\) when the LP optimum has at most \(n+8\) nonzero components, building on the foundational relaxation introduced by Held and Karp (1970–1971).
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that every metric TSP instance has a tour costing at most \(4/3\) times its subtour-elimination LP optimum; equivalently, a determination of whether the integrality gap of the subtour LP on metric instances is at most \(4/3\).
why: It would establish the exact strength of the most important TSP relaxation, pinning down the worst-case gap between the LP bound and the true optimum.
key_works: Held and Karp (1970–1971); Villa, Vercesi, Barta, and Mastrolilli (2026), *The Integrality Gap … Is 4/3 if the LP Solution Has at Most n+8 Non-Zero Components*.

title: Strong matroid secretary conjecture
open: Is there an online algorithm that, for every matroid, selects an independent set of weight at least a \(1/e\) fraction of the maximum offline weight when elements arrive in uniformly random order? That is, does the optimal secretary constant extend from classical settings to arbitrary independence constraints?
status: The constant-competitive matroid secretary conjecture was reported solved in September 2026 (Singla, *The Matroid Secretary Conjecture Is True*, arXiv:2609.14555). The stronger \(1/e\) target for all matroids remains open; a separate 2026 preprint by Abdi, Banihashem, Hajiaghayi, and Mittal (*On the Strong Matroid Secretary Conjecture and Beyond*, arXiv:2609.19118) achieves \(1/e\) for linear matroids.
solved_when: A single algorithm achieving \(1/e\)-competitiveness for every matroid in the random-arrival model is proven.
why: It would pin down the optimal classical secretary constant under general independence constraints, closing the gap left by constant-competitive results.
key_works: Singla (2026), *The Matroid Secretary Conjecture Is True*, arXiv:2609.14555; Abdi, Banihashem, Hajiaghayi, and Mittal (2026), *On the Strong Matroid Secretary Conjecture and Beyond*, arXiv:2609.19118.

title: Efficient 1/e secretary algorithms for represented linear matroids
open: Is there a polynomial-time 1/e-competitive algorithm for the linear matroid secretary problem when the matroid is given explicitly by a matrix representation? The known 1/e-competitive guarantee exists only in a computationally unrestricted model, and it remains open whether it can be realized efficiently with bounded bit complexity.
status: A 1/e-competitive linear-matroid secretary result was established by Abdi, Banihashem, Hajiaghayi, and Mittal (2026) in *On the Strong Matroid Secretary Conjecture and Beyond* (arXiv:2609.19118), but only in a computationally unrestricted model; turning it into an efficient algorithm given an explicit matrix representation remains a distinct, open algorithmic issue, and any success criterion must account for bit complexity and representation assumptions.
solved_when: A polynomial-time algorithm, respecting the bit complexity of the input matrix representation, achieves 1/e-competitiveness for the linear matroid secretary problem.
why: It converts the optimal competitive guarantee from a pure existence result into an implementable online selection method, e.g., for online selection of linearly independent measurements in experimental design.
key_works: Abdi, Banihashem, Hajiaghayi, and Mittal (2026), *On the Strong Matroid Secretary Conjecture and Beyond*, arXiv:2609.19118.

title: Sharp pass–space tradeoff for Max-Cut
open: How many streaming passes over the input are needed before a small-space algorithm can beat the trivial Max-Cut approximation? Formally, prove a lower bound of the form \(p\,s=\Omega(\sqrt n)\) for any \(p\)-pass, \(s\)-space algorithm that achieves more than the trivial approximation.
status: Singer's 2025 formulation of the problem records weaker tradeoff lower bounds, including an \(n^{1/3}\)-scale benchmark from recent work on multipass streaming lower bounds by Fei, Minzer, and Wang (2025); the sharp \(\sqrt n\) bound remains open.
solved_when: A proof establishes that any \(p\)-pass, \(s\)-space streaming algorithm beating the trivial Max-Cut approximation must satisfy \(p\,s=\Omega(\sqrt n)\).
why: It would precisely quantify how much repeated access to the input can substitute for memory, pinning down the fundamental pass–space exchange rate for a canonical streaming problem.
key_works: Fei, Minzer, and Wang (2025), multipass streaming lower bounds; Singer (2025).

title: Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits conjecture
subfield: Approximate counting, sampling, and average-case complexity
open: Is there a universal constant bounding the KLS constant of every isotropic log-concave distribution, independent of dimension? Equivalently, does the dimensional KLS constant admit a dimension-free upper bound?
status: The conjecture was proposed in 1995 by Kannan, Lovász, and Simonovits (*Isoperimetric Problems for Convex Bodies and a Localization Lemma*). The best current progress is a July 2026 preprint by Letwin (*The KLS Constant Is O(log^{1/4} n)*, arXiv:2607.24164), which proves an \(O((\log n)^{1/4})\) bound; the dimension-free target remains open.
solved_when: The KLS constant of every isotropic log-concave distribution in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is bounded by an absolute constant independent of \(n\).
why: A dimension-free bound would sharpen high-dimensional sampling, concentration, and convex optimization guarantees in one stroke.
key_works: Kannan, Lovász, and Simonovits (1995), *Isoperimetric Problems for Convex Bodies and a Localization Lemma*; Letwin (2026), *The KLS Constant Is O(log^{1/4} n)*, arXiv:2607.24164.

title: Certificate-aware finite-size scaling atlas for SAT
subfield: Experimental algorithms, benchmarks, infrastructure, and funding
open: Can we build a preregistered, reproducible atlas that measures both solver cost and certificate-checking cost across controlled SAT instance families? Formally, the atlas would span controlled random and structured families, multiple sizes, solver families, and hardware platforms.
status: Proposed experimental target. SAT competitions (e.g., Codel, Fazekas, Heule, and Iser 2025, *The Results of SAT Competition 2025*) provide valuable benchmarks, but competition rankings alone do not establish transferable finite-size scaling laws; classical hard/easy distributions go back to Mitchell, Selman, and Levesque (1992), *Hard and Easy Distributions of SAT Problems*.
solved_when: Such an atlas exists: preregistered, reproducible, covering controlled random and structured SAT families, multiple sizes, solver families, and hardware platforms, with measurements of both solver and certificate-checking cost.
why: It separates solver progress from instance selection, hardware effects, and proof overhead, and it prevents small finite experiments from being overstated as evidence for ETH or P ≠ NP.
key_works: Codel, Fazekas, Heule, and Iser (2025), *The Results of SAT Competition 2025*; Mitchell, Selman, and Levesque (1992), *Hard and Easy Distributions of SAT Problems*.

title: Certified planted-clique computation frontier
subfield: Experimental algorithms, benchmarks, infrastructure, and funding
open: Can we build a certified empirical map of planted-clique computation, measuring how recovery probability, wall-clock cost, memory, and energy scale with the graph size \(n\) and the planted-clique size? The experiment should use preregistered instance generators, held-out seeds for evaluation, and independent verification that reported cliques are genuine.
status: Currently a proposed measurement target only; existing theoretical thresholds and restricted-model lower bounds (e.g., Barak et al., 2016, arXiv:1604.03084, alongside the classical planted-clique literature of Alon, Krivelevich, and Sudakov, 1998) do not supply a hardware-normalized empirical frontier.
solved_when: A preregistered study exists that reports recovery probability, wall-clock cost, memory, and energy as functions of \(n\) and planted-clique size, with instances drawn from preregistered generators, evaluation on held-out seeds, and independently checked recovered cliques.
why: It shows where asymptotic algorithmic distinctions actually become observable in practice and closes off cherry-picked "below-threshold" claims that cannot be compared across hardware.
key_works: Alon, Krivelevich, and Sudakov (1998); Barak et al. (2016), arXiv:1604.03084.

title: Proof-certified MCSP benchmark corpus
subfield: Experimental algorithms, benchmarks, infrastructure, and funding
open: Can we build a public corpus of truth tables for circuit minimization in which every known case carries an independently checkable certificate of its circuit-size upper or lower bound? The corpus should also flag the genuinely unknown cases and include train/test splits designed to control isomorphism and transformation leakage.
status: This is a proposed data target. Existing hardness theorems, including Hirahara and Ilango (2025), *NP-Hardness of the Minimum Circuit Size Problem from Well-Studied Assumptions*, do not supply a standardized, certificate-backed empirical benchmark for circuit minimization. The proposal draws on a metacomplexity open-problem collection, with related concerns in machine-learning benchmark leakage and certified circuit optimization in hardware synthesis.
solved_when: A publicly released benchmark corpus exists containing truth tables with machine-checkable circuit-size upper and lower certificates, explicitly marked unknown cases, and train/test splits that control both isomorphism and transformation leakage.
why: It enables meaningful, reproducible evaluation of search, synthesis, and learned circuit-minimization methods, which currently lack a standardized empirical footing.
key_works: Hirahara and Ilango (2025), *NP-Hardness of the Minimum Circuit Size Problem from Well-Studied Assumptions*; metacomplexity open-problem collection.

title: Adaptive-adversary dynamic-graph benchmark
subfield: Experimental algorithms, benchmarks, infrastructure, and funding
open: Can we build a replayable benchmark for dynamic graph algorithms in which the adversary is adaptive — that is, each graph update may depend on the algorithm's previous outputs — with explicit correctness certificates and measurements of worst-case latency, rebuilds, memory, and random-seed exposure?
status: Currently only a proposed benchmark target; no such benchmark exists. The theoretical distinction between oblivious and adaptive adversaries is not captured by ordinary fixed update traces.
solved_when: A replayable benchmark exists in which updates may depend on prior outputs, correctness certificates are explicit, and worst-case latency, rebuild counts, memory usage, and random-seed exposure are all measured and reported.
why: It tests whether practical dynamic algorithms actually survive the adversary model claimed in their theoretical analysis, since the distinction between oblivious and adaptive adversaries is invisible to ordinary fixed update traces.
key_works: Henzinger et al. (2015), OMv framework, arXiv:1504.06148; Christiansen (2025), *Algorithms for Dynamic Graphs*.

title: Interoperable formal library of complexity reductions
subfield: Experimental algorithms, benchmarks, infrastructure, and funding
open: Can we build a shared, versioned library of machine-checked complexity reductions that different theorem provers can actually compose? Each reduction's certificate should record the source and target problems, promise conditions, computational model, encoding, and exact resource overhead.
status: A proposed engineering target, not a claim that formalized reductions do not exist; the challenge is interoperable coverage and auditable composition across theorem provers and models.
solved_when: A versioned library exists whose reduction certificates uniformly capture the source and target problems, promise conditions, computational model, encoding, and exact resource overhead, and whose reductions compose in an auditable way across provers and models.
why: It would prevent incorrect reuse of reductions and support trustworthy automated complexity research.
key_works: The mathlib Community (2020), *The Lean Mathematical Library*, arXiv:1910.09336; Cook (1971); Karp (1972).

title: Tenfold faster end-to-end trusted SAT proof checking
subfield: Experimental algorithms, benchmarks, infrastructure, and funding
open: Can the entire pipeline of SAT proof checking — generation, conversion, transport, and independently trusted verification — be made an order of magnitude faster? Specifically, can total end-to-end time be reduced by at least tenfold on a fixed benchmark suite while preserving exactly the same verified logical guarantee?
status: Proposed moonshot. Verified LRAT/LPR, GRAT, and pseudo-Boolean checkers already exist (e.g., Tan, Heule, and Myreen, *Verified LRAT and LPR Proof Checking with cake_lpr*; SAT Competition 2025 checking requirements), so basic proof-checker existence is settled; the open target is the specified tenfold end-to-end improvement.
solved_when: Total time for proof generation, conversion, transport, and independently trusted checking on the fixed benchmark suite is reduced by at least tenfold, with no reduction in the verified logical guarantee.
why: It would make certified computation less expensive than rerunning untrusted solvers, removing the main practical excuse for accepting results without proof.
key_works: Tan, Heule, and Myreen, *Verified LRAT and LPR Proof Checking with cake_lpr*; SAT Competition 2025 checking requirements.

title: Cross-platform energy-to-verified-solution benchmark
subfield: Experimental algorithms, benchmarks, infrastructure, and funding
open: Can we build a reproducible benchmark that measures the energy an algorithm actually spends, in joules per independently verified solution? The metric should account for the full cost of computing — preprocessing, failed runs, data movement, and certificate checking — not just the winning execution.
status: This is currently a proposed data and measurement target; no such benchmark exists. Runtime rankings and coarse carbon estimators do not by themselves provide this controlled comparison. Related work includes Lannelongue, Grealey, and Inouye (2021), *Green Algorithms: Quantifying the Carbon Footprint of Computation*, DOI: 10.1002/advs.202100707, and the SAT Competition 2025 methodology.
solved_when: A reproducible benchmark exists whose headline metric is joules per independently verified solution, with energy accounting that includes preprocessing, failed runs, data movement, and certificate checking, and which supports controlled comparisons across platforms.
why: It would reveal whether asymptotic or hardware speedups actually reduce total energy consumption, replacing coarse estimates with a controlled, end-to-end measurement.
key_works: Lannelongue, Grealey, and Inouye (2021), *Green Algorithms: Quantifying the Carbon Footprint of Computation*, DOI: 10.1002/advs.202100707; SAT Competition 2025 methodology.

title: Sustainable staffing and funding for independent cloud-algorithm evaluation
subfield: Experimental algorithms, benchmarks, infrastructure, and funding
open: How can independent cloud-scale algorithm evaluation be sustained as an ongoing operation rather than an occasional volunteer effort — that is, a funded cloud-evaluation track with public cost accounting, reproducible environments, archived artifacts, and enough staffing to run repeatedly year after year?
status: A concrete operational gap is documented: SAT Competition 2025 skipped its cloud track because it was too demanding for the AWS organizers (Codel, Fazekas, Heule, and Iser (2025), *The Results of SAT Competition 2025*, slide 6). Long-term funded operation is the target here, not an assertion about the current 2026 track.
solved_when: A cloud-evaluation track exists that is independently operated, publicly reports its costs, provides reproducible environments and archived artifacts, and has funding and staffing sufficient for repeated annual operation.
why: Without durable operational capacity, cloud-scale algorithm claims lose an independent comparison venue.
key_works: Codel, Fazekas, Heule, and Iser (2025), *The Results of SAT Competition 2025*, slide 6.

title: Versioned million-problem registry with resolution tracking
subfield: Experimental algorithms, benchmarks, infrastructure, and funding
open: Can we build a registry that maintains at least one million granular problem records, each carrying canonical statements, aliases, model restrictions, provenance, typed dependencies, and auditable resolution histories? In formal terms, this is an engineering target: a versioned infrastructure whose scale and validation contract go beyond existing precedents.
status: Currently a proposed infrastructure target. TOPP, SIGACT's open-problem columns, and newer open-mathematics initiatives provide useful precedents, but none offers the specified integrated scale and validation contract.
solved_when: A registry exists that supports at least one million granular problem records with canonical statements, aliases, model restrictions, provenance, typed dependencies, and auditable resolution histories.
why: It prevents solved problems from being repeatedly proposed and makes cross-domain research opportunities discoverable.
key_works: Mitchell and O’Rourke, *The Open Problems Project*; Gasarch, SIGACT open-problem archive; Tao (2026), *Open Problems, Open Mathematics*.
